MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Uiher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, in pursuance of the directions of an Act, passed in the 24th year of His present Majesty, he had issued his Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out new Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the following Places;

viz. for the County of Warwick, in the room of Sir George Augujhis William Shuckburgh Evelyn, Baronet, deceased; for the Borough of Hor/ham, in the room of Patrick Ross, Esquire, deceased; for the Shire of Dumfries, in the room of Sir Robert Laurie, Baronet, deceased; and for the Borough of Totne/s,in the room of John Berkley Bur land, Esquire, deceased.

Several Members present, and several Members returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those purposes; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Outlawries, was read the first time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a second time.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Knight of the Shire, to serve in this present Parliament, for the County of Rutland, in the room of the Right honourable Lord Carbery, deceased.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Devizes, in the room of the Right ho-Vol. 60.

nourable Henry Addington, now Lord Viscount Sidmouth, called up to the House of Peers.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Leitrim Clerk of the Crown in Ireland, to make out a new Writ Writ-for the electing of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Leitrim, in the room , of the Right honourable Nathaniel Clements, commonly called Lord Viscount Clements, now Earl of Leitrim, a Peer of the United Kingdom.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Haddington, Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the &c-W[it> electing of a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the district of Burghs of H, Jedburgh, Dunbar, North Berwick, and Lauder, in the room of the Right honourable Thomas Maitland, who, since his election for the said dillrift of Burghs, hath accepted the Oflice of Governor of Ceylon.

Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of the United Kingdom, do make their election by this day three weeks for which of the places they will serve, provided there be no question Upon the return for that place; and, if any thing shall come in question touching the return or election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the matter is in Debate; and that all Members, returned upon double returns, do withdraw till their returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this realm, except such Peers of Ireland as shall, for the time being, be actually elected, and shall not have declined to serve for any county, city, or borough of Great Britain, hath any right to give his vote in the election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That it is a high infringement of the liberties and privileges of the Commons of the United Kingdom, for any Lord of Parliament or other Peer or Prelate, not being a Peer of Ireland at the time elected, and not having declined to serve for any county, city, or borough of Great Britain, to concern himself in the election of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament, except only any Peer of Ireland at such elections in Great Britain respectively, where such Peer shall appear as a candidate, or by himself or any others be proposed to be elected; or for any Lord Lieutenant, or Governor of any County, to avail himself of any authority derived from his commission, to influence the election of any Member to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Refo'ved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing, or giving evidence, the fame is declared to be a high'erime and misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath given false evidence, in any case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the Utmost severity against such offender.

Resolved, That, in all cases of controverted elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the fitting Members, or their agents, lids of the persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the fitting Members; giving, in the said lifts, the several heads of objection, and distinguishing the fame against the names of the Voters excepted to; and that the fitting Members do, by themselves, or by their agents, within the same time, deliver the like lifts on their part to the Petitioners, or their agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Anns attending this House do, from time to time, take into his custody any stranger, or strangers, that he shall see, or be infonned of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the Iloufe, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no person, so taken into custody, be discharged out ofeustody without the special order of the House.

Ordered, That the back door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every morning at the fitting of the House, and the key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by 3

him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any person whatsoever without order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every day before the door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Tommorrow.

the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg leave to return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We have witnessed with pride and satisfaction the skill and intrepidity of Your Majesty’s Navy, the respectable and formidable state of Your Majesty’s Army and Militia, the unabated zeal and improved discipline of a numerous Volunteer Force, and the general ardour manifested by all classes of Your Majesty’s Subjects. Although the preparations for the Invasion of this Kingdom have been continued with incessant activity, we are firmly persuaded that while this spirit animates the Country, and its volun- by this House, tary exertions for its own defence subsistin their full vigour, they will be found sufficient to deter the Enemy from attempting to carry their repeated menaces into effect; and we shall never forget, that as our security has arisen from the resolution with which w e have met and provided against the danger, we can be preserved only by steady perseverance and unremitting activity.

We beg leave to return Your Majesty our humble Thanks, for having been graciously pleased to direct that a copy of the Manifesto which you have caused to be prepared in consequence of the Rupture with Spain should be laid before us, together with such papers as are necessary to explain the difeuflions which have taken place between Your Majesty and that Court; and we ashire Your Majesty that we will take them into our early and serious consideration.

While we regret the extension of hostilities, Your Majesty may rely on our constant support to such measures as may be necessary for maintaining the honour of Your Crown, and asserting the just rights of Your People.

We feel in common with Your Majesty, that on the Continent the general conduct of the French Government has been marked by the utmost violence and outrage, and has shewn a wanton defiance of the rights of neutral Territories, of the acknowledged privileges of accredited

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty onThurfday last, lvith their Address; to which His. Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return You my warmest Thanks for this loyal and dutiful Address.

It affords Me the greatest satisfaction to receive the declaration of Your full Concurrence in the sentiments which have distated My Answer to the Communication from the French Government.

The eonriftion You express, that the safety and permanent interests of this Country are closely connected with the Security of Europe, and the cordial affuranees of Your zealous support in enabling Me to prosecute the Warwith vigour till it can be brought to a safe and honourable termination, are calculated to produce the happielt eflefts in the present situation of affairs.

A Petition of the several persons whose names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and others, being lawful Electors of the borough of Knaresborough, in the County of York, was delivered in at the Table, and read; setting forth. That His Majesty’s Writ, tested the 9th day of July last past, for the election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament, in the room of William Cavendish, Esquire, who had accepted the office of Steward or Bailiff of the three Chiltern Hundreds of Stoke, and

Bonenham, in the County of Buckingham, was issued, directed to the Sheriff of York, and which was, on the 23d day of July last, delivered to James Fox, Esquire, then Sheriff of the same County of York, who thereupon issued his Precept, directed to the Bailiffs of the said Borough of Knaresborough, the said Bailiffs being the Returning Officers of said Borough, requiring them forthwith to cause a Burgess to be elected for the said Borough, in the place of the said William Cavendish, Esquire, according to the command of the said Writ; and which Precept was on the 23d day of July delivered to John Carr, one of the Bailiffs of the said Borough; and that, on the 25th day of the fame month of July, James Collins, the other Bailiff of the said Borough, together with the said John Carr, did cause Proclamation to be made, on the Market Cross in Knarejbo-rough, that the Election would be proceeded in on Monday the 30th day of the fame month of July, at eleven o’clock in the forenoon, at the Tolbooth there; and that the Petitioners, and several other persons having, or claiming to have, a right to vote for Members of the said Borough, were proceeding to the Tolbooth on the morning of the said 30th day of July, in order to give their Votes at the said election; but in consequence of a very great riot and tumult, raised by a very large number of persons, who were not Electors for the said Borough, and in consequence of violent affmilts and ill treatment committed on several of the Electors, and on the Magistrates and Constables intended to keep order at the said election, and by block-

ing up the paffflge to the Tolbooth at the said Borough, and preventing the Bailiffs, Magistrates, and Electors, from entering the fame, the said Election could not be proceeded in; and that the said Bailiffs made the following Return to the Sheriff of the said County of York, who transmitted the same to the Clerk of the Crown, annexed to the Writ where it is now filed,—"We the Bailiffs of the Borough of Knaresborough, in the County of York, having received the Precept of the Sheriff of the said County for the Election of a Member for the said Borough, in the place of William Cavendish, Esquire, did on the 25th day of July instant make a Proclamation at the Market Cross in_ Knaresborough aforesaid, that the Election would be proceeded in on the day of the date hereof, at eleven o’clock in the forenoon, in the Tolbooth there—That, in pursuance of the said Proclamation, we attempted to proceed to such Election with the assistance of Sir,

Baronet, a Magistrate for the West Riding of the said County, and of twenty special Constables, but were unable to get to the Court Room by the violence of a Mob, consisting of several hundred people, who had previously obtained possession of the flairs leading thereto, headed and instigated by the following persons, namely,

Allen, attorney at law, Richard Denies, an eniign in the Knaresborough Volunteer Infantry, Robert half

pay quarter master in His Majesty’s Forces, Thomas Abbot, serjeant of a Volunteer corps of Cavalry, William Whitehead, corporal of a Volunteer corps of Infantry, Mark Lezvty, John Turnbull, and William Turnbidl, all of Knaresborough aforesaid, and several others whole names are at present unknown, who not only insulted and pelted the Magistrate and one of the Returning Officers, but allb took the staffs from the Constables, knocked them down as well as several of the Electors, and destroyed their cloaths, and also dragged one of the special Constables, servant to the said Sir John Ingilby, a considerable distance to the river fide, threatening to drown him—That, after our return from the Court House, the said Sir John,

being afterwards accompanied by John Wat fan, Esquire, and the Reverend Charles Knozvlton, Clerk, two other Magistrates for the said West Riding, finding that it would not only endanger the lives of themselves, the Returning Officers, and Voters, if they attempted to proceed in the Election, or read the Riot Act, but would be absolutely useless, as there were no soldiers nearer than the barracks at York, being twenty miles from this place, except the

Volunteers of Knaresborough, several of whom were seen

to encourage rather than suppress the mob—From the above circumstances, we hereby certify, that we are unable to execute the precept as directed, as witness our hands, this 30th day of July 1804, James Collins, John Carr;'— and that the Petitioners, in behalf of themselves and the other Electors of the said Borough of Knaresborough, humbly beg leave to represent the premises to the consideration of the House; and therefore praying, That the House will take the premises into their consideration on an early day, and grant to the Petitioners such relief in the premises as they in their wisdom shall think meet, so that the Petitioners, and the other Electors of the said Borough of Knaresborough, may be represented in the present Parliament, and that the persons who were guilty of the violence and outrage, which prevented the election from being proceeded in on the 30th day of July lait past, may be brought to punishment.

Petition of Sheriff Rawlins and

A Petition of the there-undersigned was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners,

at Michaelmas 1801, entered Upon the Office of Sheriffs of London and Sheriff of the County of and

continued in the discharge of the fame till Michaelmas 1802; and t,hat, during their continuance in the fame, they did, by virtue of their said offices, and at a great expence, trouble, and inconvenience to themselves, pre-fide and were Returning Officers at three different strongly contested and protracted Foils, namely, the Election of a Bridgeinafter, the Election of four Citizens to represent the said City of London, and the election of two Knights of the Shire to represent the said County of Middlesex in this present Parliament; and at the close of the said Sheriffalty the Lively of the said City of London came to the following Resolution, in a Meeting or Assembly of the Mayor and Liverymen of the several Companies of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, at the Guildhall of the said City, on Wednesday the 29th day of September 1802 :—" Resolved •unanimously, That the " Thanks of this Common Hall be given to Sir William " Rawlins, Knight, and Robert Albion Cox, Esquire, late " Sheriffs of this City, and late Sheriff of the County of " Midd'efex, for their firm, manly, and conscientious " discharge of the various important duties of that high " office, in a year of unprecedented public duty; for " their liberality and humane attention to the several " prisoners confided to their care; and for the zeal they " have manifested in support of the Rights and Privileges " of their Fellow Citizens and of the Constitution,

" by preferring inviolate that great bulwark of public " liberty, the Freedom of Election—and the Petitioners ffate, that while in the execution of such office of Sheriffs of the City of London, the Petitioners having, upon the election aforesaid of four Citizens to represent the said City in Parliament, returned Sir William Curtis, Baronet, Sir John William Anderson, Baronet, Harvey Christian Combe, Esquire, and Sir Charles Price, Baronet, to represent the fame, a Petition was, by Sir Watkin Lewes, Knight, an unsuccessful Candidate at such Election, presented to the House against the Return of the four Citizens aforesaid, and against the Petitioners, for making such Return as Sheriffs of the City of London aforesaid; which Petition being by the House referred to a Select Committee appointed to try and determine the fame, was by such Committee voted frivolous and vexatious; and the Petitioners were thereby entitled to be reimbursed the heavy colts and damages they had been put to in defending themselves against such unjull charge so brought against them; but from the distressed circumstances of the said Sir Watkin Leices, Knight, the Petitioners have not to this hour, nor are at any time hereafter likely to be, reimbursed the fame, or any the smallest part thereof; and that two other Petitions were presented to the House; the one by William Mainwaring, Esquire, the unsuccessful Candidate at the said Election for the County of Middlesex, and the other by certain Freeholders of the said County in his interest, complaining of the Return made by the Petitioners of Sir Francis Burdett, Baronet, and charging the Petitioners, as Sheriff of Middlesex, and Returning Officers at such last mentioned Election for that County, with great partiality in favour of the said Sir Francis Burdett, and with other undue conduct in the course and progress of the said Election and Poll; which said two Petit ions were by the House referred to a Select Committee of the House, which was duly ballotted for and appointed on Friday the 3d day of February 1804, and continued from that day to fit on the trial of the fame Petitions until Monday the 9th day of July last; and that, on the said 9th day of July, the Chairman of the said Committee acquainted the House (among other things) that the Committee had determined, that the said Election and Return for the said County of Middlesex wore void, so far as respected the said Sir Francis Burdett; and that the Committee had also come to the four following Resolutions relative to the Petitioners, viz.— ill. That on the 13th, 14th, and 15th days of the Poll, on the first of which days there was a considerable majority of votes in favour of William Maimcaring, Esquire, the Sheriff Robert Albion Cox, Esquire, and Sir William Rawlins, Knight, wilfully, knowingly, and corruptly, did 5 admit

admit to poll for Sir Francis Burdctt Baronet, upwards of three hundred persons, claiming to vote under a fictitious right, as proprietors of a Mill purported to be situ-ated in the pari 111 of Ijleworlh, and called "The Good " Intent Mill" by which means a colourable majority was obtained in favour of Sir Francis Burdctt.—2d. That on the 15th day, towards the close of the poll, after such majority was established, they rejected persons tendering their votes under the fame circumstances.—3d. That the Sheriff at the poll acted in a judicial capacity, by admitting counsel to argue the validity of votes, and by deciding, in some instances, on the validity of such votes; that in other instances they refused to decide on the validity of votes which were objected to, and stated, that they would admit any person to poll who would take the oaths, declaring themselves to be only Ministerial Officers, thereby acting in a manner contradictory to their practice in other cases, and in flagrant violation of their duty.—4th. That the obvious tendency of their conduct was to admit persons who had no right to poll, and to afford the greatest encouragement to perjury;—and that the Petitioners, being ignorant of the Law, did, during the whole course of the said election, constantly and invariably aft under the advice of their Under Sheriffs and Deputy Under Slveritfj all of whom are Attornies, highly respectable in their profession, and long conversant in the Law, and one of them for above twenty years practised in the judicial decision of questions of the greatest value and importance; and that on the 13th day of the said last mentioned election, when the proprietors of the Mill, as mentioned in the above Report of the said Select Committee of the House, first tendered themselves to vote, their right to vote at such election for such freehold was argued very much at length by different counsel on each side; and after such argument the Petitioners did (by the advice of the aforesaid Deputy Under Sheriff, and of one of the Under Sheriffs, who were then and there present during the whole course of such argument, the other Under Sheriff not being on the said 13th day in attendance) uniformly admit such of them to vote as stated themselves upon oath to have been twelve months in possession of shares of the value of 40 a year, and did as uniformly reject such of them as appeared not to have been twelve months in pofi'eflion, or not to have shares of that annual value, the Petitioners acting therein in conformity to the advice aforesaid; and that the Petitioners admitted the said last mentioned persons to vote, from a full and perfect conviction at the time of the legality of their claim, established in the minds of the Petitioners by the repeated arguments of counsel, and the solemn oath of the parties; and they do conscientiously and fa-credly declare, that, in the admission of those, as well as all other voters during the whole continuance of the aforesaid election, they acted with the most pure and upright intention, without partiality to one Candidate or prejudice against the other; and that the Petitioners' humbly state, that, though in particular instances they did hear questions argued by counsel, yet they did not consider themselves inverted with a judicial authority, for the Petitioners were instructed to conceive, and did and do still conceive, that any Freeholder, who tenders himself to take the respective oaths required determined by divers Acts of Parliament to be taken at a County election, is entitled to have such oaths administered 'to him, and to Vote thereat, and that such persons would be rejected at the peril of an action for damages to be brought against the Returning Officers so rejecting them; nevertheless the Petitioners confess that, in divers instances, they did take such peril upon themselves when the justice and equity of the case seemed to warrant them in so proceeding, though not compellable by Law so to do; and, in order to satisfyand protest themselves in the execution of this part of their office, they were frequently willing and desirous to hear the arguments of counsel as a guide and affillance to the conduct of the Petitioners, but not as a right to be claimed by either Candidate; and that the Petitioners further state, that they in divers instances, as well relating to other tenements as to the Mill tenement aforesaid, when it appeared to them, by the confession Of the parties claiming a right to vote, that they had not Vol. 60.

been in possession of their Freehold for twelve months, or that it was not of the annual value of forly /hillings, did reject such persons; and the Petitioners submit to this House, that, from the aforesaid causes, they may seem sometimes to have acted ministerially and at other times judicially, but at no time did they aft from any interested or unworthy motives, but, on the contrary, from an anxious and earnelt desire to do justice to all parties, though at the peril of an aci ion against themselves; and the Petitioners pursued this line of conduct equally in respect to Voters tendering their votes for the aforesaid Wiliam Mainwaring, Esquire, and Sir Francis Burdett, particularly in respect to very many persons claiming a right to vote by virtue of certain offices, some of which were held under the Dean and Chapter of such as bell-

A Petition of several Owners of Estates in the Parish of Brandon Brandon, in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That there are, within the said Parish, several open and common fields, meadows, and commonable lands, and also certain heaths, warrens, and tvafte lands; and if the fame were divided and inclosvd, they would be rendered of greater value, and might be much improved; and that, in the month of September 1803, the Petitioners, having it in contemplation to apply to Parliament for an Act to inelofe the said lands and grounds, did give public notice thereof on the door of the Parish Church of Brandon aforesaid, for three Sundays in that month; but difficulties having arisen as to the terms upon which the inclosure should take place, no application was made to Parliament in the last Session for that purpose; and that, supposing it was unnecessary, notice was omitted to be given in the months of August and September last; but as soon as the Petitioners discovered their mistake, they caused notices of their intention to apply to Parliament in the present Session to be affixed on the door of the said Parish Church, upon three Sundays in the month of December now last past; and that all parties interested in the said inclosure have for some time past been apprised of the Petitioners intention to make this application, a great majority of whom are confecting to the inclosure; and that it will be a considerable detriment and loss to the Petitioners, if the Bill for inclosing the said Parish should be deferred until another Session of Parliament: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for inclosing the said Lands and Grounds, or that the Petitioners may have such other relief in the premises as to the House thall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Creevev, Lord Viscount kc.: And they are to meet Tommorrow Morning, at Nine of the clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for persons, papers, and records.

The House proceeded to take into consideration the Report which, upon the 9th day of July in the last Session of Parliament, was made from the Select Committee appointed to try and determine the merits of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Middlesex, respecting the conduct of the Sheriff of the said County at the' said Election.

And the Resolutions of the Committee were again read, and are as followeth; viz.

" Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That,

" on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the poll, on the first of which days there was a considerable * majority of votes in favour of William Mainwaring, Esquire, the Sheriff Robert AlbionCox, Esquire, and Sir " William Rawlins, Knight, wilfully, knowingly, and cor-

" ruptly, did admit to poll for Sir Francis Ba-

" ronet, upwards of three hundred persons, claiming to *, vote under a fictitious right as Proprietors of a mill pur-* ported to be situate in the Parish of and of called The Good Intent Mill, by which means a colour-" able majority was obtained in favour of Sir Francis " Burdett, who was thereby returned as having the " greatest number of legal Votes."

" Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That,

" on the fifteenth day, towards the close of the poll, after " such majority was established, they rejected persons " tendering their votes under the fame circumstanc.es."

" Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That

" the Sheriff at the poll acted in a judicial capacity, by " admitting counsel to argue the validity of votes, and by " deciding in some instances on the validity of such votes; " that in other instances they rcfiifed to decide on the " validity of votes which were objected to, and stated, " that they would admit any persons to poll who would " take the oaths, declaring themselves to be only Minis-VOL 60.

Januarli. . 23

" terial Officers; thereby acting in a manner contradio " tory to their practice in other cases, and in flagrant " violation of their duty."

" Refo ved. That it appears to this Committee; That " the obvious tendency of their conduct was to admit " persons having no right to poll, and to allord the greatest " encouragement to perjury."

A Petition of the Trustees appointed by two Acts, passed in the 7th and 14th years of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening several Roads leading from the town of Ayr, and other Roads therein mentioned, in the County of Ayr, was presented to the House, and read;

setting forth, That great progress has been made in making many of the said Roads, and large sums of money have been borrowed, and are Hill owing, on the credit of the Tolls leviable by the said Acts; but the said Roads cannot be properly repaired, and kept in repair, unless the term and powers of the said Acts are enlarged, and higher Tolls authorized to be levied on the said Roads; and that it would be of advantage to the Public, if certain other Roads in the said County, which are in bad repair, and inconvenient for travellers, should likewise be made and repaired; and that sundry regulations are necessary to be made respecting the application of the Statute Work in the said County; and it is necessary to increase the amount of the conversion thereof, and also the sum to he levied in name of Bridge Money, pursuant to an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made in 1669; and it is expedient that the said several Acts, with en-Vol 60.

larged and amended powers and authorities, should be reduced and consolidated into one Act: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Hew Hamilton,

Mr. Macdoioall, &c.: And they are to meet Tommorrow Morning, at Nine of the clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for persons, papers, and records.

A Petition of Messrs. Chalmers and Cowie, of London, Merchants, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition, with a Schedule annexed, was brought up, and read; setting forth. That, in December 1800, when the alarm and distress was general throughout England on account of the scarcity and dearness of Provisions, and a Select Committee of the House was constantly employed in devising means for the relief of the Nation, the Petitioners were applied to by that Committee to furnish information as to the nature and extent of the Swedish Herring Fishery, and the assistance to be de-

rived from that Country; and the Petitioners furnished full information in writing, accompanied with a plan for importing Swedish Herrings to a large amount, at reasonable prices, either to supply the Poor in England, or, by providing an adequate supply for the demand of the West India Planters, thereby save the entire produce of the British Fisheries for the sustenance of the lower classes of the Community; and that this plan was received with approbation by the Committee, and sanctioned by the West India Merchants, and various conferences were held by the members of the Committee with the Petitioners, as the best means of carrying it into effect, and the result was, that the Petitioners declared themselves willing to engage in the undertaking, under the fandfion of Parliament, either generally to bring the Herrings to London, and fell them at a reasonable price for the West India Plantations or for home consumption, or to import cargoes for account of Government to such ports in Great Britain as the Committee should point out; and that, in consequence of such offer, the subject was taken into consideration by a Committee of the whole House, and on the 12th December 1800, the following Report was brought up: " Resolved, "That it is expedient that S Herrings should be " permitted to be imported free of dutyand, in pursuance of such Resolution, a Bill was introduced into the House, which passed into a Law on the 31st of the fame month, to permit, for a limited time, the importation from any port in Sweden, in any British or neutral ship, and navigated in any manner whatever, any Herrings caught and cured on any of the coasts of Sweden, without the payment of any duty; and that the Petitioners, thus expressly encouraged and sanctioned by an alteration of the former laws, and prompted by the pleasing prospect of being useful to their Country at that eventful period, without any other prospect of private advantage more than the fair returns of moderate profit on the employment and risk of their capital, set about eHefting the desired object of Government, and actually dispatched a cutter express to Gothenburgh with very large private orders for this then necessary article of food, and invested a capital of about twenty thousand pounds sterling in the first cost of those purchases; and that on the 14th of January 1801, just as the Petitioners received advices that the purchases had been completed, and the lhipments beginning to take place, an Order was issued by His Majesty in Council for seizing and embargoing all Ruffian, Swedish, and Danish {hips, the wisdom and propriety of which proceeding as a public measure is undoubted; but it will presently appear to the House, that, in proportion as this necessary act of State was beneficial to the Nation at large, yet the eflefts resulting from it fell with the most distrelfing and calamitous weight upon the Petitioners as individuals, and that these Herrings, being at the time of the Embargo all purchased and ready to be shipped in Sweden, were there locked up as an unavoidable consequence of that measure, because, the moment the nervs of the seizure of all Swedish ships reached that country, similar measures were naturally adopted them, and no Swedish ship could fail for England, as being liable to seizure by the ships of war of His Majesty; and that the Petitioners were at first led to cherith a hope that no very heavy loss would result from this interruption, and instead of making complaints, and hastily abandoning the goods, and throwing themselves on the liberality of Government, they only solicited Orders in Council to permit the importation of their property in Sioedish vessels, and to guarantee the protection of such vessels from seizure and embargo, which Orders were indeed ultimately granted, and forwarded to Gothenburgh, but the Sioedish Government would not rilk their {hips to depart for England, and, even if it had done fq, the permission obtained from the British Government wrould have become useless, because from these delays and interruptions a disappointment more distrelfing arose—«• The season for sale or export of the Herrings to the West Indies wras rapidly expiring, being at the latest March and April; and that the Petitioners being deprived of the conveyance of English and Sioedish vessels, which but for the Embargo could have been had at moderate freights,

werq

45 Geo. III. 8° Februar. 4$

were necellitated to engage American vefle’s upon exorbitant terms, as the only possible expedient to prevent the article from peri tiling at Golhenburgh, and great part of the purchases being brought to these dif-

couraging circumstances, the residue of the Herrings came forward in July and August in the same year, aft er the Embargo was removed—The apprehensions of famine had then happily subsided, and the Petitioners had the misfortune to fee an immense quantity of provision, im-periously called for by the Country a few months before, coming to market after the season was completely over; exposed also to peculiar peril, from the perishable nature of the article, and with additional charges, that raised the colt of these goods above thirty thousand pounds. Still, however, as the next season of Shipping for the Indies approached, which commences in , the

Petitioners flattered themselves that they should at length be able to dispose of the Fish, although to a Iofs; but in this also they were grievously disappointed; for, while the auspicious event of a general Peace, and the plenty and cheapness of all forts of Provisions, utterly prevented the sale for home confiunption, the fame cause also induced the West India merchants to turn their views to

tite Home Fisheries, which shortly commenced at reduced prices; and that the utmost exertions were, notwithstanding, used to effect sales at almost any price, but the Petitioners and their Agents were unable to dispose of more than two thousand five hundred, out of near twenty thousand barrels originally imported; and, in order to save the rest from utter destruction, no measure was left for the Petitioners but to export them on their own account for sale to the West India Islands. Here a -ain their endeavours for the most part proved fruitless and unsuccessful, although a considerable additional expence was incurred in conveying them thither, as the previous scarcity of the article in the West India Islands in 1799 and 1800 caused an immense supply of Herrings from all parts of the United Kingdom, much beyond the ordinary consumption, in the then ensuing season. Under all these accumulated circumstances of disaster and lols, the Petitioners, after adding all charges to the cost price, and deducting the produce of the sales, find themselves in the distressing situation of being left sufferers, in actual disbursements of money, to the amount of thirty-five thousand pounds sterling, besides being nearly four years deprived of the use of a sum of money, which, in the ordinary course of their mercantile operations, might have produced them a fair or a liberal profit; and that the Petitioners, hoping, in a case of such extreme hard-fiiip. His Majesty’s' Executive Government might be induced to relieve their Losses, prCfented a Memorial to the Lords of His Majesty’s Treasury, who were pleased to refer the same to the Commissioners of Customs, with directions to investigate the Allegations of the Memorial, and report thereon; and the said Commissioners did afterwards report to their Lordships, that such Allegations had been proved to their satisfaction, and transmitted the proofs and vouchers; and the Petitioners beg leave to refer the House to the particulars of their losses, and which they have summarily Hated in a Schedule annexed to their Petition; and that the Petitioners do not urge their application for relief upon the ground of strict justice, but throw themselves upon the liberality of Parliament , in a case of complicated distress, solely arising from a necessary act of State, which they could neither foresee nor guard against; and they beg leave to urge, for the consideration of the House, the following among other grounds, upon which (hey hope it will be thought proper to extend relief to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners never imported a cargo of Fish in their lives before, and were induced to deviate from the ordinary course of their commercial dealings, and to invclt so large a sum in the instance in question, merely from a consideration of its importance to the Country, and at the pressing request of many Members of the Committee, and under the sanction of the Legislative Enactment; and that the object of the adventure being to furnish an immediate supply of an important article of food, and the success of the measure being peculiarly dependent on season, the Petitioners conceived themselves sufficiently protected by Vol. 60. '

a free importation being secured; and the Iofs which has fallen upon them, arol’e merely from the alteration in political circumstances rendering it necessary, on the part -of His, Majesty’s Executive Government, that the advantage intended by the 41ft of His Majesty, c. 18, should be almost immediately interrupted; and that the Petitioners entered upon the undertaking in question under the most perfect confidence that they should not be subject to any peril arising from political events, against which they could not insure; and then-fore the Petitioners asked for no indemnification, nor did (hey make any stipulation with the Committee to protect them from ultimate Iofs, although it will readily occur to the House that had any such protection been asked, it would have been granted, inafmurh as at 1 he fame period a bounty was given upon the importation of corn equal to the difference between the stipulated price and the market price at the time of arrival, so that the corn importers were not only protected from Iofs, but a certain price, giving a profit, was guaranteed: Persons entitled by a former Act of Parliament.to a bounty upon the exportation of Pilchards were permitted to vend them in this Country at the then high prices, and yet receive the exportation bounty; various advantages and inducements were also held out to persons who should engage in the Firth of Forth Fishery; the Petitioners therefore take leave to infer, from these wife and political measures, adopted by Parliament at the period referred to, that they might also have been guaranteed from Iofs on this importation; and they hope that their not having made such a stipulation will not weaken their claim upon the liberality of Parliament; and that it being a principle universally acted upon by the British Government in pursuing the public advantage still to protect the private interest of individuals, and this principle being extended to the subjects of foreign Princes and States, the Petitioners would hope, that the fame liberal and enlightened attention will embrace their present application; and that the Petitioners have taken every practicable measure to make the most of this unfortunate importation, and have withheld their claim upon Government for relief, while there was a possibility of rendering any part of it in the smallest degree productive; and that the circumstances which have occasioned Iofs to the Petitioners are so peculiar, that they submit any relief afforded by the House cannot be adduced as a precedent for any future claims upon Parliamentary Equity or Munificence: And therefore praying. That the House will be pleased to afford them such rglief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir John William Anderson, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, &c.: And they are to meet Tommorrow Morning, at Niqe of the clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for persons, papers, and records.

That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to acquaint I lis Majesty, that we have taken into reuPocu our raoft serious consideration the Papers which have been laid before us by His Majesty’s command, relative to the difcuflfions which have taken place with the Court of Spain:

That we observe with the greatest satisfaction, that, through the whole of the transactiou, His Majesty has carried his moderation and forbearance to the utmost extent which was consistent with a due regard to the honour of His Crown and the interests of His dominions:

That, while we fully concur in the propriety and ne-eftfity of those prompt and vigorous measures of precaution which His Majesty found himself compelled to adopt in consequence of the naval armaments fitted out by Spain, we fee at the same time a fifth proof of His Majesty’s

48 11 * Februariu A, 1805.

Majesty’s earnest defu'e to avert if possible, the extremity of war, in the fresh opportunity which He even then offered to the Court of Spain to enter on pacific negociation:

And that, impressed with these sentiments, and fully convinced of the just ice of the war, which the conduct of the Court of Spain (evidently under the influence and controul of France) has rendered unavoidable, we shall not fail to afford His Majesty our most zealous and cordial support in every measure which may be necessary for prosecuting the war with vigour, and bringing it to a lafe and honourable termination;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the first words " His Majesty," to the end of the Question, in order to insert these words: " To return His Majesty the thanks of this House, for the communications made to us relative to the rupture " with Spain:

" To express our entire conviction that the existence of an offensive treaty between France and Spain, would " have entitled His Majesty to consider Spain as a prin-" cipal in the present war, unless the obligations of that " treaty were renounced, or their execution difelaimed; " and to assure His Majesty, that we shall at all times be " ready to support Him, in giving effect so far as the interests of His dominions may require, to this just and undisputed principle:

" That we observe, however, that His Majesty was ad-" vised to waive the exercise of this right, in order to ne-" gociate with Spain, for the maintenance of her neutra-u lity—And that, without taking upon ourselves in the " present moment to decide a question of policy de-" pending so much on circumstances of which we are " still uninfoimed, we acknowledge with gratitude this " proof of His Majesty’s paternal desire to have prevented " the further extension of the calamities of war:

" But that we beg leave humbly to represent to His Majesty, that the execution of these His benevolent

* wnfhes indispensably required from His Ministers, the " adoption of some just, intelligible, and uniform prin-" cfple of negociation, declared in the outset with frank-" ness, and steadily pursued to its conclusion; followed " up by an unremitting attention to every new circum-" fiance arifi ng in the progress of so important a dif-,c cuffion; and accompanied by the most fcnipulous " care that all engagements resulting from it, should on the part of Great Britain, be defined with precision, * and performed with unquestionable good faith, mode-u ration and integrity:

" That wre have on the contrary seen with deep regret * in the whole conduct of this transaction, the clash-"ing efiects of undecided, equivocal, and contradictory *■ policy:

" That the withes for peace professed in the outset by " His Majesty’s Ministers, have uniformly been counter-" acted by their studious endeavours to keep alive both " the cause and the menace of war; a purpose equally * inconsistent with justice and with wisdom, destructive of " all confidence on the part of the Power with whom they " treated, and incompatible with the object for which " they were negociating: That during the whole course " of these difcullions, while they were continually soli-" citing from Spain unreserved communications on points " of mutual interest, their own indecision prevented them " from affording in return, any distinct statement of the terms on which Great Britain would consent to recognize the neutrality of that power: That their ground " of negociation was repeatedly shifted, their demands " varied, and their concetfious undefined; and that al-" though some agreement appears at last to have been " concluded, neither its date, nor its conditions were " ascertained with precision; yet both are repeatedly re-" ferred to, by the British as Avell as the Ministers,

" and the breach of those very conditions is alledged as " the motive on the part of Great Britain, for her actual <£ commencement of hostilities:

" That the omissions and defects which distinguish this " Iran faction as well as the fatal consequences to which " it has Jed, can only be ascribed to the erroneous prin-" ciple on which it was grounded, and to the criminal

"and almost incredible negligence willi which it has " been conducted. That it is particularly our duty to " represent to His Majesty, that in a negociation for " peace or war between Great Britain and carried

" on principally at Madrid, no instructions were sent to " His Majesty’s Minister at that Court, from the 2d‘of "June to the 24th of November in the year 1803; from " thence to the 21st of January in the ful lowing year, nor " again from that date to the 29th of September; that iu " the first of these intervals, being little less than fix " months, the negociation for a treaty of Neutrality be-* " tween France and Spain, was begun, continued, and " concluded, yet not the fmalh fi intimation was in that " long time, ever once given to Mr. Frere, of the light in " which that negociation was considered here, of the " language which it was proper for him to hold, or of ii;e " measures which it might be necessary for him to take, "although frequent communications were made to him " on the subject by the Spanish Government, who appear " to have been disposed to pay great attention in this " instance, to any representations from Great Britain:

" That during the last of the above-mentioned periods, " the fame Minister, though left again lor many months " without any instruction whatever, negocialed and con-" eluded some Agreement with Spain, on this mod important subject, of which Agreement 110 opinion was " ever expressed to him from hence, either before or after " its conclusion, nor does it ev en now appear from any " official documents, whether the fame was meant to be " allowed or disallovved, ratified or rejected, by the " Government:

" That we feel ourselves compelled to express to His Majesty, that in the farther progress of these transactions, the indecision and neglect of His Government "were succeeded by precipitate resolutions and acts of " violence, equally injurious to the honour and interests " of His Kingdom: that we Ihouhl have applauded any " endeavour, by firm but temperate representation, to " extricate our relations with Spain from the confufioir " in which they had been involved, and to bring them to "a distinct issue of acknowledged neutrality or decided " war; but that we find no trace of any such attempt: " and that, in the middle of September, on the first inti-" mation of supposed movements in the Spanish ports, " acts of hostility were decided on by His Majesty’s Government, previous to all complaint, and executed " without notice, during a period of amicable nego-" ciation:

" That the dispositions of Spain appear from the in-" formation of His Majesty’s Mini tier at Madrid, to have " continued up to that moment, friendly to Great Britain—And that the conduct of His Majesty’s Ministers, " in having, under such circumstances, anticipated all " explanation by concealed or del's for an attack on " Spanish Ships, Property, and Subjects, cannot bejufti-" fied on any ground of public law, much less reconciled " to those principles of moderation and liberality which " belong to the British character, and which, in the present situation of Europe, it is peculiarly the duty of this " Country to maintain inviolate:

" That on reviewing those difeufiions which immedi-" ately preceded the j)resent War, we cannot but represent " to H is Majesty the essential difference between the " conduct of the person left in charge of His Majesty’s " affairs at Madrid, and the tenor of the only instructions " under which he appeal's to have acted. That, the ex-" planations given to that Gentleman by the Spanish " Government, though not in all points adequate to the "just expectations of this Country, were yet such as ought " manifestly (according to those instructions) to have de-" termined him to wait at Madrid for the arrival of an "accredited Minister, authorized by His Majesty to " arrange with that Court all points of difierence; and " that we have therefore seen, with equal surprize and " disapprobation, the final decision of His Majesty’s " Ministers, not only to adopt the inconsiderate resolution " taken by the King’s representative, in withdrawing " himself from Madrid, but also to treat with utter dil-" regard the subsequent offer from the Spanish Minister " at this Court, to pursue the fame difcullions here; an

A Petition of the Trustees of the British ,being

offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, determined by His Majesty-s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That, in the 2d year of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the sum allowed them for the establishment and support of the said Museum was reduced to a capital of *£.30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the dividend of which, amounting to *£.900, was, notwithstanding their utmost attention to the forming their establishment with frugality, greatly insufficient for that purpose; upon which representation they have at fundiy times obtained from the House various sums to supply the deficiency of their income, which sums, together with the salary allotted to the King’s Librarian, yearly amounting to about *£. 250, have proved insufficient to defray the necessary expences of the said Museum; and what now remains in the hands of the Trustees is not sufficient to carry on the purposes of the trust without the aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to grant them such farther support, towards enabling them to carry on the execution of the trust reposed in them by Parliament, for the general benefit of learning and useful knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Trustees of the British being

offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the contents'of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, in the last Session of Parliament, presented to the House a Petition, submitting to Their consideration the necessity of providing a suitable Building for the reception and preservation of the Egyptian Antiquities, which His Majesty had been graciously plea-fed to place at the British Museum; and that, in consideration of the matters then Hated by the Petitioners, they obtained from the bounty of Parliament a grant of the sum of £. 8,000 for the commencement of such Building, according to the plan and estimate laid before the House, the total of the expence estimated for completing the fame amounting to the sum of £. 16,000; and that, since the end of the last Session of Parliament, the Petitioners have caused the foundations of the said building to be laid, and are at this time proceeding to the execution of the said plan; and that the further sum of *£.8,000, being the residue of the said sum of *£.16,000, will be soon wanting towards carrying on and completing the fame: All which matters they submit to the wisdom and munificence of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Address Majesty, to acquaint His Majesty, That we have taken resolved ®a* into our most serious consideration the Papers which have been laid before us by His Majesty’s command, relative to the difeuffions which have taken place with the Court of Spain.

That we observe, with the greatest satisfaction, that, through the whole of the transaction. His Majesty has carried His moderation and forbearance to the utmost extent, which was consistent with a due regard to the honour of His Crown, and the interests of His dominions.

That, w’hile we fully concur in the propriety and necessity of those prompt and vigorous measures of precaution which His Majesty found Himself compelled to adopt in consequence of the naval armaments fitted out by Spain, we fee at the same time a fresh proof of His Majesty’s earned; desire to avert, if possible, the extremity of war, in the fresh opportunitywhich He even then offered to the Court of Spain to enter on pacific negociation.

And that, impressed with these sentiments, and fully convinced of the justice of the war, which the conduit of the Court of Spain (evidently under the influence and controul of France) has rendered unavoidable, we shall not fail to afford His Majesty our most zealous and cordial support in every measure which may be necessary for prosecuting the war with vigour, and bringing it to a safe and honourable termination.

Mr. Rose reported from the Committee, appointed

yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the fame in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg leave to assure Your Majesty, that we have taken into our most serious consideration the Papers which have been laid before us by Your Majesty’s command, relative to the difeuflions which have taken place with the Court of Spain.

We observe, with the greatest satisfaction, that, through the whole of the transaction. Your Majesty has carried Your moderation and forbearance to the utmost extent which was confident with a due regard to the honour of Your Crown and the interests of Your Dominions.

While we fully concur in the propriety and necessity of those prompt and vigorous measures of precaution which Your Majesty found Yourself compelled to adopt in consequence of the naval armaments fitted out by Spain, we fee at the same time a fresh proof of Your Majesty’s earnest desire to avert, if possible, the extremity of war, in the fresh opportunity which Your Majesty even then offered to the Court of Spain to enter on pacific negociation.

Impressed with these sentiments, and fully convinced of the justice of the war, which the conduct of the Court of Spain (evidently under the influence and controul of France) has rendered unavoidable, we shall not fail to afford Your Majesty our most zealous and cordial support in every measure which may be necessary for prosecuting the war with vigour, and bringing it to a safe and honourable termination.

The said Address being read a second time;

Re/ulved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address, to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty, by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know His Majesty’s pleasure, when He will be attended by this House.

Pmtion of a. Petition of the Excise Incorporation in Scotland, kconmntion was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

»Scotland. That in virtue of Letters Patent from his late Majesty, the Persons employed in the Revenue of Excise in were, by Royal Charter, dated the 14th July 1748, erected and confrituted into a Body Corporate, for the folepurpose of establishing, by annual contributions payable by the persons above-mentioned, a Fund for the support and relief of the widows and orphan children of the Contributors; and that the Petitioners now find that their capital, when the existing arrears are all paid, will amount fully to the sum to which it is limited by the said Letters Patent and Charter; and that, at the first inhibition of the said Fund and Corporation, the total number of persons employed in the Excise in Scotland amounted only to about one half of the number now employed therein, and the limitation of the capital of the fund was» fixed on the supposition that only a number of annuitants corresponding to the number of persons then employed would come upon the Fund; but, as the number of contributors has so much increased, and may hereafter Rill farther increase, in consequence of which a proportional number of annuitants must in time come upon the Fund, the Petitioners find, that, unless they are empowered considerably to enlarge their capital, the revenue of the Fund will be altogether insufficient to answer the demands upon it; and that the annuities respectively provided to be given, as fixed at the com-tnencement of the institution, are too small, and quite inadequate to the present expence of living; they are therefore anxious to enlarge them, and, for that purpose, to collect additional contributions from the persons enjoying the benefit of the fund; and that certain addi-Vol 60.

tional regulations for collecting and managing the Fund will be necessary: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House;

A Petition of certain Manufacturers and others, rest-dent in the Town and neighbourhood of Stockport, in the County of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That an Act was made, in the last Session of Parliament, for regulating the Importation of Corn into Great Britain, and the Duties payable thereon, and the Bounties on Corn exported from Great Britain; and the Duties and Bounties on Corn imported into and exported from Ireland; and that the Petitioners have reason to believe that the said Act has contributed to cause the advance in the price of Corn and Bread Flour; and, if the fame should continue in force, it will perpetuate this grievance, whereby many branches of \Ia-mifactures will be transferred from Great Britain to other nations; And therefore praying. That the said Act may be repealed, and also such part of an Act made in the 31ft year of His Majesty, as relates to imposing additional Duties on Foreign Corn warehoused in Great Britain and taken out for home consumption; and that the House will adopt such measures respecting the trade in Corn and Grain in Great. Britaas may give the greatest encouragement thereto, and prevent the return of those calamities which have so lately and so frequently been felt from the high price of Corn and Provisions.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Robert Bowyer, of Pall Mall, in the County of Middlesex, Esquire, wa° presented to the House, and read , setting forth. That the Petitioner during the peace of the year 1783, amidst the publication of other works of Art in which he was then engaged, conceived a plan for promoting the arts of Painting and Engraving in this Country, and not doubting to receive aliiftanee from various l’ources in the prosecution of it, did, in order to the maturing thereof, resolve to pu’oliih Ionic splendid Work, in which the mod perfect specimens of engra ving from Paintings by Artists of this Country should be exhibited. and which might even tally prove a national concern and honour; and that, in furtherance of the said plan, the Petitioner has, at a very considerable expence during several years pad, formed a most valuable collection of Paintings, Drawings, and Engravings, by artists of this Country, which has been for several years publicly exhibited in Pal! Mai!under the name of The

Gallery, and the' Petitioner has, besides various other Works, proceeded to pubiiih a most splendid edition of Hume's History of England, ornamented with Engravings

by liritish Artists, and has thereby contributed to the encouragement of the arts of Painting and Engraving, and to secure to this Country a superiority in those Arts over all other nations; and that the fourees of aliiftanee upon which the Petitioner depended have in a great meal lire foiled, and he has incurred veiy great difficulties in the prosecution of his design, and it has become necessary for him to dispose of his collection of Paintings, Drawings, and Engravings, and of the Copies of his Edition of Vol. 60.

Hume's History of England, now remaining upon his hands unfold; and that the fame cannot be disposed of by the common mode of sale but at a very great loss, and unlei's the Petitioner is enabled by the aliiftanee of Parliament to dispose of the same to the best advantage, the Petitioner’s endeavours to promote the honour of this ’ Country, by encouraging the irts of Painting and Engraving, will prove highly injurious and detrimental to himself:

And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioner to dispose of his faiu collection of Paintings, Drawings and Engravings, and also the said copies of Hume's History of England yet unfold, by way of Lottery, and for affording the Petitioner such relief in the premises as the House shall think tit.

A Petition of several Planters, Merchants, Mortgagees, Petition* Annuitants, and others, interested in the Wcji India g^Trede

Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; taking Bill s notice of the Bill for the Abolition of the Slave Trade, at Weft j0(ja a time to be limited; and setting forth. That the Trade Planters, ate, to Africa for Labourers has been, for a great number of years, approved, sanctioned, and encouraged by repeated Acts of Parliament, and by Legislative Declarations; and that the British West India Colonies were settled, and have ever continued to be cultivated, under the solemn faith of those Laws, and of Royal Proclamations, alluring to the Colonists the continuance of this Trade; and that the cultivation of those Colonies cannot be carried on without a supply of African labourers; and that the settling of the interior of the Islands, which is greatly conducive to their safety, cannot be promoted if the Slave Trade should be abolished; and that, if the Bill should be passed into a Law, the Petitioners are convinced that the worst consequences will ensue from it, destructive in their tendency, not only to the properties of the Briti/k Planters, and of their Creditors, whose fortunes have assisted in opening the Plantations in those Islands, and are now secured upon them, but also injurious to the interests of the British Empire at large; and the Petitioners submit, that, if the said Bill should be passed into a Law, provision should be made iri it for due enquiry into the Losses which shall be sustained by them, and full compensation for the dellruftion or diminiffied value of their property: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pals into a Law, and that they may be heard, at the Bar of the House, by themselves or counsel, against the fame, and that they may be permitted to produce evidence.

A Petition of Edmund Pufct) Lyon, Esquire, Agent for Agent for the Island of Jamaica, w’as also presented to the House, Januuc»* and read; likewise taking notice of the said Bill; and setting forth, That the proceedings relative-to this meo.-sure, which have recently taken place, have filled the minds of his Constituents with the greatest uneasiness and alarm; and that the Colony of Jamaica was settled, and has continued to be cultivated, under the faith of Royal Proclamations and Charters, and of various Act of Parliament, fan&ioning and encouraging the trade to Africa for procuring labourers, and containing assurances of a conllant supply; and that the cultivation of the plantations of his Constituents cannot be carried on without a continuance of this trade; that the settling the interior of Jamaica is highly necessary to its safety; and that many Coffee settlements have been opened within a few years in that part of the Island, which cannot be cultivated with any prospect of advantage, if the British Legislature shall withhold a supply of African labourers; and the Petitioner submits, that the said Bill, if it should be passed, ought to contain a provision lor due enquiry being made into the Losses which shall be sustained by his Constituents, apd for full compensation for the definition or diminished value of their property: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that he may be heard, at the Bar of the House, by himself or his counsel, against the fame, and.that he may be permitted to produce evidence.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a second time.

Thomai Telford being examined, said. That there is a Promontory or point called Ardroffan in the Parish of Ardroffan, in the County of Ayr, terminated by a ridge of Rocks stretching for a considerable way into the sea, in a north-west direction, immediately opposite to which, at the distance of about half a mile to the north-west, there is an island called The Horse I fie, stretching nearly in a north and south direction towards the shore; which Promontory and ridge of Rocks on the one side, and the said Island on the other, completely protest a capacious Bay formed between them, from the winds and storms; and that there is a depth of water to the extent of about thirty feet at low water, ordinary spring tides, between the extremity of the said ridge of Rocks towards the Sea and the said Island, being the entrance to the said Bay; and within the same there is a depth of from twelve to eighteen feet, at low water, ordinary spring tides, with good anchorage ground, and the tide rises to the height of about ten feet in ordinary stre&m tides; and that the said Bay may be formed into a safe and commodious Harbour, which may be entered at all times of the tide, and with any wind, by Vessels of the largest burthen, by constructing Piers upon the said ridge of Rocks, whereby a safe and commodious station may be aftorded to Ships of War on that part of the Coast, and the Trade of that part of the United Kingdom, and the intercourse between Ireland and Scotland, may be greatly promoted; and that the Shipping resorting thereto will be further accommodated by the erection of Wet Docks and Basons, and the constructing of other Works for that purpose, for which the situation of the place is peculiarly favourable.

A Petition of Robert Eyre, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That in July 1781 the late Lieutenant Samuel Eyre, then of His Majesty’s Sloop of War the Nymph, with a small detachment of Seamen and Marines, surprized and captured the Dutch Fort and Factory of Chinfurah, which is distant from Calcutta about thirty miles; and that Lieutenant Eyre was in the complete and unmolested possession of his said conquest for several hours, and until constrained involuntarily to relinquifti the fame by a force of Sepoys under the command of Captain Chat field, in the employ and pay of the British East India Company, who thereby obtained possession, and unlawfully converted to their use immense properties, jullly the prize of Lieutenant Eyre and his detachment; and that, on the Company’s refusal to make restitution of the captured properties, the Navy Captors instituted a suit in the High Court of Admiralty, in the usual way, to obtain redress; and that the cause was first heard ten years subsequent to the said surprize and capture, when the then Judge was pleased to pronounce a joint capture through the Navy Captors and India Company’s Troops; and that against this decree, and against three subsequent and distinert decrees or orders of the said Judge, the said Company interposed as many appeals, in three of which, the decisions appealed from were affirmed by the Lords, and the fourth appeal the said Company did not prosecute; and that in 1793 the said Judge appointed certain Commissioners to examine books and vouchers at the India House, who reported that the said Company ought to account for 246,995. gs. 4 and that of the said sum the said Company have never yet paid more than £. 187,180. i8r. 4 and under the said decree of joint capture, against which the said

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That an Act was passed, 33 III. for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from Lock Gilp to Loch Crinan, in the Shire of Argyll; and that, in

1799, an Act was passed authorizing the Barons of the Coiirt of Exchequer in Scotland to advance 25,000 to the Petitioners, out of the Money arising from the sale of the forfeited Estates in Scotland, for which sum a preferable security exists on the said Canal; and that another Act was passed about the same time, to enable the Petitioners , to raise more money from the original Subscribers; and that not only the whole Money advanced by the Subscribers, but also the said loan from Government, and the sum of £.5,000 borrowed from the Bank of Scotland, together with the Tolls levied on the Navigation, have been expended in this great national undertaking, and considerable debts are now due to Contractors and others for work and materials, and for Money advanced on account of the said Canal; for the liquidation of which, and to completely fini/li the Canal, and make a Pier at the East end, and other necessary works, a further sum of money is stili wanting; and the Petitioners submit that this Canal is particularly entitled to the aid of Parliament, and, as there is no other means of completing it but by a public loan, they hope that their application for such aid will be favourably received, and that the Revenues which the Canal will produce, if finished, according to a reasonable proportion of the goods and commodities now carried by Sea, and which qannot fail to pass through it, will be an ample security to the Public for such additional loan: And therefore praying for such relief as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

III. to authorize the advancement of further sums of Money out of the Consolidated Fund for completing the said Canal and other Works; and that the said Works are in a very forward Hate, but cannot be completed according to the intentions and directions of the said Acts unless a further sum of Money be provided for that purpose, and tire powers and provisions of the said Acts are in some respects altered and amended: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.
