Edinburgh Mr. Abercromby reported from the Committee, to Pe°mion, whom the Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and reporttdi Council Ordinary and Extraordinary, of the City of Edinburgh, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and foafid that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for supplying any City or Town with Water, as the Magistrates of the said City have already brought Water into the said City at , their own1 expence, and without having been under the'

necessity of obtaining power from Parliament for that purpose; and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the 7th year of the reign of His present Majesty, for extending the Royalty of the City of Edinburgh over certain adjoining Lands, and for other purposes, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Royalty of the said City was extended over a variety of Lands, which were disjoined from the Parishes of Saint and South Leith, and

annexed to the Parish of Saint Giles .*—And a Member present informed Your Committee, that it is now become expedient to have the Royalty still further extended over certain Lands, and Grounds adjacent to and to the North of the former extension, and situated within the said Pari fli of Saint Cuthberts; and that it is found necessary to have an additional Church erected within or adjacent to the present extended Royalty, in place of one of the Churches in the antient Royalty, and to translate the Minister or Ministers thereof to the Church to be erected, and also have a Church built and endowed on the Grounds to be annexed, so footi as there shall be a certain number of Inhabitants therein, and funds for such endowment; and that it is necessary to ascertain the claim of the said Parish of Saint Cuthberts, with respect to the maintenance of the Poof, on account of the Lands already, or proposed to be disjoined from the said Parish; and that the Petitioners have at a great expence brought Water to the City, have distributed the fame among the Inhabitants of the City, and of the eight Districts on the South of the City, and a few other places, and that it has become expedient to limit the rate of Water-duty for private Pipes, and the Petitioners agree to have the fame limited, and that they shall not be entitled to raise the Rate or Duty with respect to all private FamiHes and public Stables, higher than the respective Rates contained in their Act in Council, dated the 4th of February 1801, unless the previous consent of a number of official persons shall be obtained Upon being satisfied of any considerable expence being incurred, either by unforseen accidents or bringing in an additional supply' of water, but to be raised only to the extent and to continue during the period to he ascertained by them; but with respect to Brewers, Manufacturers, Porter-dealers, and others, using a great quantity of Water, that may be charged agreeably to the quantity they may be supposed to consume.—Then another Act, passed in the 39th year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging and improving the Harbour of Leith, and for making a Wet Dock or Docks there, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Petitioners were authorized to borrow any sum or sums necessary for that purpose, not exceeding in the whole £. 80,000.—And the Member further informed Your Committee, That the sum is now found to be far short of the Sum necessary for completing the Dock and other Works, and therefore it has become necessary to authorize the Petitioners to borrow an additional sum of money upon the security granted by the

former Act, and that various other powers will be necessary for effecting these purposes.

Mr. Abercromby reported from the Committee, to Petition of whom the Petition of the Excise Incorporation in Scotland, was referred; That the Committee had examined the in Scotian^ matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to re- reported. . port the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and. he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Toprove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. David Robert fan, being examined, said, That by virtue of Letters Patent from his late Majesty, the Persons employed in the Revenue of Excise in Scotland, were by Royal Charter, dated the 14th July 1748 (produced to Your Committee) erected and constituted into a Body Corporate, for the sole purpose of establishing, by annual contributions payable by the persons above-mentioned, a Fund for the support and relief of the Widows and Orphan Children of the Contributors; and that the Petitioners now find that their Capital, when the existing arrears are all paid, will amount folly to the Sum to which it is limited by the said Letters Patent and Charter; and that at the first Institution of the said Fund and Corporation, the total number of persons employed in the Excise in Scotland amounted only to about one-half of the number now employed therein, and the limitation of the Capital of the Fund was fixed on the foppo-fition that only a number of Annuitants corresponding to the number of persons then employed would come upon the Fund; but, as the number of Contributors has so much increased, and may hereafter still farther increase, in consequence of which a proportional number of Annuitants mull in time come upon the Fund, the Petit oners find, that unless they are empowered considerably to enlarge their Capital, the revenue of the Fund will be altogether insufficient to answer the demands upon it; and that the Annuities respectively provided to be given, as fixed at the commencement of the Institution, are too small, and quite inadequate to the present expence of living; they are therefore anxious to enlarge them, and for that purpose to collect additional contributions from the persons enjoying the benefit of the Fund; and that certain additional regulations for collecting and managing the Fund will bo necessary.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the powers of the Excise Incorporation in Scotland: And that Mr. Abercromby and Mr. Robert Dundas do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Your Committee having taken the said Report into Consideration, proceeded to examine, Mr. Thomas Loveland-, who informed Your Committee, That the whole-l'ale price of a bushel of Salt is eighteen shillings; but he

mull remark, that the greater part of the Bakers buy it at the retail price, which is ao s.per bushel, as fixed by the Court of Aldermen—That the increased price of Salt per bushel in consequence of the proposed New Duty is five shillings, and the Salt Merchant has laid sixpence extra—That the increased expence to the Baker in baking a sack of Flour by means of the increased price of Salt, is sixpence, because every sack of Flour upon the average takes five pounds of Salt to manufacture it into Bread—>

That all the articles mentioned in the Report of last Session, remain the fame in price—That the allowance is the fame for baking a sack of Flour, whether the price is two pounds or five pounds per sack, notwithstanding a much larger capital is employed in the latter case; and an encreased rilk from bad debts: Whereupon it appeared to the Committee, That the Bakers are entitled to a half Assize, or twenty pence per sack in addition to

That there are within the said Parish several Commons and Waste Lands, and if they were divided, inclosed and fold, or otherwise disposed of, and the money arising thereby applied in or towards defraying the expences of certain purposes for the benefit and accommodation of the said Town, and in aid of the Poors Rate, it would be of great advantage to the Inhabitants thereof; and that the Poor belonging thereto are become very numerous, and are supported at a very great expence to the Inhabitants; and if a suitable House was provided for the reception of such Poor, and proper Powers were given for their regulation, employment and government, it would not only be of great advantage to all Persons paying to the Poors Rate, but would tend to the better support, relief, and comfort of the Poor themselves:—And the Witness being further examined, said. Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the desire of the Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills and one Private Bill therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, their Royal Highnesses the Duke of York, the Duke of Cla, the Duke of Kent, the Duke of Cumberland, the Duke of Sussex, the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor, the Lord Walsingham, and the Lord named

also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty additional Duties in Great Britain on Horses used in riding or for drawing certain Carriages, and forconfoiidating the said additional Duties with the present Duties thereon:

An Act for granting additional Duties on Salt in Great Britain:

An Act for granting to His Majesty additional Duties in Great Britain on the Amount of Assessments to be charged on the Profits arising from Property, Professions,

Trades, and Offices:

An Act for punishing Mutiny and Desertion; and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters:

An Act for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the CanalNavigation from Manchejlcrto or near under

Lyne and Oldham, more effectually to provide for the discharge of their Debts, and to complete the said Canal, and the Cuts and Works thereto belonging:

An Act for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the Peak Forest Canal more effectually to provide for the discharge of their debts, and to complete the said Canal, and the Cut, Railways or Stone Roads, and other Works thereof:

An Act for naturalizing John Antony.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Gorft, Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the said County, being examined, said, That the business of the General Quarter Selbons held by Adjournment within the Hundred of Salford;for the determination of such matters as arise within the said Hundred, is of peculiar magnitude and importance, owing to the very great population of the District, and the prevailing influence of the Trade and Mann facia re established and carried on therein—That the population of the said Hundred of Salford, with respect to the whole of the said County, is as 281,404 is to 672,731, and out of which number 116,543 are employed in Trade and Manufacture—That during the interval of the last five years, there has been tried at the said Quarter Sessions held for the said District, 1,632 prisoners for various offences, at an expence of more than Jf.6,800; besides T raverfes and A p pea Is, and other business of a more summary nature, directed by various Acts of Parliament That the said Sessions formerly began on the Thursday, and generally concluded on the Saturday, but of late years, the commencement was altered to Wednesday, and the same are not always terminated in that week, but have frequently gone into the following week :—And the Witness added. That the duties of a Chairman at the said Sessions held within the said District, cannot be effectually discharged, but by a Personpofiefled of a very considerable degree of legal knowledge, and whose regular attendance may be fully depended on; and that he conceives such a Chairman cannot be obtained, unless some provision can be made for his remuneration, and that unless some such Chairman shall be found, it is apprehended, that in the course of a short space of time, the business of the said adjourned Sessions will be greatly impeded or wholly flopped, whereby the trade and business of the District will be liable to great interruption, difficulty, and danger, and the Inhabitants in general will be essentially inconvenienced.

A Petition of several AI after Printers in the Cities of London and Westminster, was presented to the House,

and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have for many years carried on the Printing Business, to the general dist'ufion of Literature, the promotion of Commerce, the facilitating of every kind of Business, and to the great benefit and accommodation of the Public at large; and that, from the extraordinary increase of the Printing Business for several years pall, a great variety of modes of Printing has been introduced, and various expedients have been adopted to facilitate its execution, in consequence whereof disputes have frequently arisen with the Workmen, but as the Matters Profits have always been in proportion to the Wages paid to the Journeymen, the Petitioners, Handing as they do between the employer and the employed, have constantly been induced to allow the utmost advanced prices they thought themselves juf-tified in paying, but have not always been enabled to satisfy the demands of their Journeymen, who in the Metropolis consist of two branches, denominated Competitors, and Prellincn; and that the Compositors are paid by a liandard generally reckoning upon the number of Letters contained in a page, and tire PrelTmen by the number of Sheets printed; that feales for both descriptions of Workmen have been formed and advanced upon in different periods from the 'year 1786 to December 1800, when the last advance was made in consequence of the then unusually high price of bread and every necessary article of life; and that the Workmen have lately become dissatisfied, and have made exorbitant demands, although the preffiire of the times is b y no means so great as at the period above ftuted, and the Masters do not therefore think themselves justified in making any further advance upon the fixed prices, as they conceive that, if such demands were to be complied with, the price of elementary Books for the Inllruetion of Youth, and many other useful tracts of Literature, would be so enhanced as to place them out of the reach of many, and the encouragement of the Export Trade, so beneficial to the Revenue aswell as to the Petitioners, and to the numerous individuals interested in the sale of Books, would be nearly-precluded; and that within the last month nearly all the Preffmen usually employed by the Petitioners have voluntarily left their work, thereby putting all public and private business nearly to a stand, and utterly preventing the possibility of completing in due time many important Papers actually wanted by Government, as well as the various Periodical Publications for the ensuing month, to

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed, That a Committee be appointed to examine whether any and what Securities have been taken on behalf of the Public, for the liquidation of a Debt of £.81,625. 18 s.lid. which by the last Account of the Balances of Public Accountants, laid before this House, appears to be due from John Fordyce, Esquire, to the Public, and at what period, and from whom the said securities have been taken, and particularly to examine whether an Assignment of all the Property of the said John Fordyce, was not made by him to Trustees for the Lords of the Treasury, as a security for his Debt in 1783, and to examine of what that property then consisted, and whether any of the profits and proceeds thereof, have been applied by the said Trustees in the liquidation of the said Debt, and to examine w hether any and what proceedings have been instituted by the Lords of the Treasury against either the said John Fordyce or any part of his property, or upon any of the Securities in the possession of the Lords of the Treasury for the liquidation of his Debt; and to examine whether any and which of the engagements entered into by the said John Fordyce with the Lords of the Treasury for the liquidation of this Debt, and which are referred to by him in the Appendix to the First Report of the Commissioners for examining the Public Accounts in 1780, and in the Appendix to the Eighth Report of the Finance Committee, 1797, have been performed; and to examine what film now remains due from the said John Fordyce to the Public, for principal and interest upon his said Debt; and to report upon all such matters to this House.

And the said Motion was, with leave of the House, withdrawn.

A Petition of the Roman Catholics of Ireland, whose names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and of others His Majesty’s subjects professing the Roman Catholic Religion, waspresented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are stedfastly attached to the Person, Family, and Government of their Most Gracious Sovereign; that they are imprefied with senti-ments of affectionate gratitude for the benignant laws which have been enacted' for meliorating their condition during His paternal reign; and that they contemplate, with rational and decided predilection, the admirable principles of the British Constitution; and the Petitioners most humbly state, that they have solemnly ami publicly taken the oaths prescribedbv Law to His Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects as tests of political and moral principles; and they confidently appeal to the sufferings which they have long endured, and the sacrifices which they Hill make, rather than violate their confidences, by taking oaths of a religious or spiritual import contrary to their belief, as decisive proofs of their profound and fcrnpulous reverence for the sacred obligation of an oath; and the Petitioners beg leave to repvefent, that, by these awful tests, they bind themselves, in the presence' of the all-seeing Deity, whom all dalles of Christians adore, " to be faithful, and bear true allegiance to their Most Gracious Sovereign Ix>rd King George the Third,

" and Him to defend, to the utmost of their power, against " all conspiracies and attempts whatsoever that shall be " made against His Person, Crown, or Dignity; to do " their utmost endeavours to disclose and make known " to His Majesty, and His Heirs, all treasons and traito-" rous Conspiracies which may be formed against Him or " thgm; and faithfully to maintain, support, and defend, " to the utmost of their power, the succession to the " Crown in His Majesty’s Family, against any Person or "Persons whatsoever;" that, by those oaths, they renounce and abjure obedience and allegiance unto any other Person claiming or pretending a right to the Crown of this Realm; that they reject and detest, as unchristian and impious, to believe that it is lawful in any ways to injure any person or persons whatsoever under, pretence of their being Heretics, and also that unchristian and impious principle, that no faith is to be kept with Heretics; that it is no article of their faith, and that they renounce, reject, and abjure the opinion, that Princes, excommunicated by the Pope and Council, or by any authority whatsoever, may be deposed or murdered by their fuhje :,s, or by any person whatsoever; that they do not believe that the Pope of Rome, or any other foreign Prince, Prelate, State, or Potentate, hath, or ought to have, any temporal or civil jurisdiction, power, fupe-. riority, or pre-eminence within this Realm; that they. firmly believe, that no act, in itself unjust, immoral, or wicked, can ever be justified or excuied, by or under pretence or colour that it was done for the good of the Church, or in obedience to any ecclesiastical power whatsoever; and that it is not an article of the Catholic Faith, neither are thereby required to believe or profess, that the Pope is infallible, or that they are bound to obey any order, in its own nature immoral, though the Pope, or any ecclesiastical power, /hould ift’ue or direct any such order; but, on the contrary, they hold that it would be sinful to pay any respect or obedience thereto; that they do not believe that any fin whatsoever, committed by them, can be forgiven at the mere will of any Pope, or of any Priest, or of any person or persons whatsoever; but that any person who receives absolution for the fame, without a liticere sorrow for them, and a firm and sincere resolution to avoid future guilt, and to atone to God, so far from obtaining thereby any remiftion of his fins, incurs the additional guilt of violating a Sacrament; and, by the fame solemn obligation, they are bound and firmly pledged to defend, to the utmost of their power, the settlement and arrangement of property in their Country, as established by the laws now in being; that they have disclaimed, disavowed, and solemnly abjured any intention to subvert the present Church Establi/liment, for the purpose of fub-ilituting a Catholic Establishment in its Head; and they have also solemnly sworn, that they will not exercise any privilege, to which they are or may become entitled, to disturb or weaken the Protestant Religion, or Protestant Government of Ireland; and that the Petitioners most humbly beg leave to /hew, that however painful it is to their feelings, that it /hould still be thought necessary to exatt such tests from them, and from them alone, of all II is Majesty’s subjects, they can, with perfect truth, affirm, that the political and moral principles which are thereby aliened, are not only conformable to their opinions and habits, but are expressly inculcated by the Religion which they profess; and the Petitioners most humbly trust, that the religious doctrines which permit such tests. to be taken, will be pronounced by the House to be entitled to a toleration not merely partial but complete, under the happy Constitution and Government of this Realm, and that His Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects, holding those principles, will be confulered as subjects, upon whose fidelity the State may repose the /irinest reliance; and the Petitioners further most humbly /hew, that twenty-six years have now elapsed since their Most Gracious Sovereign, and the Houses of Parliament in Ireland, by their public and deliberate act, declared, that, from the uniform peaceable behaviour of the Roman Catholics of Ireland, fora long series of years, it appeared rea/onable and expedient to relax the disabilities and incapacities under which they laboured; and that it mull tend not only to the cultivation and improvement of this 13 Kingdom,

45 Geo. III. 25° Marlii. 169

Kingdom, but to the prosperity and strength of all His Majesty’s Dominions, that His Majesty’s subjects, of all denominations, should enjoy the bJeffingsof a freeCon-fiitution, and should be bound to each other by mutnal interell and mutual afiection, a declaration founded upon unerring principles of just ice and found policy, which Hill remains to be carried into full ellect (although the Petitioners are imprefied with a belief, that the apprehensions which retarded its beneficial operation, previous to the Union, cannot exist in the Parliament of the United Kingdom) for the Petitioners most humbly shew, that, by virtue of divers Statutes now in force, His Majesty’s Homan Catholic Subjects, who form so great a proportion of the population of Ireland, and contribute so largely to the resources of the State, do yet labour under many incapacities, restraints, and privations, winch a Refit them with peculiar severity in almost every station of life; that more especially they are denied the capacity of fitting or voting in either of the Houses of Parliament, the manifold evils eonfequont upon which incapacity they trust it is uuneeHTary to unfold or enumerate to the House—they are disabled frorh holding or exercising (unless by special dispenlaiion) any Corporate Office whatsoever in the Cities and Towns in which they re-fide; they are incapacitated and disqualified from holding or exercising the offices of Sheriffs and Sub-fheritls, and various offices of trust, honour, and emolument in the State, in His Majesty’s Military and Naval Service, and in the administration of the laws in this their native land; and that the Petitioners, declining to enter into the painful detail of the many Incapacities and Inconveniences avotvedly inHifted by those Statutes upon His Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects, beg leave however most earnestly to solicit the attention of the House to the humiliating and ignominious system of exclusion, reproach, and suspicion, which those Statutes generate and keep alive; for the Petitioners mod humby shew, that in consequence of the hostile spirit thereby fanCtioned, their hopes of enjoying even the Privileges which, through the benignity of their Most Gracious Sovereign, they have been capacitated to enjoy, are nearly altogether fmftrated; insomuch, that they are in efleet shut out from almost all the honours, dignities, and offices of trust and emolument in the State, from rank and distinction in His Majesty’s Army and Navy, and even from the lowed fixations and franchises in the several Cities and Corporate Towns throughout His Majesty’s Dominions; and that the Petitioners severely feel, that this unqualified interdiction of those of their Communion from all municipal stations, from the franchises of all Guilds and Corporations, and from the patronage and benefits annexed to those fixations, is not an evil terminating in itself, for they beg leave to ftaX, that by giving an advantage over those of their Communion to others by whom such fixations are exclusively possessed, it establishes a species of qualified Monopoly universally operating in their disfavour, contrary to the spirit, and highly detrimental to the freedom of Trade; and that the Petitioners likewise severely feel, that His Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects, in consequence of their exclusion from the offices of Sheriffs and Sub-iherills, and of the host ile spirit of those Statutes, do not fully enjoy certain other inestimable privileges of the British Constitution, which the law has mod jealously maintained and secured to their fellow subject.s; and that the Petitioners most humbly beg leave to solicit the attention of the House, to the distination which has conceded the elective and denies the representative franchise to one and the fame class of His Majesty’s subjects, which detaches from property its proportion of political power, under a Constitution whole vital principle is the union of the one with the other, which closes every avenue of legalized ambition against those who mud be presumed to have great credit and influence amongst the mass of the population of the Country, which refuses to Peers of the Realm all share in the legislative representation, either arinal or virtual, and renders the liberal profelllon of the Taw to Roman Catholics a mere object of pecuniary traffic, despoiled of its hopes and of its honours; and that the Petitioners further most humbly shew, that the exclusion of so numerous and efficient a portion of His Ma-VoL. 6o.

jesty’s subjects as the Roman Catholics of this Realm from Civil Honours and Offices, and from advancement in His Majesty’s Army and Navy, actually impairs, in a very material degree, the most valuable resources of the British Empire, by impeding His Majesty’s general service.

Hiding the most honourable and powerful incentives to military and civiPmcrit, and unnecefl’arily restricting the exercise of that bright prerogative of the Crown which encourages good subjects to promote the Public Welfare, and excites them to meritorious actions by a well regulated distribution of public honours and rewards; and that the Petitioners beg leave most humbly to submit, that those manifold incapacities, restraints, and privations, are absolutely repugnant to the liberal and comprehen-five principles recogniscd by their Most Gracious Sovereign and the Parliament of Ireland, that they are impolitic restraints upon His Majesty’s Royal Prerogative, that they are hurtful and vexatious to the feelings of a loyal and generous people, and that the total abolition of them w ill be found not only compatible with, but highly conducive to, the perfect security of every Establishment, religious or political, now existing in this Realm; for the Petitioners most explicitly declare, that they do not seek, or with in the remotest degree, to injure or encroach upon the " rights, privileges, immunities, possessions, or " revenues, appertaining to the Bishops and Clergy of " the Protestant Religion as by Law established, or to " the Churches committed to their charge, or to any of " them," the foie object of the Petitioners being an equal participation, upon equal terms, with their fellow subjects, of the full benefits of the British Laws and Constitution; and that the Petitioners beg leave most humbly to observe, that although they might well and justly infill upon the firm and unabated loyalty of His Majesty’s Roman Catholic Subjects to their Most Gracious Sovereign, their profound respect for the Legislature, and their dutiful submission to the Laws, yet they most especially rest their humble claims, and expectations of relief, upon the clear and manifest conduciveness of the measure which they solicit to the general and permanent tranquillity, strength, and happiness of the Empire;

and that the Petitioners, entertaining no doubt of its final accomplishmenf from its evident justice and utility, do most solemnly allure this honourable House, that their earnest solicitude for it, at this peculiar crisis, arises principally from their anxious desire to extinguish all motives to disunion, and all means of exciting discontent; for the Petitioners most humbly state it as their decided opinion, that the enemies of the British Empire, who meditate the subjugation of Ireland, have no hopes of success save in the disunion of its Inhabitants; and therefore it is, that the Petitioners are deeply anxious, at this moment, that a measure should be accomplished which will annihilate the principle of religious animosity, and animate all descriptions of His Majesty’s subjects in an enthusiastic defence of the heft Constitution that has ever yet been established: And the Petitioners therefore most humbly presume to express their earned but respectful hope. That the House will in its wisdom and liberality deem the several Statutes now in force against them no longer necessary to be retained; and that His Majesty’s loyal and dutiful subjects professing the Roman Catholic Religion may be effectually relieved from the operation of those Statutes, and that so they may be restored to the full enjoyment of the benefits of the British Constitution, equally and in common with their fellow Subjects throughout the British Empire.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of John Duke of Atholl, was presented to Petition of the House, and read; setting forth. That the Isle of Man, was granted in sovereignty by King ienrxf the Fourth l«ve to to the Petitioner’s ancestors, and confirmed to, and made unalienable in, the Petitioner’s family, by an Act passed in the 7 th year of King James the First, and they continued Proprietors thereof, with sovereign rights, until it was thought necessary by Parliament, for purposes connected with the protection of the British and Irish Revenues, to vest the fame in His Majesty, by an Act passed in the 5th year of His Reign; and that the Petitioner is well satisfied that it was not intended in that transaction to deprive his family of the full benefit of the principle that has invariably governed the Legislature in all cases in which the public safety has required that the rights and properties of individuals should be resigned or purchased for the protection of great national interests, namely, that of giving full compensation to th'ofe who are called upon to make such sacrifices; and that the compensation then given to the Petitioner’s family was estimated on an erroneous supposition, that the greater part of the Revenue produced to him by the said itland was derived from illegal sources, and from the introduction of articles which were afterwards smuggled into His Majesty’s Dominions, to the great detriment of His Majesty’s Revenues; and that, notwithstanding the lapse of time (a great part of which has been employed in invef-ti gating the nature of the interests of the Petitioner’s family in the said island, and in the improvement of the Revenues derived by His Majesty from the same) the Petitioner is able, by original documents and evidence, to prove that the Revenue fairly arising to his family from the fair duties at the rates payable in 1765, accruing on articles introduced into the island for the purposes of consumptiononly, independent of trade, would have produced an annual income, for which, together with the regalities that were attached to it, the sum given could not be deemed an adequate compensation; and that fub-sequent experience, founded on the system introduced after the reveftment of the said island in His Majesty, has fully confirmed that the compensation thus given was not adequate to the property taken from the Petitioner for the public service, and has also proved, that if a plan, similar to that which is now pursued, for regulating the supply of articles for the use of the island, had been adopted *in 1763, His Majesty’s Revenue would hifve been protected, and the interests of the Petitioner’s family in the said island would have been secured, and their value increased instead of diminished; and that the Revenue now raised in the said island greatly exceeds what Parliament had in contemplation at the time of the purchase, and the Petitioner, being satisfied that it was not the intention of Government at that time to procure a benefit to the Public by sacrifices made by his family, without giving full compensation, rolls allured that the House will not deprive him of the full benefit that his family ought to have received for the resignation of their rights for the Public Service; and that the Petitioner has observed, that there is a Bill now before the House for encouraging the Trade, and for the improvement of the Revenues, and for prevention of Smuggling to'and from the Isle of Man; and that the Petitioner was not able to obtain His Majesty’s recommendation to the object of his Petition until the day appointed by the House for receiving private Petitions had elapsed: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to present a Petition for his relief.

Ordered, That, in consideration of the particular cir- L?av? given, cumstances set forth in the said Petition, leave be given to present a Petition as desired.

The Order of the day being read, for the second reading of the Bill for the establishment of Provincial Asylums for Lunatics and Idiots in Ireland;

, A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Bill be now read a second time;

The Amendments following were proposed to be made to the Question; viz.

To leave out the word * now,'’ and at the end of the Question to add the words " upon this day six months."

And the Question being put. That the word " now," Hand part of the Question;—-It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the words " upon " this day six months," be added at the end of the Question;—It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Questioji, so amended, being put;

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a second time upon this day six months.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read:—And Mr. Robert Barf eld, being examined, said. That the Commissioners appointed by the said Act, have proceeded in the execution thereof, and have made considerable improvements, and erected several useful and expensive Works within the said Harbour, and for such purposes have borrowed considerable sums of Money on the credit of the Tolls and Duties thereby granted; and that the several Piers and other Works within the said Harbour are now in want of considerable repairs, and such Harbour still requires many alterations and improvements, in order to afford safe and commodious Moorings for Vessels coming into the fame; but such alterations and improvements cannot be made, or the works and repairs now absolutely necessary for the preservation of the said Harbour, be executed, or the Money now due and owing on the Tolls and Duties, thereby granted be paid off and discharged, save and except such Tolls and Duties are encreased, and the powers and provisions of the said Act altered and enlarged.

Resolved, That, in furtherance of the intention of the House of Commons, expressed in such Resolutions. His Majesty, by His Warrant, dated 26th June 1782, directed that the Salary of the Treasurer of the Navy should be increased to the sum of X. 4,000. per annum, in full satisfaction of all Wages and Fees, and other Profits and Emoluments theretofore enjoyed by former Treassurers.

Reffved, That it appears to this House, That, during the Treasurership of the Right honourable Isaac Barrf the conditions of the aforesaid Warrant were ft rift ly complied with; that the whole of the money issued from the Exchequer to Mr. Barr} for Naval Services was lodged in the Bank; that it was never drawn from thence previously to its being advanced to the Sub-Accountants, to be applied to the Public Service; that, during the time Mr. Barr^ after! as Treasurer and Ex-Treasurer, he had not in his possession or custody any of the Public Money, and that neither lie, nor the Paymaster of the Navy, did derive any profit or advantage from the use or employment thereof.

Resolved, That the Right honourable Hairy Dundas, now Lord Viscount Mdv'die, fuceecded to the office of Treasurer of the Navy on the 19th August 1782, when a further addition was made to the Salary of* the said Office, in order to produce a net annual income of X. 4,000. after the payment of all taxes and charges oil the fame; and that this additional Salary was considered by the said Lord Viscount Melville as granted to linn in lieu of all Wages, Fees, Profits, and other Emoluments, enjoyed by former Treassurers.

Resolved, That the said Lord Viscount Melville continued in the said office till the 10th of April 178^; that, being nfkcd whether he derived any advantage from the use of the Public Money during that period, he, in his examination before the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry,

declined answering any question on that head; but that he has, in a letter since written to the said Commi dinners, and dated the 28th March last, declared, " that, previous " to 1786, he did not derive any advantage from the " use or employment of any money iifiu d lor r arrving " on the service of the Navy;" but Mr. Douglas, who was Paymaster, being dead, and his Lordship having re-fused to answer any questions on this head, as aforesaid, no evidence has been obtained as to the Application of Monies issued for the Service of the Navy, or the mode of drawing the fame from the Bank during this period.

Resolved, That the Right honourable Charles Townf hend, now Lord Banning, held the office of Treasurer of the Navy from the nth of April 1783 to the 4th of January 1784; and that, from the examination of his Lordship, it appears, that, during his Treasurerthip, no part of the money issued for the Service of the Navy was applied to his private use or advantage, and that he does not believe that Mr. Douglas, who aided under him as Paymaster, derived any protit or advantage from the use or employment of the Public Money, except the inoney* issued for the payment of Exchequer Fees.

Resolved, That the Right honourable Henry Dundas was re-appointed Treasurer of the Navy on the 5th of January 1784, and continued in the said Office until the ill of June 1800.

Resolved, That, in the year 1785, an Act of Parliament was passed (25 Geo. III. c. 31.) intituled, "An Act " for better regulating the Office of Treasurer of His Ma-" jetty's Navy," whereby it is directed, that no money shall be issued from the Treasury to the Treasurer of the Navy, but that all monies issued for Naval Services shall be paid to the Bank on account of Naval Services, and placed to the account of the Treasurer of the Navy, and shall not be paid out of the Bank unless for Naval Services, and in pursuance of drafts signed by the Treasurer, or some person or persons authorized by him, which drafts shall speci/y the heads of service to which such sums are to applied; and that the regulations under the said Act /had take place from the 31st of July 1785.

Resolved, That the execution of the said Act was post-ponedtill the month of January 1786; and that from that time till the month of June 1800, when Lord Melville left the office of Treasurer, contrary to the practice efta-b! filled in the Treasurer/hip of the Right honourable Isaac Barr}, contrary to the Resolutions of the House of Commons of the 18th of June 1782, and in defiance of the provisions of the above-mentioned Act of 25 Geo. III. c. 31. large sums of money wrere, under pretence of Navy Services, and by a manifest evasion of the Act, at various times drawn from the Bank and inverted in Exchequer and Navy Bills, lent upon the security of Stock, employed in discounting private Bills, in purchasing Bank and East India Stock, and used in various w ays for the purposes of private emolument.

Resolved, That Alexander Trotter, Esquire, the Paymaster of the Navy, was the person by whom, or in whose name, the Public Money was thus employed; and that in so doing he acted with the knowledge and consent of Lord Viscount Melville, to wdiom he was at the same time private Agent, and for w hose use or benefit he occasionally laid out from ten to twenty thousand pounds, without confiilering whether he w as previously in advance to his Lordship, or whether such Advances w ere made from Ins public or private Balances.

III. c. 31, has been guilty of a gross violation of the Law, and a high breach of Duty;

A Petition of several Electors of the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, in behalf of themselves, and the other Electors, in Common Hall assembled, was presented to the House, and read; congratulating the House upon the result, so glorious to the character of Parliament, of the dilcuflions which took place in the House, on the 8th and 10th days of this instant April, respecting the gross malversations in certain branches of the Executive Government, which have been disclosed in the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval Inquiry; And praying the House to follow up that virtuous line of conduct, which has diffused such signal satisfaction through the whole country; and the Petitioners intreat the House to fist to the bottom the mass of Abuses which the aforesaid Commissioners have traced and exposed; and to renew, without loss of time, and extend, if necessary, the powers so faithfully executed by those Commissioners; and the Petitioners implore the House to pull down guilt, however protected, to save from rapacity, peculation, and fraud, a People who contribute cheerfully to the real wants of the State, and who never complain but when their generous temper is abused and imposed upon: So shall the Commons of England take the most efficient course possible to vindicate the sullied honour of the Government; to confirm the public confidence; and to plant in all good hearts the most un-. feigned admiration of the British Constitution.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Liverymen, of the City of London, in Common Mali assembled, was all'o presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have uniformly concurred in and supported such measures as have appeared conducive to

the iafety and welfare of His Majesty’s dominions, and have cheerfully submitted to the most unexamp’ed burthens, under a confidence that the resources of the Country were faithfully and hpneftly administered; and that they learn, with the utmost concern and astonish-ment, from the Reports of the Commissioners for Naval Enquiry, now before the House, that the Right honourable Henry Dundai Viscount Melville, late Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, has been guilty of a gross violation of the law and a high breach of duty, whereby iromenfe Sums of the Public Money have been perverted to private emolument; and that they conceive it to be a high aggravation of such offence, that these disgraceful transaelions were carried on during a period of unprecedented difficulty, when the very existence of the Country was said to be at flake; and that the person so abusing his trull, so violating the law, Wa9 in the enjoyment of several high and lucrative offices} and evetf among the foremost in laying additional burthens Upon the people, and calling upon them to submit to the most painful privations; and that they are duly impressed with a high sense of the virtue, integrity, and firmness of the House, and strongly participate ill the sentiment which so generally pervades all ranks of His Majesty’s faithful subjects, of the wisdom and fidelity with which it has discharged its most sacred trull, by the progress it has made towards protecting the people against such gross violations of the law and breaches of Public Duty;

‘and that the Petitioners approach the House, as the Guardians of the Liberties and Property of the People; under a full conviction that such shameful abuses will induce the House to do ample justice to the outraged feelings of the Country, by bringing to condign punishment convicted criminality; and that they beg to submit to the House, that it would be highly derogatory to His Majesty’s Government, prejudicial to the Public Service* and insulting to the House, and the Nation at large, for Lord Melville any longer to Continue in His Majesty’s Councils, or to hold any place of trust, profit, or honour, in or under the Government; and that they conceive all other persons who may be implicated in, or have Connived at such abuses, to be incapable any longer of serving the Country with honour or advantage, and ought equally to be brought to a severe account: And therefore praying, That the House, taking these matters into their serious consideration, will vigorouffy promote and prosecute those enquiries, and cause the powers of the said Commissioners to be prolonged and extehded, and other measures to be adopted, in order that such further enquiry may be made into the Receipt, Management, and Expenditure of the Public Money, and the conduct of the Public Offices, as may lead to the detection of all abuses and the punishment of all offences, and that such a fyltem of vigilance and economy may be eilablithed, as may effectually guard against the recurrence of such flagrant abuses.

A Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the New Sarum, City of New Sarum, was likewise presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have pe-rufed, with much concern and interest, the Resolutions of the House of the 8th and 10th days of this instant April; with concern, that any charges of the nature , therein implied should attach upon any individual in high official situation, and with interest, that the repre- * feutatives of the Nation have, under the circumstance of such charges, marked such individual with their censure and reprobation; and that the Petitioners beg leave to state, that, in common with the Nation at large, they have to lament the weight of the burdens to winch the Legislature has found it necessary to submit them, but they claim for themselves, in common with the Nation at large, the merit of having borne them with patience, , readiness, and equanimity, trusting that what had been granted liberally would be applied faithfully; but when a suspicion is gone forth, under the authority of Parliamentary Commissioners, and that suspicion apparently adopted by the House, that peculation has been hard at work, the Petitioners take leave to call upon the National Representatives for red refs, reminding them, that it is of little consequQtice as a public grievance, of little con-

P

,{That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That feme " regulations ought to be adopted. For the pijrpose of " k-flening and keeping down the Balances of Public " Money, which appear to have usually been in the hands " of the Treasurer of the Navy; and it would be bene-" ficial to the Public, if the first and other Clerks in the " different branches belonging to the said office, were " paid by fixed and permanent Salaries, in lieu of all Fees, * Gratufties, and other Perquisites whatsoever:"

" That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from * henceforward the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s " Land Forces and the Treasurer of the Navy for the " time being, shall not apply any sum or sums of Money * imprested to them, or either of them, to any purpose of * advantage or interest to themselves, either directly or " indirectly

" That it appears to this Committee, That the Com-. " missioners appointed to examine, take, and hate the " Public Accounts of the Kingdom, have, so far as " appears from the Reports which they have hitherto " made, discharged the duty intruded to them with great " diligence, accuracy, and ability; and, if Parliament * shall carry into execution those plans of reform and " regulation which are suggested by the matter contained " in the Reports of the said Commissioners, it cannot but " be attended with the moil beneficial consequences to " the future welfare and prosperity of this Kingdom."

* Resolved, That, in furtherance of the intention of the House of Commons, express’ed in such Resolutions, His Majesty, by His Warrant, dated 26th June 1782, directed that the Salary of the Treasurer of the Navy should be increased to the sum of £. 4,000 per annum, in full fafcisfafction of all Wages and Fees, and other Profits and Emoluments, theretofore enjoyed by former Treasurers/

‘ Resolved, That it appears to this House, That, during

tfte Treasurership of the Right honourable Isaac the conditions of the aforesaid Warrant were ft rift ly complied with; that the whole of the Money issued from, the Exchequer to Mr. Barr} for Naval Services was lodged in the Bank; that it was never drawn from thence previously to its being advanced to the Sub-Accountants, to be applied to the Public Service; that, during the time Mr. Bar?-} acted as Treasurer and Extreasurer, be had not in his possession or custody any of the Public Money, and that neither he, nor the Paymaster of the Navy, did derive any profit or advantage from the use or employment thereof.’

‘ Resolved, That the Right honourable Henry Dtnidas, now Lord Viscount Melville, succeeded to the oflice of Treasurer of the Navy on the 19th August 1782, whew a further addition was made to the Salary of the said Office, in order to produce a net annual income of £. 4,000, after the payment of all taxes and charges on the lame; and that this additional Salary was cou-fidered, by the said Lord Viscount Melville, as granted to him in lieu of all Wages, Fees, Profits, and other Emoluments, enjoyed by former Treasurers: ’

* Refohed, That the said Lord Viscount Melville continued in the said office till the 10th of April 1783; that, being asked, whether lie derived any advantage from the use of the Public Money during that period? he, in his examination before the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, declined answering any question on that head; but that he has, in a letter since written to the said Commissioners, and dated the 28th March lait, declared, " that, previous to 1786, he did not derive any ad-*, vantage from the use or employment of any Money " iff'ued for carrying on the service of the Navy;" but Mr. Douglas, who was Paymaster, being dead, and his Lordfiiip having refused to answer any questions on this head, as aforesaid, no evidence has been obtained as to the Application of Monies iff’ued for the service of the Navy, or the mode of drawing the fame from the Bank during this period: ’

III. c. 31.) intituled, "An " Act for better regulating the office of Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy," whereby it is directed that no Money shall be issued from the Treasury to tire Treasurer of the Navy, but that all Monies issued for Naval Services shall Be paid to the Bank on account of Naval Services, and placed to the account of the Treasurer of the Navy, and shall not be paid out of the Bank unless for Naval Services, and in pursuance of drafts signed by the Treasurer, or some Person or Persons authorized by him, which drafts shall specify the heads of service to which such sums are to be applied; and that the vegu'a-tior.s under the said Act shall take place from the,3 ill of Juiy, 1785

Befolved, That it is the Opinionof this Committee, That it is expedient that the Lord Lieutenant, or other Chief Governor or Governors of Ireland for the time being, should be enabled to advance, out of the Consolidated Fund of Ireland, such parts of such sums of Money as shall be preferred by Grand Juries for the purpose of making or' completing Poll Roads in their respective Counties, for the more secure and speedy conveyance of the Mails, as he or they shall think proper, the repayment thereof being to be made out of the monies arising from such Presentments.

A Petition of Peter Stuart, Printer and Publisher of a Morning Newspaper, intituled, " The Daily Advertiser, " Oracle, and True Briton," was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, for the publication of that part of his Paper of Thursday last, deemed highly offen-five to the House, he feels the deepest regret; and, although certain expressions in that paragraph be indif-creet and unguarded, and such as have incurred the displeasure of so important a branch of the Constitution, yet that the Petitioner humbly hopes, on this acknowledgement of his sincere sorrow, that the House, in the plenitude of its condescension and liberality, will be pleased to pardon him for a transgression solely attributable to the hasty composition of a Newspaper, and not to any deliberate design of offending the House; and that the Petitioner is emboldened to solicit the indul* gence and forgiveness of the House on his well-founded assurance, that, during the several years in which he has conducted a Newspaper, it has uniformly been his principle and pride zealously to support the character and dignity of the House of Commons; and that it has frequently fallen to his lot to have vindicated both from the charges of societies, expressly instituted to bring them into public disrepute and contempt; and that, in any observations which the Petitioner may' have published on the conduct of Lord Melville, he could not but bear in mind, that the views of those societies, abetting domestic treason, and allifted by the co-operation of the resolutionary power of France, would, he verily believes, have efli rted the destruction of the British Constitotion, had not the wife and efficient measures brought forward by that Administration, in which Lord Melville held so conspicuous a situation, been adopted, and the House would not, in that case, perhaps, have been now in existence either to censure Lord Melville or to pardon the Petitioner; and that, if any thing could increase the Petitioner’s regret, it would be its being supposed, that the objectionable paragraph was directed also against the Right honourable the Speaker of the House of Commons; that the Petitioner has no hesitation to declare, that no idea was ever more remote from his mind, and that the Petitioner would he the very last person to in-fiimate any thing difrefpertful of a Character, whom he,: in conjunction with the whole Nation, highly etieems as a private gentleman, and most profoundly' venerates as the head and public organ of the House: And the Petitioner, therefore, most humbly hopes, that the House will consent to his release.

So it was resolved in the Affirmative:

He was accordingly brought to the Bar; where he received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker, and was ordered to be discharged out of custody, paying his fees.

The Reprimand was as followeth; viz.

Peter Stuart,

You having confessed that you were the Printer and Publisher of a Paper, which has been complained of to the House, as containing libellous reflections upon its character and conduct;—this House resolved that you were thereby guilty of a high breach of its privileges; and ordered you to be taken into custody.

By your Petition you have this day expressed your sorrow for your offence, and acknowledged the justice of your punishment; and thereupon this House, in its lenity, has ordered that you be now brought to the Bar, to be reprimanded and discharged.

I have now, therefore, to reprimand and admonith you, as a warning to others, that this House doth and will resent it, as a high offence in any man, who shall presume to slander its character and conduct, and endeavour to degrade it in the public estimation.

You being now reprimanded, it is my duty further to acquaint you, that you are discharged;—paying your fees.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That what has been now said by Mr. Speaker, in reprimanding the said Peter Stuart, be entered in the Journal of this I louse.

A Petition of the Freeholders of the County of Petition fi-cra dlesex, convened by the Sheriff on Thursday the 2d of Muidiefex, May 1805, was presented to the House, and read; setting Tenth Report forth. That the Votes of the House on the 8th and 10th on Naval of April last, founded upon the Tenth Report of the Com- En<luir/-missioners of Naval Enquiry, have interested the whole Nation, and no part of the Nation more deeply than the Petitioners; and they humbly crave the liberty of Hating, that no measures ever yet issued from the Commons of England, which had diifufed more gladness, or raised more expectation, than the said Votes of April the 8th and 10th, declaring Lord Viscount Melville to be guilty of a grols violation of Law, and a high breach of Duty, thereby supporting the upright and virtuous discharge of the falu-tary duties of the said Commissioners, whole conduct has excited the gratitude and the confidence of the whole Country; and that the renewal of the said Commission is a subject of unfeigned joy to the Petitioners; and they entreat the House to be careful to make the new Law effectual and adequate to its end; and they pray the House to attend particularly to those parts of the Tenth Report, which have detailed the obftaelcs thrown by persons in office in the way of the investigations of the said Commissioners, and to guard against their repetition; and they submit to the House, whether the Agents of corruption will not be eager to shelter their contumacy under the example of their superiors, unless the enlarged authority of the Law defeat their artifices; The House being informed, that the Sheriffs of the City of London, attended at the door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Ix>rd Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have observed, with infinite concern and difquictude, a Petition lately presented to the House, by " the Roman Catholics of Ireland, on behalf of them-" selves and of others, His Majesty’s subjects professing " the Roman Catholic Religion," pray ing a repeal of the several Statutes by which they are precluded from offices of trust and power, the only remaining bulwarks now in exigence for the preservation and security of the Protestant Reformed Religion, as finally settled at the glorious Resolution of 1688; and that the Petitioners conceive they would incur the imputation of criminal indifference, ' as the first Municipal Body in His Majesty Dominions, were they lightly to regard an application to the Legis-laturc so formidable in its claims, and so mischievous in its tendency to the Religion, Laws, and Liberties, which it has ever been their glory to admire, and their ambition to guard and secure in every perilous situation; and that

the Oaths of Supremacy and Allegiance are an integral part of the Bill of Rights, proposed, as the Declaration of the Lords and Commons of 1688, expressly Antes, " in " order to such an Establishment as that their Religion,

" Laws, and Liberties, might not again be in danger of " being subverted that the abrogation of or dispensation with those Oaths, to any class of His Majesty’s subjects, would not only weaken at present, but ultimately destroy, those solid foundations on which the wisdom and virtue of our ancestors erected our free and happy Constitution, the envy and admiration of the world; and that the Petitioners regard, with veneration and gratitude, those unextinguishable principles which led the Legislature of that day to provide for the happiness and freedom of their Posterity, by so carefully guarding the Protestant succession, which has placed the House of Brunswick on the Throne of the United Kingdom; and they rely, under Providence, that the spirit of our Forefathers will animate and strengthen the virtue and pa-triotism of their honourable successors, the Commons of the Imperial Parliament, to preserve, uninjured, the glorious fabric they have rai fed; and that the Petitioners conceive every equality is already allotted to the Roman Catholics, in common with the rest of His Majesty’s subjects, consistent with the safety of the Church and State; but that, to grant an indiscriminate participation of ower, without requiring and enforcing the Oaths of upremacy and Allegiance, taken by every other cb.Cs of His Majesty’s subjects, must be productive of future unavoidable anarchy and misery: And therefore praying.

That the remaining salutary restrictive Statutes, respecting the Roman Catholics, may not be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

onfrom Mr. Wilberforce reported from the Committee, to

(Vk,&c. whom the Petition of the Clothworkers and Shearmen of Sthe the Counties of York, Some Gloucester, and;

anuucturc, of the Weavers of the Counties of Somerset, Gloucester, tpcrtai. an(j Wilts, and other parts of the United Kingdom; and of the Clothiers of the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,—An Act, passed in the zd and 3d year of the reign of King Philip and Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act touching Weavers;" and also an Act, passed in the 4 th and 5th year of the said reign, intituled, "An Act touching the making of Woollen " Clothsand also an Act, passed in the 5th year of the reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, "An Act contain-" ing divers Orders for Artificers, Labourers, Servants of " Husbandry and Apprentices," were severally read: —And, Mr. Francis Berry, being examined said. That he has been concerned in the Woollen Trade upwards of 35 years; that the object of the above recited Acts was to secure the good and skilful Manufacture of Woollen Cloths; and that the provisions thereof, which prevented 1 persons from weaving or making, or putting to weave or make Woollen Cloths, or for using or exercising the art, mystery, or occupation of Woollen Cloth Weavers, unless they should have been Apprentices thereto for the space of seven years, have been found highly beneficial, and have greatly contributed to the excellence and fuc-cess of the said Manufacture, and the prosperity of the Kingdom—That the Penalties imposed by the said Acts are by lapse of' time, and by the alteration which has taken place in the value of Money, insufficient for enforcing the due observance of the said Provisions—That the provisions of the said Act of Queen Elizabeth, which require that one of the Parents of such Apprentices should have Estates of Inheritance or Freehold of £. 3. annum, are inapplicable to the present fiate of Society in this Kingdom, and the enforcing thereof would greatly diminish the number of persons capable of being employed in the said Manufacture, and to the great injury of the persons who might be so employed, and of persons employed in the said Manufacture who are willing to take Apprentices :—And being further examined, he laid, That the employment of Weavers and other persons engaged in the Woollen Trade, to spin and weave and make Cloth at their own houses, has produced effects highly beneficial, by improving the condition and comfort of the persons so employed, and by preserving their morals, inculcating habits of iudustry in their families, increasing the population of the Country, and promoting and diffusing the wealth of the Counties in which such employment should be encouraged; and that the life, by individuals or partners, of numerous Looms and Spinning Jennies in the fame Manufactory, should be prohibited.

—Then, an Act, passed in the 5th and 6th year of King Edward the Sixth, intituled, "An Act for putting down " of Gig Mills," was read; by which it appeared, that in many parts of this Realm was newly and lately devised, 'erected, budded, and used, certain mills called Gig Mills, VOL. 60.

Mail 235

for the perching and burling of Cloth; and that the true drapery of this Realm was wonderfully impaired, and the Cloth thereof deceitfully made, by reason of the using of the said Gig Mills:—Then,

Mr. John Tale, being examined, said, That he has been concerned in the Woollen Trade 16 years; that, notwithstanding the said Act, divers Gig Mills, or Machines constructed on the fame or a like principle, and adapted to the fame purpose, have been set up, and Cloths have been thereby unduly stretched and otherwise injured; and that doubts have arisen, whether the word " burling," in the said Act mentioned, applies to the Gig Mills, or other Machines now in use, although those mills or machines cause the fame injurious eftefts in the said Manufacture; and that it is expedient that such doubts should be removed:—Then,

Mr. Bern) being again examined, said, That it is important to the due encouragement of the domestic Manufacture of Woollen Cloths, that Machines called Spinning Jennies, should be limited in regard to the number which may be lawfully employed in one House or Factory, by or for the benefit of one and the same person, or two or more persons being partners:—Then,

Mr. James Jones being examined, said. That he has been concerned in the Woollen Manufacture years,;

, and being further examined, said. That notwithstanding there are divers Statutes now in force, to prevent the Master Clothiers, Weavers, and other Persons concerned in carrying on the Woollen Manufacture, from paying their Workmen in Goods by way of truck, or in any other way than in money for their Labour; yet the Mailers and other persons do in many instances pay their Workmen with Goods by way of truck, or in some other way equally injurious:—/then,

Mr. Tate being again examined, said. That the law respecting Sealers and Searchers and Inspectors of Woollen Cloths, have been greatly evaded, and are in many places totally neglected; and that the Wages or Fees now payable to the said Sealers, Searchers, and Inspectors, are an inadequate reward for the duties to be performed by such Sealers, Searchers, and Inspectors respectively.

nquiry. share the National Gratitude to the House, for the memorable and virtuous Votes of the 9th and xoth of April lair, founded upon the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, declaring the Lord Viscount Melville guilty of a gross violation of the Law, and a high breach of Public Duty :—Never were Parliamentary measures received with more exultation by the Country than the said Votes, and nothing, the Petitioners are persuaded, could cause more disappointment to the Nation, than the House flopping short of those great ends of Justice, which the Public intered demands, and the hohour the House has acquired by the said Votes, exacts and enforces at their hands; and that the pure, the moderate, the faithful, the independent, and the dignified discharge of the functions with which the Law has inverted the said Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, has filled the Country with the most unqualified admiration of their conduct, the renewal of their authority is a source of the most unfeigned pleasure to the People at large; and the Petitioners do most eariieftly supplicate the House, that, in the construction of the new statute, their attention will be fixed upon the contumacious obstrudion to full enquiry, which is so clearly pointed out in the said Tenth Report; and that they will carefully guard against its repetition; and, that the Petitioners beg leave to state to the House, that a civil suit against Lord Melville and Mr. Trotter, unaccompanied by criminal prosecution, would be infinitely short of the Public hopes, because it is so of Public justice: It is not the refunding of money, that of itfclfisof real consequence to the Nation, it is the infliction of an exemplary vengeance upon proved and powerful Delinquents; it is the manifestation to the whole world, that high criminals are not above the reach of punishment; and that the corrupt or wanton violation of Law, shall feel the strength of its arm; and that, above all things, the Petitioners entreat the House not to permit the Public feeling to be sported with; and in the formation of enquiries similar to the Naval Commission, that they will take care that the power constituted be equal to its profefted objects, both as relating to the vigour of the authority, and to the integrity of those w ho are to put it in execution; for they submit to the House, whether, if any thing can be worse than a deep rooted wide-spread lyftem of abuse and peculation in the management of Public Money; it w ould not be the institution of a system of revision, in its nature a bnrlcfque upon investigation, and in its result a mockery of justice; and that to all these points they beg the bed attention of the House; and beseech them to pnrftie with efil d what they have begun with so much honour; and that the Petitioners entreat the House not to relax in their efforts till they have brought Lord Melville to condign punishment, and given to all who shall be found to have committed similar crimes, a signal demonstration that in the Representatives of the People, instead of abettors of their iniquities, they will find only the faithful Guardians of the Nation, and the zealous Vindicators of the Law s: And therefore praying the House to take the premises into ronsideration, and to grant such relief as to the House thall seem meet.

Lord George Augufius Henry reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Freeholders and Inhabitants in the Hundred of High Peak and Manor of Cafileton, in the County of Derby, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Shaw, being examined, said, That from time immemorial, Plea hath been held every three weeks, or so often as requisite, in all personal Actions arising within the jurisdiction of the two several Courts Baron, of and appertaining to the said Hundred and Manor respectively, where the Debt or Damages have been made under the sum of Forty Shillings:—Then an Act, passed in the 33d year of King George the Second, for regulating the proceedings in personal Actions, in the respective Courts Baron of the Hundred of High Peak and Manor of Cafileton, in the County of Derbi], was read:—And, the Witness said, That under the powers and directions of the said Act, Justice hath, in the most strict and impartial manner, from time to time, been administered in the said several Courts Baron, to the great benefit of the Inhabitants within the jurisdiction of the fame— That the jurisdiction of the said Hundred and Manor is very extensive, and includes a populous and increasing district of the County of Derby—That the Town of Derby, where the superior Courts for the County are holden, is upwards of forty miles distant from the most populous part of the said Hundred and Manor—That on account of the very great expence attending the recovery of Small Debts of the amount of Forty Shillings and upwards, in the superior Courts, by reason of thediftance thereof, many Creditors are discouraged from attempting to recover the Debts due to them, and many evildisposed Persons, who have contracted small Debts within the said Hundred and Manor, are enabled to refuse or delay the payment thereof, to the manifest injury of their lawful Creditors—That it would be of great benefit and advantage to the Inhabitants within the said Hundred and Manor respectively, if the powers and provisions of the aforesaid Act were extended to the recovery of Debts of a larger amount than Forty Shillings, and if the said Act was to be explained and amended, and further powers granted.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, past’ed in the 33d year of his lute Majesty, for regulating the proceedings in personal Actions in the respective Courts Baron of the Hundred of High Peak, and Manor of Cafileton, in the County of Derby, and for extending the powers of the said Courts:

ion A Petition of several Proprietors of a certain Manufac-tory, called the Herculaneum Pottery, situate in To.vteth LFen* Park, near Liverpool, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for improving the passage between the Town of Liverpool and the County of Chester, at the Rock Ferry, on the River Mersey, and for levying Tolls on Vessels using the fame; and letting forth. That the Petitioners, and those from whom they derive title to the said manufactory and premises, have, for many years last past, had the uninterrupted use and enjoyment of a certain Road which leads from the said Pottery along the strand of the said River to Liverpool, which Road the Proprietors and Occupiers of Land adjoining have, for time immemorial, used and enjoyed; and the said Road is intended, should the said Bill pass into a Law, to be entirely blocked up, which would very much, injure and impede, if not wholly destroy, the use of the said manu-factory and premises; and that the Petitioners are also possessed of at least ten thousand tons of Copper Dross, in and upon the said Premises, which they fell for the purpose of ballasting vessels, and, by blocking up the said Road, the fame would be rendered of little or no value: And therefore praying. That, in case the said Bill should pass into a Law, sufficient Clauses may be inserted . therein, for the purpose of effectually securing to them the full, free, and uninterrupted use and enjoyment of the said Road, or, that another Road, equally convenient and as advantageous to the Petitioners, may be substituted; and that they may be heard, by themselves, their coun— fel or agents, against such parts of the said Bill as affect their interests.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit connfel to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.
