A Petition of the Freeholder^ of the County of Oxford; Petition front was presented to the House; and read; setting forth,

That the Petitioners have seen; with the deepest coriCem; Petition of that a Petition has been presented to the House by the Cathoiit* Roman Catholics of Ireland, praying that the Laws by which they are at present excluded from being Members of the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ixeland\ and from filling the principal Offices in the executive Government and Civil and Military Administration of Ireland, may be repealed j and the Petitioners humbly tract, that they are not deficient in those feelings of moderation and tolerance, by which an allowance is made for difference of opinion on religious subjects, and by which a protection is afforded to the exercise and practice of those different opinions; but they are at the same time persuaded, that, to grant power and authority to Persons whose religious principles are hostile to the Constitution. of the Country, is neither, required by liberality, nor confident with the distates of found policy or self-preservation; and that the Petitioners are convinced, by the experience of all ages, that the principles of the Roman Catholic Religion are incompatible with both Civil and Religious Liberty; that they are particularly repugnant to the genius and spirit of the Constitution of this United Kingdom, so that it is impossible that Protestants and Roman Catholics should ever agree in administering together the powers of Government, and that such an attempt would be productive of the moil mischievous distractions and weakness in the public Councils of the Kingdom; and that though the petitioning Roman Catholics disclaim some of the mischievous Doctrines of the Church of Rome, yet they still admit that they acknowledge some of the most dangerous ones, amongst which must be reckoned the acknowledgement of the Supremacy of a foreign power in matters of their Religion, which must have a moil important influence on their moral and political conduct; and that the Petitioners cannot but remember, that the partiality of King James the Second for the Roman Catholics, and the influence which he gave them in the Public Councils of the Country, were the sources of all those grievances which imposed upon our Ancestors the necessity of effecting the Resolution in 1688, and of establishing those securities by which a recurrence of those grievances was guarded against and prevented y and the Petitioners are persuaded, that no measure could be devised more disrespectful to that great event, or to the illustrious Characters that were instrumental in effecting it, or more repugnant to the principles established by it, than the attempt to give to the Roman Catholics a power in the Government of this United Kingdom; and wiat the Petitioners cannot but further recollect, that, by the existing Laws, no Roman Catholic can wear the Crown of this United Kingdom, a restriction which the Petitioners conceive to be founded in the soundest policy and wisdom; nor can the Petitioners help thinking, that the fame wisdom and policy requires their exclusion from the other branches of the Legislature; and for this, amongst many other reasons, that nothing seems more incongruous to the Petitioners, than that the King should be obliged to discharge his share of the Government upon Protestant principles, and that his Council should consist of persons devoted to a Church, of principles not only of a different but of a repugnant nature: And therefore praying, That the Laws by which Roman Catholics are at present excluded from being Members of the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great and Ireland, and from filling the principal Offices in the executive Government and Civil and Military Administration of Ireland, may not be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Order of the day, for the second Wand-reading of the Bill for amending an Act, passed in Ireland, Bin *0 amend

A Petition of the Chancellor, Masters, and Scholars, of Petition fro* the University of Oxford, was presented to the House, Oxford and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have seen, rt^'ing’the by the Votes of the House, that a Petition from certain Petit on of Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, Roman Catholics of Ireland, whose names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf Ireland, of themselves and others His Majesty’s subjects pro-fefling the Roman Catholic Religion, hath some time since been presented to the House, complaining of divers restraints and incapacities to which, notwithstanding the various indulgences heretofore granted them from time to time, they arc frill subject by the several statutes now in force against them; and praying that they may be effectually relieved from the operation of the said statutes, as being now no longer necessary to be retained; And, that the Petitioners contemplate, with much concern and anxiety, the alarming extent of the . prayer of the said Petition, and the consequences which, in their apprehensions, must inevitably follow, if the fame should be complied with; and that the Petitioners, notwithstanding the allegations contained in the above-mentioned Petition, do verily believe, that, by the wisdom and liberality of the Legislature, every safe and practical indulgence hath already been extended to their Roman Catholic fellow subjects in Ireland, and that the restraints and incapacities to which, by the statutes now in force, they are Hill subject, and of which they now complain, are no other nor greater than are indispensably requisite to the maintenance and security of the Protestant Government and Protestant Church, as they are happily by law established in that part of the United Kingdom; and that the Petitioners fee also much reason to apprehend, that a compliance with the prayer of the above-mentioned Petition would lead, and, they fear, determined by direct and necessary consequence, to the removal of every similar restraint now subsisting within this Realm of England, and to the abrogation of those oaths, declarations, and tests, which are by Law required of every person admitted to fit or vote in either House of Parliament, or to exercise offices of trust and power; all which, they are thoroughly persuaded, are still essentially necessary to the permanence and security both of our Civil and Religious Establishments: And therefore praying. That the House, in its wisdom, would be pleased still to maintain and preserve inviolate those Law's, which they sincerely believe to be the best safeguards, under Divine Providence, of our present happy Constitution both in Church and State.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, Commons, and Citizens, of the City of Dublin, in Common Council aiVemblod, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have seen with the deepest regret a copy of a Petition, presented to the House by certain persons in the name of the Roman Catholics of Irelawj, containing demands of political power, which, if yielded, would be ruinous to our happy Constitution in Church and State; and that the good conduct of the Roman Catholics, as recognized by the Irish Legislature in 1770, hook place under the operation of severe Laws, which linee 1779 have been from time to time repealed, so as to place the Roman Catholics of Ireland upon a footing of political power not enjoyed by any other Dissenters from the established Religion in any other State; but though the Roman Catholics declared, at tire time of relaxing those Laws, they would be fully content,.vet the Petitioners are lorry to observe, that that cordiality and union of fentimeat which would be so desirable in Ireland has not yet taken place; and further, the Petitioners cannot but observe, that the Petition of the Irish Roman Catholics, though profcffmgto explain the tenets of that feet, as ailecting political duties, is notsigned by a single Ecclesiasfiic of that perfuufion; and that the assertion in the said Petition, that Irish Roman Catholics are excluded from the privileges of Corporations, is wholly unfounded, inafmueh as they are admissible into all Guilds and Corporations on taking the.oaths in their own Petition recited; and that many of them do at this time actually enjoy and exercise such privileges; but the Petitioners observe, that the object of this assertion seems to be to induce the Legislature to compel the Protestant Corporations of Ireland to elect Roman Catholics into their Franckifes, in such numbers as to overbear and de-ffoy the Protestant interest, an attempt which was made both va England and Ireland during the short and arbitrary reign of that unfortunate and infatuated King James

V 01* 60.

the Second, and which, with other serious innovations, led to the glorious re-assertion of the Constitution in Church and State, under the great King William; and the Petitioners beg leave most humbly to irnprefs upon the House, that the lower order of Roman Catholics in Ireland are in possession of the fame degree of civil, religious, and political liberty, that is enjoyed by Protestants of the fame rank and fiation; and even the restraints complained of by the said Petition affect a very inconsider- * able number of Roman Catholics'; the Petitioners there-:' fore humbly conceive, that the inducement held out by the Petition to the House, viz. " That granting the demands of the Roman Catholics would ex-

" tinguish all motives to disunion and means , of difeon-" tent," is utterly fallacious; and they most humbly: submit, that if the demands contained in the said Petition were acceded to, all the fences and. securities of our. excellent Constitution; in Church and State, established; by Protestant Legislators from the time of the Reformation to the reign of His present Majesty, would be destroyed and annihilated: And therefore praying the House will continue to preserv£ unimpaired our excellent Con*, stitution, and reject the demands of the Roman Catholics of Ireland.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

"Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Stationers, and other persons who 11.all purclia e Stamps for Receipts in Ireland to the amount of ten pounds, in consideration of their making no charge to the Public for the paper stamped for Receipts, shall have an allowance at the rate of seven pounds ten shillings for every 100 of the amount of the Duties on such Stamps, over and above the allowance on the present payment of Stamp Duties to the amount of twenty pounds and upwards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties and Allowances shall be paid and payable, according to the amount thereof, in British Currency; and that in all cases where any Duties of Stamps in Ireland, or any Allowances in respect thereof, are directed to be ascertained by the amount of any sum in respect whereof such Duties are imposed, or such Allowances are made, such amount, as well as the rate of Duty or Allowance in respect thereof, shall be taken in British Currency (except where the amount of any sum shall, in the Instrument on which any Duty is imposed, be expressed to be in Irish Currency, in which case such amount shall be taken according to the amount expressed in such Instrument.)

That the Umpire appointed by the said Engineers did, by a deed poll, in the nature of an Award, bearing date the 10th day of September last, in pursuance of the reference so made to him, give his opinion in writing, as to the works, matters, and things requisite to be done, and the mode of executing the fame, and on the whole of the cause or subject of the reference to him; which opinion is by the first-mentioned Act made final and conclusive, and therefore no further controversy can arise as to the form and dimensions of the said new River or Cut.—Then, Mr. William being further examined, said. That the Commissioners have laboured unde? great difficulties, and taken infinite pains to make the proper and necessary rates and assessments, and have from time to time made certain rates or assessments, as accurate as the information they had then obtained, enabled them to do, and that many persons have paid the said rates and assessments; but an opposition has been made thereto, in feme cases, and further opposition is likely to arise, if the Petitioners proceed to enforce the fame—That they have expended nearly the whole of the Monies received by them under the said Acts, in forwarding the objects and directions therein contained, and there are now considerable sums due; and that the Commissioners are unable, by virtue of their present powers, to collect the said Taxes, and to complete the new River or Cut set out by the said Umpire, and the several other works directed to be executed by the first-mentioned Act; and that the said Act is defective and imperfect in various respects, and it is necessary that the fame should be amended.

Resolved, Thnt it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there.be charged upon all Spirits made in Ireland, which shall be warehoused for Exportation, and shall remain in warehouse above a certain period, a Duty after the rate of ten pounds for every one hundred pounds by the year, on the amount of the Duties of Excise payable on such Spirits.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Distiller in Ireland, who shall make use of any Still, the body whereof only shall contain one thousand gallons or upwards, shall be allowed a Bounty after the rate of sixteen pounds for every one hundred pounds of the Duty on Spirits paid by such Distiller; and every Distiller making use of any such Still containing five hundred gallons, and not containing one thousand gallons, shall be allowed a Bounty after the rate of eight pounds for every one hundred pounds of the Duty on Spirits paid by such Distiller.

Mr. I.eyre Her reported. That the Managers had pret Conference the Lords at the Conference; which was managed on the ^'reported, part of the Lords by the Duke of N; and that the Conference was to acquaint this House,

That the Lords, always dertrous that a good intelligence and right unrterstanding rtiould be maintained betwixt the two Houses; and, persuaded that nothing can tend more effectually thereunto than a dole adherence to the antient and regular methods of proceeding between the two Houses, have desired this Conference upon the subject matter of the Metlage sent by the House of Commons, for leave for the Lord Viscount to attend the Select Committee of that House, in order to be examined, to communicate to the House of Commons;

That it appears undeniably, by an uniform series of precedents down to the present time, that the course adopted by the Lords, respvfting the giving leave to the Members of their Lordships’ House to go down to the House of Commons, has been to permit the Members of their Lordships’ House, on their own request, to defend themselves in the House of Commons, if they think fit, on any points, on which that House has not previously passed any accusatory or criminating Resolutions against them; and also, to permit the Members of their Lordships’ House, on the request of the House of Commons, to give evidence, if they think fit, before that House, or any Committee thereof, on those points only on which 110 matter of accusation or charge is at that time in any manner depending against them before that House, whether the same shall then have been resolved by the House of Commons or not.

That the Lords had also directed them to acquaint the House of Commons, That their Lordships, relying with the most perfect confidence that the House of Commons are at all times as desirous to preserve the Privileges of the Lords as to maintain their own, have given leave to the I>ord Viscount Melville (who had also previously made it his own unqualified request) to go down to the Select Committee of the House of Commons, to whom the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry (respecting the Office of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy) is referred, to enquire into the application of any Monies issued to the Treasurer of the Navy for Naval Services, to purposes not Naval, and whether any and what representations were made to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, or the Chancellor of the Exchequer, respecting the withdrawing from the Bank any sums of Money so issued since the parting of the Act of 25 Geo. III. c. 31.; and also, into the Proceedings had for the recovery of the Debt due to the Crown by the late Adam Jcllicoe;in order to be examined at that Committee, if lie shall so think fit; his Lordship, lievertheless, conforming himself in all respects to the course directed to be communicated to the Commons as above.

That the detection of Men, who are now found to have been, for a series of years, in the constant habits of misapplying the Public Money, will warn the House not to rely too much upon the specious professions of their colleagues for the punishment of offences, through which they have themselves derived a corrupt support to their own power; and that the Petitioners trust, rather, the period is at length come, at which the Representatives of the People, returning to the examples and the maxims of former times, will shew themselves determined to pursue hereafter a system of vigilance and jealously, instead of reposing an implicit and indiferimi-nate confidence in the Advisers of the Crown.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Petition from A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of York, rcibecting the conv^ne^> pursuant to request, by the Right honourable Tenth Report the Lord Mayor, and assembled in the Guildhall of the on Naval said City on Monday the 13th day of May 1805, was q,uiry» presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the . Petitioners feel the deepelt gratitude to the House for its patriotic Votes of the 8th and ioth days of April lait, founded on the Tenth Report of the Commi (honors of Naval Enquiry; the one declaring Lord \ i (count Melville to be guilty of a gross violation of the Laws, and a high breach of his Public Duty; and the other ordering inch Resolution to be laid at the foot of the Throne, the whole House attending; the Petitioners are convinced that no act of any branch of the Legiftature has ever been received with more satisfaction by the People of this Country than the said Votes; and they are further convinced that nothing can possibly be a greater disappointment to the People, than any remission in the House of the vigorous and necessary efforts with which they have thus commenced the career of Public Justice; and that the faithful and dignified discharge of the powers vested in the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, their indefatigable indullry, their resolute perseverance, their unexampled fortitude, and their incorruptible integrity, have demanded and have obtained the admiration and applause of the whole Nation; and a continuance at lead, if not

an extension of the powers vested in them, and also a general enquiry into the conduct of every other Depart* ment of Finance, are essentially requisite to the prosperity of the British Empire; and the Petitioners anxiously request of the House, that whenever hereafter this subject may come before them, they will fix their attention on the obstructions to full enquiry, so evidently pointed out in the said Tenth Report of the Naval Commissioners; and they intreat the House that they will, in the institu-tion of other enquiries into the Public Expenditure, take especial care that the power they shall delegate be equal to its object, both as referring to the facility of enquiry and to the integrity of those to whom enquiry shall be committed; for the Petitioners submit to the House whether any thing short thereof will not be deemed illulive and unavailing, and rather contribute to the continuation than the prevention of future abuse and peculation: And that, on all these matters, the Petitioners re-quest the House, steadily to pursue what they have with so much honour begun, and not to relax their efforts, till Guilt , wherever it exists, shall be pursued to detection, and till exemplary and deserved punishment shall have overtaken, as well those who have themselves been fraudulent, as those who have connived at fraud.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

petition from A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders ‘ of the County of Norfo'k,convened by the High Sheriff Tenth Report the said County, at the Castle at Norwich, in the Shire-on Naval house there, on Tuesday the 14th day of May 1805, was En<lulry' presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners beg leave to express their gratitude to the House, for the steps which they have already taken towards the detection and punishment of those servants of the Crown, wrho have defied the Laws, broken their trull, and applied enormous sums of the Public Money to their own corrupt purposes of emolument and power; and that, in the name of a loyal and suffering People, the Petitioners implore the House not to relax in their exertions; they intreat them to consider, how patiently the Petitioners have seen Millions added to Millions of the National Debt, the rapid advance in every article of consumption, their burthens encreasing, and their means of bearing them diminiffiing, in the just hope that. While engaged in extensive wars, what they contributed with | cheerfulness would be applied with fidelity, and as the

! Law expressly directed; and that, faithful to Their first

duties, the House. have recorded, by the Resolutions of the 8th and 10th of April, that the People of England have been grossly wronged by Lord Melville; and the Petitioners humbly represent to the House, the necessity of effectually protecting the Nation against future depre-. dations: And therefore praying the House, First, to in-veftigate and fist to the bottom the remaining charges of 1 abuse in the application of the Public Money, cont ained

in the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry: Secondly, to examine minutely into the nature of those irregularities brought to light in the Eleventh Report of the said Commissioners, and likewise whatever may appear culpable or suspicious in any of their future Reports: Thirdly, to institute immediate and rigorous enquiries into the Expenditure of every other Department of Executive Government; and that in performing these acts of necessary and expefled justice, the Petitioners are persuaded, that the House w ill take no other guides than its own wisdom and refe>lution; and that, 1 W’amed by the example of detected guilt, and awake to

the frauds which have been practised upon their own facility, as well as upon the Public purse, the House will perceive the necessity of resorting to those principles, Which prevailed in the better days of our Constitution, and of acting upon a lyftem of vigilance and jealously, in preference to one of blind and implicit confidence in Ministers.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lio Upon the Table.

A Petition of the House of Keys, of the Isle And also, the Duke of

A Petition of several Inhabitants and Proprietors of Atholi: Estates within the Isle of Man; House of

Were severally presented to the House, and read; ey*' setting forth. That the People of Man not being *fletant* represented in Parliament, the Petitioners hope, of Man. that when a measure affecting them and their posterity is introduced into the House, they may be deemed peculiarly entitled to its protection; and that the centrical position of the Isle, and the comparatively low rate of Duties paid to the feudal Lord, made the Isle the place of deposit for contraband goods for the purpose of clandestine conveyance to the neighbouring coasts— . the privilege of subordinate sovereignty being thus abused, by which the feudal Lord benefited equally with the Trader, the necessity of re-ac-qulring it became obvious; and the Treasury Was therefore authorized, in the year 1726, to purchase the Isle from the then Proprietors: In the year 1735 the Atholi family became possessed of the Isle; and from that time it would feefn that the Proprietors expected to fell, until the year 17 65,when the bargain was concluded between the Treasury and the then Duke and Duchess of Atholi, for JJ. 70,000, the sum asked by the Noble Proprietors; and that this bargain received the function of Parliament; and besides the price required, His Majesty was pleased, as an act of gracious bounty* to bestow on the Duke and Duchess a pension of £. 2,000. a year upon the Irish Establishment; and that the late Duke of Atholi surviving this sale about nine years, made no complaint of inadequacy of price; and the prefetit Noble Petitioner, for sixteen years after the death of the late Duke, although the House have witnessed other measures on his part designfed to act’efft the Isle, yet no difedvery appears to have been made of this alledged inadequacy; and that in the year 1790 a Bill, affirming the possibility of this inadequacy, was, indeed, laid before the House, but it was afterwards withdrawn; and that in the year 1801 application was made to His Majesty for further compensation, which was referred to the Privy Council, and by them to the then Attorney and Solicitor General, whose report, and that founded on ex parte evidence, the Petitioners have reason to believe was against this claim; the Petitioners, then, viewing this compact between parties, in stations so ele-* vated, thus deliberately and advisedly made, thus solemnly ratified, thus long acquiesced in, thus confirmed by the acceptance of additional Royal Bounty, which has already doubled the price demanded, do most humbly enquire, if such a compact, forty years after its completion, be suffered to be questioned, what then is sacred and binding between man and man ? and that the Revenue of the Island has been greatly increased within these few years, by additional Duties laid on Importations by the tlritish Parliament at the recommendation of the Duke of Atholi, and with, a view, as it now appears, to the present appli* cation. If this increased Revenue is to be made subject to a Rent-charge payable to his Grace, the Petitioners cannot consider these additional Duties in any other light than a direct Tax on the People for his Grace’s private advantage: And therefore praying. That they may be heard by their counsel, against the imposing on the Revenue of the Isle of Man any hereditary Rent-charge or other burthen in favour of the Duke of Atholi.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered , to lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners have received the Votes of the House, of the 8th and 10th days of April lad, with a satisfaction as great as have been their afio-nishment, indignation, and sorrow, at the gross and flagrant system of negligence and peculation which has been disclosed by the commissioners of Naval Enquiry; and, with a gratitude proportioned to the extensive security and important national advantages thence to be expedited, the Petitioners beg leave to date their firm conviction, that nothing can so much contribute to the happiness of the People, the fuceefs of the conted in which the Nation is engaged, and the ultimate tvell being of the Country, as a fydem of economy planned with prudence, adhered to with firnmefs, and conducted, in its details, with diligence, caution, and integrity; impressed as they are with this conviction, the Petitioners entreat the House to accept their grateful thanks for the enquiries which it has already indituted: To the further prosecution of the object above-mentioned, they earnefily pray the attention of the House, and beseech them to pursue with efiect, that which they have begun with so much honour, and that they will institute and persevere in a general fydem*of Enquiry which flia.ll be eo-extensive with the Abuses which may exist in the expenditure of the Public Money.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners unite with their Constituents Tenth Report at large, in thanking the House for their Resolutions of the 8th and 10th of April, founded on the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry: By the first of those Resolutions the House vindicated the character of their Country', by censuring a M miller proved to have been guilty of a gross violation of Law, and a flagrant breach of Duty; by the second, the House laid before the Sovereign, the sense of His People, and enabled Him, by a ready compliance with their wishes, to endear 1 lim-self more than <ever to their loyal and act’eftionate hearts; and the Petitioners implore the House, ftend'dy to per-severe in detecting all other abufos which are poiiVcd at, as well in the Tenth as in the Eleventh Report of the said Commissioners; attentively' to investigate all irregularities wdiich may be brought to light by any of their succeeding Reports; impartially, minutely, and refolntely to examine into the Public Expenditure in all the other branches of Administration, and to inflict exemplary puniliiment on all who shall be found guilty of, or in anywise aiding, abetting, or conniving at (molar frauds and depredations: And that the Petitioners are thoroughly persuaded that it is needless for them to urge any f ein motive to the House, in order to induce them to a3opt suchmeasures: They rely upon the knowledge the House have of their duties, and upon their sympathy and fellow feeling with their constituents, who, during a long, a difficult, and trying period of war, in times of severe hardships and scarcity, have chearfully submitted to the heavielt burthens, that what they granted liberally should be applied honestly, was the least the Petitioners could hope, from men, whose conscientiousness and bounden duty enjoined a faithful discharge of the great trull reposed in them; disappointed of this hope, and finding on the contrary that a Minister, filling many great and lucrative offices, high in the confidence of his Sovereign, one of the foremoll in his pretended efforts to reform abuses, has been at length himself de-tested in conniving for a series of years at the foulest peculation: The Petitioners now approach the House with their claims to protection and just ice; and they trull, therefore, that in profeculing the enquiries necessary' for these ends, the House will proceed in that spirit of firmness and integrity which dictated the Resolutions of the 8th and 10th of April; and that they will not , trull this great cause out of their own hands, nor again suffer themselves to be deceived by the plausible promises of men, who openly violate the taws of the Legislat ure, and hold in defiance and contempt the wholesome guards they enact against the possible malversations of oflice; and that the Petitioners also trust that the example of the pall, will aft upon the House as a warning for the future; that they will fee and acknowledge thejuft value of those principles on which our Ancestors established the power and authority of the House of Commons; that the House w ill feel their office to be that of controid over the servants of the Crown; and that jealously and vigilance, instead of confidence and compliance, are their true and distinguishing characteristics: To this fyf-tem, the Petitioners humbly hope that the House will direct their immediate and unvarying attention, as the system by which the Country may bell be defended, and as the only one under which the Constitution can be safe.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and County Petition fro of the Town of Southampton, was presented to the House, Soiltll:n'n"tM. and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners would feel Tenth themselves criminally indifferent were they not to ex- on. Naval £». press their gratitude for the Votes of the House on the <luiry'

8th and iotli days of April last, which declared Lord Viscount Melville guilty of a gross violation of the Law, and a high Breach of Duty, Votes which have diflufed joy and confidence throughout every part of the United Kingdom; and that, among the various Irregularities mid Abuses which have been detected and exposed by the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, none has created more jealously and alarm in the breads of the Petitioners, than the application of Monies, appropriated by the Legislature for the uses of the Navy, to other purposes, a practice replete with danger to the Constitution and to the liberty of this Country; and that the detection of such malversations in one Department of the State, induces apprehensions that others may not be more faithfully and honellly administered: And the Petitioners, therefore, think it their duty to implore the National Representatives, That their intention, already manifested, of instituting Enquiries into every branch of the Public Expenditure, may be speedily carried into effect, a mea-fiire calculated to compose the Public Mind, to confirm the confidence, and to secure the unanimity and energy, of the People.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, Petition from of the County of Northumberland, held at Morpeth on the 24th of May 1805, was presented to the House, and ing the Tenth read; setting forth, That the Petitioners beg leave to congratulate the House, on the result of the difeuflions qUiry. that have taken place in the House, respecting the gross peculation and misapplieation of the Public Money, in open defiance of the Law, that have been detected by the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry; and they pray the House to persevere in that virtuous line of conduct, which on that important occasion difi’used such general satisfaClion throughout the Country; and they intreat the House not only to continue their enquiries into the abuses in the department of the Navy, but to extend the fame into every branch of the Public Expenditure, and to adopt a solid and permanent system of Economy, well convinced that rigid frugality alone can enable this Country to support the present enormous weight of public burthens, and fiiftain the awful contest in which we are engaged: And the Petitioners implore the House to punifit guilt, however protected or exalted, and to refeue from peculation and plunder a loyal People, who have ever willingly contributed to the real exigences of the State, and who never complain but wdien their generous temper is imposed upon, and thus will the Commons of the United Kingdom confirm the confidence of the People, and instil into the hearts of all good men, a warm and Heady attachment to the British Confutation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Charles Price reported from the Committee, to London whom the Petition of the Wardens and Assistants of the ‘ Fellowship of Carmen, of the City of London, was refer- reported*, red; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,—An Act of Common Council, made in the year 1665, was produced to Your Committee; whereby it appeared, that the President and Governor of CkrijTs at

London, were entrusted with the Rule and Government of the Cars, Carts, Carroons, Carters and Carmen, and other Persons; and by the said Act the number of Carts allowed to wurk for Hire within the said City and Liberties, were limited to Four hundred and twenty, and the respective Owners thereof were directed to pay the sum of Seventeen shillings and four-pence per annum, for the exclusive privilege of working such Carts for Hire within the said City and Liberties, to the President and Governors of the said Hospital.—Then an Act of Parliament, made in the 40th year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts,

« and other Works, for the greater accommodation and security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within " the Port of London," was read; by which, certain Powers and Authorities were given, for the making of satisfaction and compensation for the loss and damage that the several Free Carmen of the City of London might sustain, by means of the trade or business carried on from the present legal Quays, and from the other Quays and Wharfs called Public Foreign Sufferance Wharfs, being diverted :—And Mr. Thomas be-

ing examined, said. That the Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, directed by the said Act to he. made, are nearly completed; and that the Trade and Business from the old Quays to the new Docks, is now diverted; by which the Petitioners (who have spent the greatest part of their lives in the business of Carmen) are very much injured; and that, unless some immediate relief is granted to them, it will tend to the utter ruin of their Families.—And the Witness further said. That the powers and authorities of the last mentioned Act, which directs compensations to be made to the Carmen for their Losses, are totally insufficient for enabling them at this time t® bring such proofs of the loss and damage sustained, as is by the said Act directed to be eompenfated forinaf-much that such compensation is not to be fixed and settled till after the expiration of three years from the q present

Petition from A Petition of the Governors and Committee of the fcavaiAfylura. Naval Asylum, whofb Names are thereunto subscribed, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Mali, . 1805.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; felting forth. That the Petitioners have observed and deplored, that, in this Nation, no provision whatever was made for the Orphans of those brave Men, whose lives have been devoted on board of His Majesty’s Royal Navy to the defence of His Empire, and therefore undertook to form an Asylum for the reception of- such Orphans, aided by the munificence of the Royal Family, and by the liberality of the Public, where to not only the brave Defenders of their Country may look for the future support and protection of their Orphans, but wherein Orphans of like description are now’ reared by the Petitioners for the service of their King and Country; and that, in order to carry their objects into full efteft, the Petitioners do humbly petition Parliament for Public . Aid; and, in conformity with their former exertions, they trull, that by their application of any Grant now made to them, the present liberality of Government will prove fnture economy to the Nation; and that, with respect to the sum requisite for the purchase of Ground and the erection of Buildings for the Asylum, the Committee repose on the Geuerofity of Parliament, while they beg leave to point out tw’o precedents; the one is a Grant, during the space of fifteen years, from 1756 101771 inclusive, of <£. 33,000. per annum, on an average* to the Foundling Hospital; the other is a Grant, last year, of £. 32,400. after preceding annual Grants to a much larger amount, to the Military Asylum at Chelsea: And < the Petitioners hope also, that Parliament will, as in the case of the Foundling Hospital, be pleased to render the Asylum and its limits free from all Parliamentary and parochial Dues and Rates, except those already imposed thereon, and from all parochial Jurisdiction whatever, civil and ecclesiastical.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir John Borlafe Warren, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, &c.: And they are to meet Tommorrow Morning, at nine of the clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for persons, papers, and records.

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Uffier of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Petition from Cornwall, re (petting the Tenth Report on Naval Enquiry.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the County of Conin'nil, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Abuses in the Expenditure of the Public Money, which have been lately brought to light by the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry,'have filled the minds of the Petitioners

with alarm and indignation, and they call upon the

House for the fpoedy remedy of such Abuses, and for the exemplary pun ithment of the offenders; and that Abuses in the Expenditure of the Public Money (at all times matter of grievance) are peculiarly felt at this time, when so great a weight of Taxation falls upon all ranks of People; and that a Defence has been attempted, of the guilt of the offenders, by the assertion that no actual mif-chief has been sustained by these gross breaches of trull and offences against Law, as if the direct violation of a Statute were not a high Crime and Misdemeanor, without the aggravation, that the violation, of which the Petitioners complain, was fvhematic, and committed by a confidential Servant of the Crown, himself the framer of the Act which he has broken, and enjoying an increased salary under that very Act, in full satisfaction of all wages and fees, and other profits and emoluments theretofore enjoyed hv former Treasurers; and that such a Defence naturally increases the fear, that Peculation in the Expenditure of the Public Money is not confined to the Naval Department; and that the Petitioners have long submitted to severe privations, in the perfualion that they were necessary to the welfare and safety of the Country, and they claim, as theiif right, that the Money which is liberally granted shall be legally applied: And that the Petitioners, look with a confident hope to the House, after their Votes of the 8th and ioth days of April left, that, as Constitutional Guardians of their Liberty and Property, they will neither be deterred nor diverted from a full and impartial enquiry into all Abuses, in whatever department they may exilt; and that the enquiry now begun will not cease, until all Abuses in every Public Board be remedied, finee so only will the minds of the Petitioners be satisfied, the credit of the Government he upheld, anti that free Constitution be preferred inviolate, wdiieh is the sacred birthright of Lnglijhmen; and that Lord Viscount Melville, having been declared guilty of a high misdemeanour, by the Vote of the House of the 8th of April, a Civil Action is inadequate to the end proposed, and in itself incapable of faljsfying the demands of Public Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 33d year of his late Majesty King George the Second, to continue an Act, made in the 12th year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the better encouragement of the making of Sail Cloth in Great Britain, which was to continue in force until the 29th day of September 1767, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by three Acts, made in the 8th, 14th, and 22d years of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 29th day of September 1788, and from thence to the end of the then Vol. 60.

next Session of Parliament; and by an Act, made in the 29th year of His present Majesty, was amended and further continued until the 29th day of September 1795, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; and by twro other Acts, made in the 36th and in the 39th and 40th years of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 29th day of September 1S04, from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 9th year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the further encouraging and regulating the Manufacture of British Sail Cloth, and for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on Foreign Sail Cloth imported into this Kingdom, which \ftis to continue in force from the 24th day of June 1736, for the term of five years, and from thence to the encl of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the 13 th, 24 th, and 31ft years of his said Majesty’s reign, and the 4th, 12th, 18th, and 26th years of His present Majesty’s reign, was further continued until the 29th day of September 1792, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; and by another Act, made in the 33d year of' His present Majesty, was amended and further continued until the 29th day of September 1795, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; and which was, by two other Acts, made in the 36th and in the 39th and 40th years of His present Majesty, further continued until the 29th day of September 1804* and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament •, is near expiring, and fit to be made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Commi ttee. That an Act, made in the 19th year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on Foreign-made Sail Cloth imported into this Kingdom, and for charging all Foreign-made Sails with a Duty; and for explaining a doubt concerning Ships being obliged, at their first setting out to Sea, to be furnished with one complete set of Sails, made of British Sail Cloth, which was to continue in force from the 24th: day of June 1746, for the term of seven years, and from, thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the 26th and 32d years of his said late Majesty, and of the 6th, 14th, 22d, 29th, 36th, and 39th and 40th years of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 29th day of September 1804, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be made perpetual; with Amendments.

A Petition of several Ship Owners of North and South Shields and neighbourhood, was presented to the House, to and read; setting forth. That the greatest quantity of Coal* Shipping employed in the Coal Trade from the River c Tyne to London belongs to the Towns above-mentioned; Navigation* and that the Petitioners, from the depressed state of the

Shipping

45 Geo. IIL 7° J'unit.353

Shipping interest in general, have lately memorialized the Lords of the Committee of Privy Council for Trade, respecting the too liberal employment given of late to Foreigners, to the prejudice of the Petitioners and others* who have embarked their Capitals in Shipping; but they are not less alarmed by perceiving an intention to introduce Coals into the Metropolis by means of Inland Navigation, a measure fraught with the greatest evils: And therefore praying, That the House will not pass into a Law any Bill that may be brought in for introducing Coals into the Capital by means of Inland Navigation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

dangerous state, the wall on the north side being 4 feet under ground; that the Church will accomodate with feat room about 350 people; that he did not know the number of the Inhabitants, as he did not live in the Parish; that he believed there were near 200 houses in the Parish; that the Church was 60 feet long besides the belfry, and 25 feet wide; that he believed the Church would not admit of repair, for if the roof was taken off the walls would fall out, being ten inches out of the perpendicular, and parted in several places; that it would be almost impossible to repair it, and that he would not undertake to do it for £. 500 as it ought to be done; that it was not in a state to admit of enlargement; and believed it could not be so enlarged as to accommodate the inhabitants who would go to Church; that if it was large enough, which it is not, for the Inhabitants, it would be as cheap to rebuild it, as to repair it, under all the circumstances, if the advantage of the Parish was considered; that the' Church has been shut up about 4 years; that the Tower wanted much repair; that the aisles of the Church were of various widths; the north aide being in some parts 3 feet wide, and in other parts only 2 feet; that the pews were irregular and ruinous; that the principal aisle was 5 feet wide at one end and 3 feet at the other; and that no pews could be added for the accommodation of the Inhabitants, in the body of the Church.

Sir, Wimbledon, nth June 1805.

Having observed, in the Votes of the House of Commons, that a Committee has been appointed to consider of the Tenth Report of the Commissioners of Naval and having obtained a copy of a Report which that Committee has submitted to the House of Commons; I take the liberty of requesting that the House will allow me to be admitted, and heard, on the subject of those Reports.

I hgwe the honour to be. Sir,

Re faked, That Lord Viscount Melville be admitted in, and heard.

Whereupon a Chair was set by the Serjeant a little within the Bar, on the left hand the coming in.

And the Serjeant had directions to go with the Mace, and acquaint Lord Viscount Melville, that he might come in.

And the doors being opened, and the Bar down, his Lordship came in uncovered, making his obeifances in the padage and at the Bar, which was then lifted up, and came up to the Chair prepared for him; and Mr. Speaker acquainted his Lordship, that he might, if he pleased, repose himself in the Chair.

Whereupon his Lordfiiip fat down in the Chair, and was covered; and, after a little space, arose lip again, find, being uncovered, and Handing behind the Chair, spoke to the House, addressing himself to Mr. Speaker.

And having ended his speech, withdrew uncovered; making his obeifances at the Bar, and in the passage, in like manner as at his entrance.

and the full Rates and Duties as soon as the Dock and I>ock should be finished and completed, so as to admit a Ship or Vessel to be moored therein :—That the one h.ili of the Dock Duties, at present payable and received, amounted in the first year to *£.1,933- 1. 10. in the second year to *£.2,091. 14. 11. in the third year to j£.2,236. 3. 11. and so far as the fourth year has gone they are (fill en-creasing, and the fame will increase very considerably as soon as the Dock shall be finished:—Tliatbefides Ihefe Funds the annual produce of the grounds or areas belonging to the Community of the City of Edinburgh is by the said recited Act of the 39th year of the reign of His present Majesty, directed to be applied in aid of the Funds for completing the said Docks and other Works, and that if the first Dock and Lock were completed, the Petitioners will be entitled to levy the fall Rates and Duties by the said Act of the 39th year of His present Majesty granted and made payable; but to eftect this, will require an additional sum of between^. 20,000, and £.30,000.; and that upon the completion of such Dock and Lock, the produce of the Funds will be sufficient not only to pay the interest of the Sums already borrowed and to be borrowed for completing the said Dock and Lock, but to raise a Sinking Fund for paying off the principal Sums so borrowed and to be borrowed; it would disablo them from fulfilling tlmir Contra ft s for quarrying and furuishing Stones and other materials; and it would occasion a demand from their Creditors for paying oil the principal Sums borrowed as well as the interest thereof, which the Petitioners would be unable to satisfy:—And that, prior to the Union between England and Scotland, a Stock or Fund was provided to antwer the Salaries of the Judges of the Court of Session, by different grants from the Scotch Parliament, amounting to ,£. 23,833. which, upon the Salaries receiving an adequate augmentation, to be paid in future by the Crown, was directed by an Act of the 26th year of the reign of His present Majesty, to be paid into the Receiver General of His Majesty’s Land Rents and Casualties in Scotland, for behoof of the Public; that the above Sum was accordingly paid to the then Receiver General, and at his death in 1795 remained still unapplied, and his Representatives being unable to pay the Money, an heritable security was granted to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury for £. 21,000 of the above sum, payable to their Lordships for behoof of I Iis Majesty; Thomas Hope, Esquire.—Have you examined the

Collection of feulptuied Marbles, Vases, and Terra Cottas, lately in the possession of Charles Esquire,

so as to be able to Hate to the Committee, your opinion of the value of that Collection ? I have not examined it so as to have a decided opinion of its value.—Do you believe that Collection to be of the value of 20,000. or upwards? I think it is fully worth that sum, exclusive of the Etruscan and Ala ha ster Vases, and of the Bronze Statues of Apollo and Hercules; which Statues however, I consider of very high value.—Do you believe the possession of that Collet ion, on the part of the Public, if made properly accessibleto Artists and the Public, would be materially beneficial to the cultivation of the Fine Arts in this Country ? I believe it would be highly beneficial to the cultivation of the Fine Arts. [Withdrew.

Joseph Nollekens, F.squire.—Have you examined the

Collection of sculptured Marbles, Vases, and Terra Cottas, lately in the possession of Charles Townley, Esquire, so as to be able to state to the Committee your opinion of the value of that Collection ? I am perfectly acquainted with that Collect ion, having known it from the beginning, which is 37 years: I a (Tided in procuring some of the articles.—Do you believe that Collection to be of the value of £. 20,000. or upwards, exclusive of the Etruscan and Alabafler Vases and the Bronzes? I do; more than that film; but I think the Bronze Statues of Apollo and Hercules, and particularly the latter, of very high value.—Do you think the Collodion worth considerably more than £.20,000. ? I should think it Worth £. 30,000. honestly.—Do you believe that the possession of that Collection on the part of the Public, if made properly accessible to Artists and the Public, would be materially beneficial to the cultivation of the Fine Arts in this Country ? Undoubtedly. [Withdrew.

John Fhrman, Esquire.—Have you examined the Collection of sculptured Marbles, Vases, and Terra Cottas, lately in the possession of Charles Esquire,

so as to be able to state to the Committee your opinion of thp value of that Collection ? I am wrel! acquainted with the Collection, and have paid a great deal of attention to it as a Sculptor, and have a general irba of the value.—Do you believe that Collection to be of the value of ,£.20,000. or upwards, exclusive of the Etruscan and

Alabaster Vases, and of the two Bronze Statues of Apollo and Hercules? Indeed I do think it richly worth that sum to the Country; but I think the Bronze Statues of Apollo and Hercules of very high value.—Do you believe that the possession of that Collection on the part of the Public, if made properly accessible to Artists and the Public, would be materially beneficial to the cultivation of the Fine Arts in this Country? I am certain of it.— You have stated, that you have a general opinion of the value of this Collection; state the principles upon which you entertain such opinion ? I first consider the labour as works of excellent Sculpture: I next consider their value from the relative and critical light they are capable of throwing upon that Art; and, lastly, their great value towards forming a School for the study of Sculpture in this Country; and on thele accounts it appears to me they would be well worth the sum above-mentioned in any Country enlightened in the Arts.—Is it your opinion that this Collection, if now brought to sale, either together or separately, would produce the sum of ^C.20,000 ? I really cannot positively afiert, fovnuch would depend upon a variety of eircurnstances; but I think I may add, that if the peHons of taste, who are qualified to appreciate this Collection, have sufficient places for the articles, I have no doubt but they would produce 20,000. Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presentod the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

HIS Majesty thinks proper to acquaint the House of Commons, That the Communications which have taken place, and are still depending, between His Majesty and feme of the Powers of the Continent, have not yet been brought to such a point, as to enable His Majesty to lay the resultof them before the House; or to enter into any farther explanation with the French Government, con-' fiftently with the sentiments exp re fled by His Majesty at the opening of the present Session :—But His Majesty conceives that it may be of essential importance, that He should have it in His power to avail Ilimself of any favourable conjuncture, for giving el left to such a concert with other Powers, as may aflord the bell means of refilling the inordinate ambition of France, and may be most likely to lead to a terminat ion of the present contest, on grounds confident with the permanent safety and interests of His Majesty’s Dominions, and the security and independence of Europe. His Majesty therefore recommends it to the House of Commons, to consider of making provision for enabling His Majesty to take such measures, and enter into such engagements, as the exigencies of aft airs may require.

G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s said most gracious Message be referred to the consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to Mis Majesty,

The Lord Glenbervie reported from the Committee of Secrecy, to whom so much of the Eleventh Report of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry, as relates to the advance of One hundred thousand pounds for Secret Naval Services, was referred; and who were empowered to report their opinion and observations thereupon, to the House; That the Committee bad considered the mat-

unit.

ter to them referred; and, had come to a Resolution thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the lame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have taken into their consideration, the subject referred to them; and having examined various persons, and called for and perused certain Letters and other Documents relative thereto, they have agreed on the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinionof this Committee, That the said^C. 100,000. was advanced for an object, to which the Supplies granted for Naval Services were applicable; that the Application thereof to that object, was a measure in which the interests and honour of this Country were concerned; that it was issued determined by the Comptroller of the Navy, und*T Orders from the Lords of the Treasury, with the knowledge and authority of the First Lord of the Admiralty, and in the fitted mode for answering the end proposed; that the Clearing Bill for <£\ 97,000. part of the said sum of £. 100,000. was granted on just and proper grounds; that the circumstances of the Application of the money, were of such a nature, that a disciofure of them, either at the period when they took place, or at any time since, would have been attended with public inconvenience; that it must be matter of regret, if any thing has occurred, in the mean time, which may have tended, in any degree, to'such a disciofure; and that the reasons against such disciofure still com’ ae, and render it the duty of the Committee to abstain from entering into any farther particulars on the subject.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed, for the Members of the House.

'of respeHaWe character, property, and unimpeached loyalty, who, hearing that the Petitioner was severely in lifposed, called to visit him, was, in consequence of his visit, arrested and detained in custody during the period of sixteen days; and that, some time after the committal of the Petitioner, he received from the Right honourable William Wickham, then principal Secretary Vol. 60.

to his Excellency the Earl of Lord Lieute-

nant of Ireland, a tender of liberation, provided he w'ould go to England, and remain there at large; and that the Petitioner, conscious of the most perfect innocence, and, considering that acquiescence in such a proposal w'ould imply guilt, re Ip ect fully declined it, at the same time tendering to Mr. Wickham the moll ample satisfaction that an unreserved examination upon oath could aliord, and intreating a speedy trial; and that the Petitioner has remained ever since in elofe custody, now for twenty months, sustaining all the rigours of a Military Prevot, and, added to them, the unw holesome dampness of a new, undried, and unfinished edifice, to the material injury of his health; and that the creditors of the Petitioner, induced by the coneluiions they drew of his danger and guilt from so rigorous an imprisonment, and his total seclusion, by order of the General, from them and all his friends, came down upon him at once with their demands, to satisfy which, lie relinquithed to them his moderate income, and has ever since been confined for subsistence to the mere Jail allowance; and that the Petitioner is now very infirm, and of the age of fifty-two }rears, thus of-prelfed, untried, and unheard: And therefore praying. That the House w ould be pleased to take his case into its consideration, and grant him such redress for the heavy calamity he has sustained in the loss of liberty and time, of health, reputation, and pecuniary credit, as to its judgment and benevolence may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Innkeepers, Publicans, and Victual- petition of lers, of the Town and Borough of , in the innhoUicnof

County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; ,mon* setting forth. That the Petitioners are burthened with heavy expences, not only in common with their brethren, in consequence of the small allowance of an halfpenny a day for the lodging, use of kitchen and other utensils, vinegar, salt, and firing,* found for each Soldier quartered on them, but from their residence in an intermediate Town between Exeter and Plymouth; and that, from the numbers often quartered on them, more than they can accommodate, they are compelled to expend one flailing weekly for each Soldier placed out by them in private lodgings, exclusive of the halfpence so allowed the Petitioners, which they usually give to such Soldiers to induce them to consent to be removed :• And therefore praying for such relief as to the House may seem meet Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

and that the Petitioners rely, with confidence, on the continued and persevering exertions of the House, for the further detection and punishment of offences of so dangerous a nature; but at the same time feel it to be a duty which they owe to themselves, and to their posterity, to express to their Representatives, the natural and constitutional guardians of the purse of the People, their just sentiments of indignation, and their earned duplications for full and ample redress; and that the Petitioners respectfully represent to the House, the great and increasvng neeeffily for its rigid and vigilant attention to the due application of Public Money, to the Services to which it shall be appropriated by the wisdom of Parliament; the practices which have of late prevailed tending nianifellly not only to the encouragement of fraud and peculation, but to the fub-veriion of the fundamental principles of the Conditution: And therefore praying the House, to persevere in the enquiries so happily begun; b bring all Delinquents to condign and exemplary punishment; to exert the ancient and indubitable privilege of the House, of watching and controlling the exercise of every branch of the Royal Prerogative; for the exelufion from His Majesty’s Councils of every person w ho has committed, countenanced, or favoured the abuses and evil practices so judly complained of; and toeflabli/h in every department that wife, liberal, and comprehensive fyfiem of economy, which the exigencies of the times, and the circumstances of the arduous con tell in which the Country isengaged, require, and which is due equally to the intereds ami to the feelings of a People, who have submitted, with exemplary fortitude, to unparallelled sacrifices and burthens.

Your Committee having examined the present state of the new Building, and considering the propriety of providing a suitable place for the reception of Mr. Tottfnley'i Collection of Antique Sculpture, as soon as possible,~ib as not to lose the present feaforu have endeavoured to accommodate the Plan, already proceeded in, to that purpose, rather than to adopt any plan entirely new:—

Your Committee have therelore determined; that an Enlargement is necessary in the connecting Galleries and the two Tribunes; and they have taken upon themselves to recommend that alteration; though they are sorry to find it will be attended with some additional Expence; a rough calculation of which is contained in the Evidence of the Architect. On the other hand, they have re^ trenched somewhat from the expence of another part of the intended Building, which it appeared to them might be omitted without disadvantage.

George Sanders, Esquire, called in, and examined.—

What will be the increased expence of widening the Galleries, and the two Tribunes, to contain Statues as proposed ? I think it will amount to about .£. 2,500.; to which must be added the expence of the Foundation of that part of the Building which is to be altered.—What will be the saving in omitting the blank Colonade ? That has been considered in the foregoing Estimate, and allowed for, amounting to £. 700.

Articles exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the name of them (elves and of all the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and,

against Henry Lord Viscount Melville-, in maintenance of their Impeachment against him, for High Crimes and Mifikmeanors.

Whereas the Office of Treasurer of I Iis Majesty’s Navy is an Office of high Trust and Confidence; in the faithful and uncorrupt execution whereof, the Subjects of this Kingdom are moil deeply interested: And whereas the ancient Confutation of the said Office of Treasurer of the Navy, and of other Offices concerned in the receipt, disbursement, and controul of the Public Money, having been found to be highly inexpedient in conference of the increased expenditure of the Country, did become the subjoCt of frequent long and serious deliberation in Parliament: And whereas by an Act of, Parliament made and passed in the 20th year of the reign of His present Majesty, and by several subsequent Acts of Parliament, for appointing and enabling Commissioners to examine, take, and ltate, the Public Accounts of this Kingdom, and for other purposes therein mentioned, certain Commissioners were constituted and appointed for examining, taking, and dating the Accounts therein particularly mentioned, and also for examining and fluting in what manner, and at what times, the receipts, ifl'ues, and expenditures, of the Public Monies Vol. 60.

were accounted for; and for considering of and reporting determined by what means and methods the Public Accounts might in future be patted, and the Accomptants compelled to pay the balances or monies due from them in a more expeditious, more effc6tual, and less expensive manner: And whereas the said Commissioners did inquire into and report upon the Public Accounts by the said Acts referred to their examination, and did discover and point out various abuses in many of the Public Offices entrufied with the receipt and expenditure of Public Money, and in particular in the Office of the Treasurer of I lis Majesty’s Navy; and did propose and recommend fundrv good and wholesome provisions and regulations for the reformation of the fame, and particularly for preventing the Public Money issued for Navy Services from coming into the possession and custody of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, or the officers or persons employed under him; for depriving him and them of all opportunity of using and misapplying the Public Money to private purposes, and thereby expos-ing the same to the risk of loss; for making the Bank of England the foie place of deposit for the fame; for removing, from thenceforward, all temptations and inducements to applications for more Public Money than was necessary for the Public Service; for preventing ail unnecessary delay in passing the Public Accounts of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, and in restoring to the Public the Balances remaining in his hands: And whereas the House of Commons having taken the Reports of the said Commissioners into consideration upon the! 19th day of June 1782, did (among other things) resolve that some regulations ought to be adopted, for the purpose of lettening and keeping down the balances which appeared to have usually been in the hands of the Treasurer of the Navy; and did further declare their opinion, that from thenceforward, the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and the Treasurer of the Navy for the time being, thou Id not apply any Sum or Sums of Money imprested to them or either of them, to any purpose of advantage or interest to themselves, either directly or indirc6lly.

And whereas for the more effectually carrying into execution the said Resolutions of the House of Commons, His Majesty, by Warrant under His Royal Sign Manual, bearing date the 22d day of June 1782, was most graci-oufiy pleased to augment the income of the Right honourable Ij'aac Barre, as Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, and to add thereto the sum of 2,150. that the said income might in future amount' to 4,000. which His Majesty was then graciously pleased to grant to the said Ifaae Barre, clear of all dedu6tions, in full satisfaction of all wages and fees and other profits and emoluments theretofore enjoyed by former Treasurers of His Majesty’s Navy: And whereas by Letters Patent bearing date the 19th day of August 1782, His Majesty was graciously pleased to give and grant unto the Right honourable Henry Dundas now Lord Viscount Melville, the Office of Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy Royal and Ships, and Receiver General of all sums of Money appointed, or from time to time to be appointed and payable for the support, maintenance, and reparation of I Iis Majesty’s Navy Royal and Ships, for emptions and provisions appertaining to and necessary for the said Navy and Shipp, and for wages, falaties of officers, servants, and other persons whatever, belonging to the said Navy or Ships, or any other matter or thing whatsoever, in any manner touching or concerning the Navy Royal or Ships; and for the exercise and occupation of the said Office, and for and in satisfaction of all wages and fees of three pence of lawful money for every pound to be received and paid by the said Henry Dundas, by virtue of his said office. His Majesty was further graciously pleased to give and grant unto him by the said Letters Patent, an annuity or yearly payment of 2,000.

And whereas on the 17th day of February 1785, the House of Commons ordered that leave should be given to bring in a Bill for better regulating the Office of the Treasurer ofl lis Majesty’s Navy, and that (together with other Members of the said iloufe of Commons) Mr. Henry Dundas, now Lord Viscount Melville, should prepare and bring in the fame; and, in pursuance of the liiid order, the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville, on the 29th day of April 1785, did present to the House of Commons a Bill for belter regulating the office of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy; and the said Bill having pa fled the House of Commons, was, in pursuance of an Order of that House, carried by the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville to the House of Lords; to which Bill be (in the name of the House of Commons) desired the concurrence of their I>ordftnps:

And whereas the said Bill, in the 25th year of His Majesty’s reign, patted into a law, intituled, "AnACt " for better regulating the Office of the Treasurer of " His Majesty’s Navy;"—The ill, 3d, 4th, and 5th ScClions whereof, are as follows:

" Whereas it appears by the Reports made by the " Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and state " the Public Accounts of the Kingdom, that Regtila-" tions are necessary for better conducting the bufi-" ness in the Department of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy; Be it therefore Enacted by the " King’s Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the Ad-" vice and Consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, " and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, " and by the Authority of the same, That from and after " the first day of July 1785, the Treasurer of His Majesty's Navy for the time being, in all Memorials to be " by iiim presented to the Treasury, for Money for Navy " Sendees, shall pray that such sum as he requires may " be issued to the Governor and Company of the Bank " of England on his account, and shall transmit with " each Memorial a copy of the letter or letters from the " Commissioners of the Navy, Victualling, and Sick and " Hurt Boards, directing him to apply for such sum or " films; in which letter or letters the said Commissioners " shall, and they are hereby required and directed to " specify for what particular service or services the said " mottey is wanted, and shall also state the balances then " in the hands of the Treasurer of the Navy under each " head of service respectively; And whereas the provisions contained in the said last mentioned Act of Parliament, were thereby directed to take place on the i It day of July 1785: But the execution of the said Act, with respect to the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville, opening an Account or Accounts with the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, as thereby directed, was postponed by him until the 13th day of January 1786, when the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville opened an Account with the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, intituled, " Right " Honourable Henry Dnndas, Act of Parliament New " Account;" and which said Account was continued by him until he quitted the said Office on the 31st of May 1800, and was the only Account kept by the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville, as Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, with the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, under and in pursuance of the said Act of Parliament for regulating his said Office.

And whereas on the 10th day of January 1786, whilst the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville held and enjoyed the said Office of Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, he did constitute and appoint Alexander Trotter his Pav-maller; and the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville did, on the said icth day of January 1786, duly authorize and empower the said Alexander Trotter to draw on the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for and upon the account of him the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville as Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, all and every sum and sums of Money that then were or should thereafter be wanted for the Public Services, under the care of payment of the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville, the said Alexander Trotter being particularly careful to specify on each $nd every draft the service for which the Money should be drawn.

And whereas it was the duty of the said Hennj Lord Viscount Melville, during all the time he held and enjoyed the said Oflice of Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, to abstain from applying himself, and to prevent all persons acting under him from applying any part of the Money issued from His Majesty’s Exchequer for Navy Services, to any purpose of advantage or interest to himself or themselves, either directly or indirectly, or to any other purposes than for Navy Services, and from deriving any profit or emolument therefrom: And from and after the passing of the said Act of Parliament of the 25th year of His Majesty’s reign, for better regulating the Office of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, it was the duty of the said Lord Viscount Melville to observe and pursue the provisions and directions of the said Act of Parliament; Yet the said Henry Lord Viscount Melville, not satisfied with the ample revenue so provided for him as aforesaid, nor regarding the duty of his high and important Office, or the express provisions of the said Act of Parliament, did, whilst he so held and enjoyed the said Office, aft and conduct himself fraudulently, corruptly, and illegally, in the several instances herein set forth.

Mr. Speaker, Duke of

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, Athoir* Bill. That the Lords have taken t he Message of the Commons, of the fifth day of July instant, relating to the Message of the Lords, requelling the Commons to communicate to the Lords the Evidence upon which they passed the Bill, intituled, An Act for settling and securing a certain Annuity on John now Duke of At holt, and the Heirs general of the seventh Earl of Derby-, and inform the Commons, that the Lords intended by their Message, to requell the Commons to communicate the information laid before the Commons relating to the fafts stated in the said Bill as the ground and foundation thereof; and the Lords conceive, that it is according to the practice ol Parliament for the Lords to requell of the Commons such information touching Bills passed by them.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House proceeded to take the said Message into Message to

consideration. in aXcA

Ordered, That a Message be font to the Lords, to acquaint their Lordships, that the Commons have taken their Lordships Message, of this day, into consideration; but inasmuch as the nature of the Bill, mentioned in their Lordships Message, was for the express purpose of making a disposition of Public Money, the Commons conceive that the claim asserted in their Lordships Mef-sage is not warranted by the practice of Parliament, and doth intrench upon the Rights and Privileges of the Commons; from which they can never depart.

Ordered, That the Lord Glcnbervie do carry the said Message.
