Extract of a Dispateh from J. II. Frere, Esquire, to Lord Hawkesbury; dated Escurial, 9th October 1803. (Received 9th November.)

I have to announce to your Lordship the conclusion of the negotiation between this country and France, agreeably to the conjcdure which I hated in my lait report to your Lordship upon the subject; namely, that, for the present moment, the difference would be patched up with money; and that it can only be for the present moment, lour Lordship will easily conceive from the exorbitance of the sum, which is no leis than six millions of livres a month y a sacrifice beyond the ability of -Spain to furmlh, and, as I have distinctly explained

to the Prince of Peace, far exceeding the limits of any thing but a mere temporary connivance on the part of England.

On the 3d instant, M. Herman arrived from Paris, and the fame evening had a conference with the Prince of Peace at this Sitio. The next day, there was a second conference; at which M. Cevallos was present; and, on the following day, the Prince of Peace sent to acquaint me that every thing was settled; that they had made every sacrifice to preserve their Neutrality; and that they had finally consented to pay fijt millions of livres a month.

The terms, it seems, which M. Herman bad been inflruded to demand, included the payment of arrears pretended to be due since the beginning of the war, at this fame rate, together with a payment in advance, the amount of which I could not learn. The result of these conferences was, to reduce them simply to the monthly payment of six millions of livres. Upon M. Herman’s return to Madrid, General Bournonville set off himself for the Sitio. He had two successive conferences with the Prince of Peace: which terminated in obtaining some further addition to the terms which had been extorted by M. Herman, the exact nature of which I have not yet been able to learn. When I pressed the Prince of Peace upon the subject of the Treaty, he said that there was nothing but an additional article about the transit of French woollens to Portugal. I then asked what security was obtained for that country; he said that was settled: Portugal was to pay a million of livres a month; that the demand upon Spain was extravagant in comyarifon; and that had been made so, he believed, with a view of a future ground of quarrel, in case they should find themselves unable to fulfil the engagements which they had been forced to enter into. He said, however, that orders had been sent to M. Azara to lign a Treaty; and that they should think no price too great for the maintenance of their Neutrality; and he added some-thing, which implied a preemption that such a neutrality might continue through the War. 1 interrupted, and reminded him of what I bad said on a former occasion on the same subject, that I thought it possible that Great Britain might connive at a trifling sacrifice, such as that which w as exacted from Portugal, or even at the present, if considered merely as a temporary measure, and intended to give time till the disposition of the great Powers of Europe should be more decidedly known, and till those Powers themselves should be acquainted with the circumstances and fituction of this country. He aiked, How was it possible for Spain to ad otherwise ? that their conduct was the effect of their weakness, and not of any *real hostility to! England. I admitted it; but added, that the effects were the fame: that a Sub fidy, such as they were about to grant, was a much greater injury to the interests of England than any that could be apprehended from their hostility. He admitted this; but pleaded the utter im-poflibiiity of resistance, and the necessity of submitting to demand* which were backed by such a force. I said, that I hoped that these considerations would induce England to forbear for a time, and that I would most earnestly recommend it to him to look to foraething beyond the present, which could serve as nothing but a temporary expedient.

I have reserved for afeparate Dispateh some particulars which may perhaps appear interesting to your Lordship, with a view to forming a judgement resperiing the measures to be pursued by Great Britain, in consequence of those which have been adopted by this Court in their present emergency; and I mention them the rather as they may perhaps appear necessary to justify my remaining here, which I have determined to do till such time as I can receive instrudions from home. No. 10.

Extract of a Dispatch from J# H. Frere, Esquire, to Lord Hawkesbury; dated Madrid, 7th December 1803. (Received 30th December.)

Since the date of my last the events of this Court have proceeded hi the channel to which they seemed naturally tending; and the ratification of the Treaty has taken place. It has been agreed, that of the six millions which were stipulated to be paid monthly, two are to be set apart for the reimbursement of the Spanish claimants upon the French Government, and are consequently to be kept by this Government, in order that they themselves may satisfy the demands of their own subjects. Since the arrival of the ratification a new claim has however been set up, for the payment of arrears amounting to about a million sterling, and which are pretended to be due since the beginning of the war. As yet no payment has been made either upon this account or that of the monthly subsidy.

remaining difference is with respect to its limits, which have been construed to comprehend West Florida.

1 have the honour to be, kc.

J. U. Frere.

(Inclosure in No. 12.)

Letter from J. H. Frere, Esquire, to Sir Edward Pellew; dated Madrid, 28th January 1804.

Sir,

It appears that this Court have it in contemplation to send out a considerable expedition from the port of Ferrol, confuting, at the lowed efiimation, of about six thousand men.

Though it is not evident that they have any immediate object of hoffility in view, yet, in the present situation of the two countries, I should consider myself as wholly incxcufable if I were to connive at the execution of a measure of such an important, and, under all its circumstances, of so suspicious a nature. I mud therefore recommend it to you as an object (as it appears to me) of the utmofr consequence to llis Majesty's service, that the failing of the above-mentioned armament should be opposed; fird, by a declaration of your being authorized to oppose it by force, and finally, by the execution of force, if unhappily such an extremity should become necessary.

The expedition cannot I suppose be in a date to put to ica for some weeks; and it is possible that the protefls, which I shall think it my duty to make, may lb far delay it, as to render it possible to receive instrudions from England. In the mean time however, arid unless you should yourself receive instrudions to the contrary, I beg to be considered as charging myself with any responsibility which may attach to the measure which I recommend.

As it is my wish to avoid any needless appearance of menace, t would advise the utmost lecrecy upon the subject of this letter. 1 shall myself communicate it to the Miniders here, but to no one else. They will, 1 apprehend, be much more disposed to give way, when they find that our discretion enables them to do so with decency.

(Signed) J. II. Frere*

To Sir Edward Pellew, Bart.

Sir,

His Majesty's Government having received frequent complaints from several Commanders of llis Majesty's ships of war, of the unfriendly treatment to which they are exposed in the ports of Spain, (more especially in that of Ferrol,) and of the refusal which they have experienced, in many instances, of permission to purchase in those ports provisions, and other necessaries for the use of the respective ships of war under the command of those officers; I have to signify to you His Majesty's pleasure, that you make the most forcible repre-fentations upon this subject to the Spanish Ministers; and that you date to them llis Majesty's just expectation, that the Commanders of his ships of war shall have full liberty to purchase, in the ports of Spain, provisions, and any other necessary articles of which they may be in want; and, generally, that they may be treated precisely in the same manner as the Commanders of the ftiips of war of the French Republic, or of any other country which may be at peace with his Catholic Majesty.

I am, &c.

The Subsidy paid by this country to France had been regularly acquitted up to the month of May, at the rate of 800,000 dollars per month. A new expedient has since been hit upon for enabling the French Government to avail itself of the relourccs of Spain to au extent which will not be limited by those difficulties which muff sooner or later have put a stop to the extraction of specie. A loan of five millions of dollars has been negotiated at Paris in favour of this Government, or more properly speaking, in favour of that of France, as it is not to be imagined that any part of it will ever find its way into this country, or be applied to any other purpose than that of the payment of the ttipulated tribute. It is agreed that the capital is to be repaid at the end of three years; the annual interest to be fix per cent., with an allowance of three per cent, for commission upon the whole capital subscribed; there is besides a further advantage allowed to the contractors, namely, a privilege of exporting, free of duty, a quantity of dollars, to the amount of the capital subscribed; this cannot be calculated at less than fix per cent., and may be much more. These sums therefore, divided amongst the three years, make at ieaft an additional three per cent., and give nine per cent, as the

Dispatch from Lord Harrowby to B. Frere, Esquire; dated Downing-street, 29th September 1804.

Sir,

The preceding Dispatch is written with the view of being read in extenso to M. de Cevailos, in your conference wish him; and if you should find it necessary to make any communication in writing, you will frame it in exact conformity to the instrudions contained in that dispatch.

After the step which has been taken by the Court of Spain, it is impoflibie to rely implicitly upon any assurances, however positive; and you will therefore take the most speedy and effectual means of learning, with certainty, at Ferrol, at Carthagena, and at Cadi/, whether the armaments have been countermanded, and the orders for that purpose are actually in the course of execution; and you will forward, without delay, the intelligence you may receive from those ports.

In every view in which the subject has been considered here, it has appeared so improbable that any explanations can be given by the Court of Spain, of the motives of this armament, which can induce His Majesty to acquiesce in its continuance, that I have not adverted to that case: but if, contrary to expectation, any explanation should be offered, which in your judgment appears satisfactory, you are authorized to suspend your departure from Madrid until His Majesty's pleasure can be taken; but you will expressly declare, that you have no authority to suspend, during that interval, the execution of those measures of precaution which His Majesty has already thought necessary to direct to be taken,

B. Frere, Esquire.

No. 21.

Translation of a Letter from the Chevalier d'Anduaga to Lord Ifarrowby.—(Received the 23d December 1804.)

My Lord, Fortlatid-Place, and December 1804.

After the abrupt and unexpected manner in which the British Charge d'Affaires at Madrid has broken off all diplomatic communication with the Spanish Cabinet, I might well dispense with recalling to your Excellency's attention the completely pacific proceedings which have constantly marked the fyfterfi followed by my Court towards England; but deliring, conformably to his Majesty's orders, to shew to the last moment that spirit of conciliation which confututes the essence of my million, and the distinguishing characteristic of my Sovereign, 1 have thought it my duty to make yet one more effort, tending to shew in its true light the frank and friendly conduct which the King has not ceased to displuy since the rupture between France and England, amidll the difficulties of his situation with regard to the two belligerent Powers.

From the very moment that the King had learned the commencement of lioftilities between France and England, his Majesty gave all his attention to the manner in which he should conduct himself, in order to prevent all room for discontent on the part of these two states, and to the system which he would have to follow in such a conjundure, in order to conciliate his engagements as the Ally of France with his duties of friendship towards England. Although his Majesty knew very well, that his quality of auxiliary to the first of thele Powers was in nowise incompatible with that of friend to the second, he was, from the very first, perfectly sensible, and his opinion has been since confirmed by accounts from his Minister at London, that the British Government would, with difficulty, coufent to his fui niftiing to France succours, such as are stipulated by the Treaty of 1796. In this persuasinn, and, in order to remove every hostile appearance in his connections with the latter Power, he resolved to propose to his Ally the conclusion of a new Treaty, by which pecuniary succours should be substituted for the succours in troops and ftiips, which he had engaged to furnifti to France by the Treaty of Alliance. After long and difficult negotiations, the King congratulated himself on having at last obtained the object of his amicable views, by the conclusion of a Treaty of Sublkly.

Confiding in the uprightness of his intentions, and in the pacific

575

sentiments which had prompted him to take this step, his Majesty was fully persuaded that the British Government would not fail to appreciate this very unequivocal mark of friendship. The complaints brought forward soon afterwards by Mr. Frere against the above-mentioned Convention—complaints which he baa at different times renewed, though always in very vague terms, and without ever making 1 V an essential and decisive point of them—were therefore a real subject of surprize to his Catholic Majesty. Nevertheless, answers full of moderation and candour were by his order made to them, in which answers were set forth the motives which had led him to make a Treaty of which the English Government had the less room for complaint, as it was solely out of regard to them that his Majesty had determined to conclude it.

At nearly the same time, His Britannic Majesty's Minister having addressed to my Court representations on the armaments which he pretended were carrying on in our ports, and which he supposed to be directed against England, his Majesty ordered answers to be fn like manner made to him, 44 That the views of the Spanish Government were very far from any motive of hostility; that His Britan- nic Majesty could not mistake pacific intentions of the King of 44 Spain, who had given Him so many incontestible proofs of friend- ship; and that these proofs were manifested as well in the sacrifices 44 made by the King to secure Peace, as in the severity exercised,

44 even before it was demanded, towards those of his subjects who 44 had acted contrary to the duties of Neutrality. In fine, that, according to these data, there did not exist the least cause for appre- bending that Spain would engage in further armaments, for that 44 would be acting against her pacific system."

At the same time, as the Court of Madrid was not enabled to form an exalt and fixed judgment of the principles and the conduct which the British Government proposed to follow, on account of the equi«* vocal language in which Mr. Frere always enveloped his representa-tions, it invited him to express himself in a clear and precise manner as to the intentions and the views of his Government with regard to Spain. It was in conlVquence of this frank and friendly invitation, that His Britannic Majesty's Minister at last particularized to my Court, in a Note which he transmitted to it on the 18th February last, the conditions on which his Government would be disposed to recognize the Neutrality of Spain. These conditions were, the suspension of all ulterior armament, and the prohibition of the sale of prizes in his Majesty's dominions. Not having exuded others, it is perfectly clear, that the British Ministry engaged itself thereby to respect the Neutrality, as soon as the King, my raafter, should acquiefee in these conditions.

His Majesty, who had resolved to make every sacrifice compatible with the welfare of his people, in order to secure to them the benefits of a solid Peace, determined to forbid the sale of prizes in his kingdoms; which prohibition took place on the 23d March last. And with regard to the armaments be renewed the assurances, which the British Government had already received on this head; assurances the fmcerity of which was well guaranteed by the lively interest which his Majesty has constantly attached to the maintenance of Peace, since the rupture between France and England.

This eagerness of the King to fulfil all the wishes of the British Cabinet, and the painful sacrifice which his Majesty had just made of the advantages which the sale of prizes in the ports of Spain held out to Spanish commerce, ought to have completed the confidence of England, and to have eradicated from the opinion of its Government every atom of doubt on the pacific sentiments of my Court; Accordingly, the English Minister feeined to have felt all the value of such sacrifices, since he brought forward no more complaints, and that the most perfect harmony seemed every day to unite more and more the two Governments.

Such were the relations subsisting between the two nations, when, in the month of September last, fonie discontent having broken out in Biscay, his Majesty ordered the embarkation of a part of the troops which were in garrison at Ferrol, in order to their being transported without delay to the place where the disorder had occurred. Then it was, that the enemies of Spain, founding the alarm, under the pretext that considerable armaments were carrying on in her ports, fought to communicate their feigned uneafmefs to the British Government, by placing before them in the most hostile colours, a measure as foreign to the interests of England, as it was indispenskble to the (lifting in their birth, movements which had manifested themselves in a province of Spain. Then it was, that the British Charge d'Aftairesy hurried on by reports which malevolence had exaggerated, and without examining either the nature, the extent, or the well-known object of these pretended armaments, made complaints of them in a Note, dated the 27th September last, in which he representf d them as an hostile aggression against his Government, and as a defiance given to England; and expressed himself in other terms not less injurious to the reputation of the King, than contrary to the relations which fub-fifted between the two countries.

Although such reproaches, in return for the proofs which the King had always given of his eagerness to strengtheo the bonds of friendship

No. 24.

Extract of a Letter from Lieutenant General Nugent to the Right honourable Lord Ilobart; dated Jamaica, 14th January 1804.

I have just received the enclosed Extract of a Letter from St. Jago de Cuba, of the 8th instant; and, as the intelligence is fully credited by the gentleman who forwarded it to me, I have advised the Admiral of its contents. The French troops alluded to are parts of the garrisons of Port au Prince, under General La Valette; Cape Nicola Mole, under General Noailles; and Jeremie; which escaped from our cruizers; together with a considerable number of fiek and cou-valefcents, whom it was considered as unsafe to bring away, or to retain in Jamaica. I am sorry that the reduction in our numbers here will not permit me to reinforce Providence; but I am confident in the efticaey of our naval force for the protection of that Aland and its dependencies.

We shall look with a very jealous eye towards Cuba, in which island the French troops have been, contrary to the pretended Neu trality of the Spanish Government, moll glaringly permitted to remain embodied, and privateers to be fitted out, notonously the property of, and manned by Frenchmen.

Every precaution, however, has 1 think been taken, and it is extremely improbable that they can arrive without notice being given of their approach; and effectual refinance made to their progress, by the vessels which have been employed for this purpose.

Indeed, by an account received from the coast of Cuba, I think that it is likely that General Noailles has been recently killed in an action which took place on that coast with one of the armed private vessels from this port, the Captain of which very imprudently permitted him felt* to be boarded in the night-time by a French vessel, having on board about 350 French soldiers; the Captain of the British vessel was killed, together with a great number of his crew, and the vessel captured. I under and that eighty or ninety of the French soldiers were killed in the action, and that General Noailles died of his wounds.

(Inclosure in No. 35.)

Translation of the Governor of Corunna's answer lo Captain Wallis’s first letter, dated Coiunna, 17th August 1803.

Sir,

I haV£ received your letter of yesterday’s date, and being desirous ta serve you in whatever lays in my power, 1 have mentioned to the British Agent here that he may get you supplied with water, or whatever refreflunents you may require; and the fame I will do whenever it lays in my power.

It has been repeatedly reported here that you have captured several vessels from St. Domingo, which, on account of the epidemic fever in that island, has spread universal alarm throughout; and the Health Board, as well as myself, have received the ftri&elt orders from Court to enforce a quarantine in all vessels coming from the West India Islands, or those who may have had any intercourse with them; for which reason it lays me under the disagreeable necessity to inform you the Board of Health will not consent that any of your officers or men come on shore, nor have any intercourse with the inhabitants; nor can 1 permit your vessel to enter this port without (he is to perform quarantine.

In regard to the salute, the orders we have, are, to treat all men of war in amity with his Catholic Majesty as we do our own; and it is only by the late Treaties with Russia and France that gun for gun is returned, otherwise I should find great pleasure in being able to comply with your request, not only in this, but in any thing else you think I can be of service to you; and remain truly,

Sir,

Y’our attentive humble Servant.

By your letter of the 31ft to me, you expressed your readmefs to me to comply with my request; and as a neutral Nation 1 had a right, it being merely water and refreshments. Understanding I could get those things with more facility at Ferrol, 1 applied to the Governor of that place, who advised me to go to Corunna, where I might anchor, and get whatever I wanted.

Under all these circumstances, I came off here last evening, and was piloted to an anchorage by a Pilot, authorized by you to do so.

Before iun-set I sent an Officer from this /hip on shore with the rank of Captain of Infantry, with a letter to your Excellency; this Officer was treated with great insult, and obliged to return to me without being permitted to deliver the letter he was charged with, and this too in the presence of the Officers belonging to the french frigate.

No. 44.

Letter from Don Diego Contador, Governor of Ferrol, to Sir Edward Pellew, Baronet; dated 14th February 1804.

I am informed by the Governor of the Cattle of Palmo, that a Wit belonging to the squadron under your command, and having an English officer on board, has passed through the mouth of this harbour, and entered it in the middle of the night, without obeying the Governor's orders not to proceed to their delunation before daylight, according to the edublished orders for all boats and small vessels, either national or ft rangers.

I am also informed, that the squadron under your command has anchored at the mouth of the harbour between the batteries, which greatly annoys the coming in or going out.

Your Eminence knows that I have strictly conformed myself to the la\*s of Nations and of Neutrality, not only by facilitating the supplying the squadron Under your commarid with meat, bread, and all other provisions, refreshments, and succours, according to the rules of hospitality, but that even I did not object to yotir ships entering the harbours under my command, when the hardships of the sea and the damages sustained by the weather made it neeefiaVy; but as it is contrary to the fame laws and rules of Neutrality that the boats of the squadron under your command should enter this port contrary to orders, in the night-time, which is not allowed even with flags of truce; or that the fame squadron, without being forced to it by distress of weather, or any other necessity, should anchor at the harbour’s mouth, and in the very entrance of it, I find myself obliged to requell your Eminence to acquaint me with the motive which may have induced you to ad in this manner; and I have no doubt that henceforward your Eminence will tahe example by my conduct, and faithfully observe the laws of Nations and Neutrality, by not fending your boats at night into our ports, and making use of the Spanish territories; harbours, and succours, but as much as hospitality requires, and so as not to give room to suspect that I connive at the abuse of that hospitality to the prejudice of other Nations, which are equally on terms of neutrality with this Country, and have ships of war in this harbour.

I beg, &c. he. &c.

(Signed) Diego Contador,

, Governor of Ferrol, he. he.

No. 45.

Letter from Sir Edward Pellew, Baronet, to Don Diego Contador* Governor of Ferrol; dated on board His: Majesty s ship Tonnant, off Ferrol, the 16th February

1804.

Sir,

I was last evening honoured with your Excellency's Letter of yesterday's date, and am concerned to find that it wears so much the complexion of real complaint. The want of a person to translate the Castilian language has delayed my reply; and I have to apprehend that we have not put a proper constructiou on all its parts. I did not, however, lose a moment in calling to account the Officer who had broken my pofttive orders, by entering your harbour in the night. His defence I enclose herewith, observing only, that this young Officer was actuated by no improper motive whatever: it was the giddiness of youth. The boat was certainly not armed, and was the smallest in the cutter. But so little am I disposed to justify the opinion, that I have put him under arrest, to be tried by a Court Martial, where he will meet the punishment due to his inlubordi-nation.

T trust, however, (and have great pleasure in the expectation) from the personal inclination your Excellency has so uniformly evinced, by affording the squadron of His Britannic Majesty every supply confident with neutrality and friendship, that this trivial circumstance (which I could not controul) will not lead to disturb the good understanding and harmony so happily commenced. I shall maniteft, by every means, my strong inclination for its continuance, and my regret at any event which may disturb it. With respect to the occasional anchorage of the ships under my command, your Excellency has been misinformed, i trust it is not such as can give umbrage to your Excellency, or to the Spanish nation. I am sent upon the coast of Galicia by the King, my matter, to protect the commerce of his sub-

jedts trading to the ports of Spain. In performing this service, it cannot with truth be said, that I have given trouble to the (Trips of any nation, either entering or departing from them. I have acted up to the spirit of exact Neutrality, and the existing Treaties; and, with the exception of the cutter (to which your Excellency had giveb permission to go into Ferrol to receive supplies) there is no ship anchored within the batteries, but in the open ocean. In eailerly winds I occasionally anchor to prevent being blown off, and in westerly winds I anchor to prevent being shipwrecked upon the coast. I cannot give your Excellency two more powerful reasons; and I entertain no doubt that they will prove satisfactory, and that I shall continue to experience the fame attention and respect to the flag of my Sovereign as is shewn to that of any other neutral nation enjoy-ing the benefit of amity and peace.

I have the honour to be, with great respect, &c. he. he.

(Signed) Eduard Pellew.

To his Excellency Don Diego Contador,

Governor of Ferrol, &c. &c. &c.

(Inclosure in No. 45.)

Declaration of the Officer in the boat, inclosed in the Letter of Sir Edward Pellew, Bart, to Don Diego Contador, Governor of Ferrol; dated on board His Majesty’s ship Tonnant, the 16th February 1804.

Having been sent on board the Nimble cutter, to be ready to go early in the morning for provisions to Ferrol, it was discovered about midnight that the buoy of the cutter s anchor was gone, and it was doubted if it had not broke from the rope, and drifted up the harbour; upon which I jumped into the boat, with two men and two boys, to look for it. The tide was setting strong into the harbour, and in a few minutes the boat was hurried up under Castle Palmo, and hailed by the sentry, and ordered to go back; upon which I answered in French, that it was an English boat, looking for a buoy broke from the cutters anchor, and begged to go on; after calling, a serjeant, I believe, said I might do so. The boat was unarmed, and I returned in a few minutes. I had no improper motive whatever; and I know the most positive orders were given again!! any boat moving by night. The hurry of the moment, and the rapidity of the tide, gave me no time for reflection, and to that alone is the circumstance to be attributed, and for which I aip very sorry.

It is surmised by some, that they are to remain in readiness in the event of the squadron at Ferrol being able to evade the vigilance of Sir Edward Pellew, and appearing off to join them, and to proceed to the Mediterranean.

(Ihclosure in No. 16.)

Sir, Ship Enterprize, Havanna, 17th January 1803.

According to my Instru&iohs from the High Court of Admiralty of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, I have to inform you of the proceedings in this port since my arrival on the 12th ' of this month. On my being in fight of this port, the figfcal was mad© for an English ship. The French General here sent a French privateer out for the express purpose of taking my ship; but not being of force sufficient to attack the ship, (he thought proper to haul off. There are five privateers now here, of different descriptions; one Brig fitting out on purpose to take this ship when (he fails; The said brig mounts 18 guns, and full of men. One schooner of 6 guns; and the others mount 4 guns each, and (carry) from 50 to 60 men. I under-(land they are determined on taking the ship. I shall have on board, when failing, 30,000 sterling; and unless I have some protection, I am undetermined on foiling.

One of the before-mentioned privateers has brought in here a large ship, named the British Queen, of St. John's, that failed with the last convoy from Jamaica. She parted with the fleet, and came through the Gulph. She was captured off Cape Antonio by a privateer of one gun. These privateers make prizes of Danes, Americans, and every thing unarmed. 1 have also to communicate to the Admiralty of Great Britain the conduit of this Government. And have the honour, &c.

Cufar Lawson.

No. 17.

Naval Occurrences; reported by Mr. Duff, His Majesty's Consul at Cadiz, for May 1804.

The squadron of the fifteen ships continues nearly in the fame date as in the preceding months. Upon the 16th of May, the King's Urea or storeship the Santa Appolonia, left this port; her destinatioa for the Havannah, conveying stores for that department, recruits, Ac. Upon the 31ft ditto failed his Majesty's Urea Visitation; her destina-tion Ferrol; two others are preparing here to follow her, the Santa Justa and Liebre; the whole said to be intended to proceed to the Havannah, with stores, and to return from thence with timber for the arsenals. Orders are said to have been received for laying the keels of some ships and frigates, and to begin to build as soon as timber may arrive*

Upon the 7th April the frigate Amphitrite failed from the Havait-nah; she had gone from this, and with her failed the frigate Neuftra Senora Delao, of that department; their destinatioft for Vera Cru*; there to join the frigates Sabina and Venganza, there to take aboard treasure, to be conveyed to this place, where they may now soon bn expelled. They will probably bring with them from ten to twelve million of dollars.

Of the ships which have been fitted out at Ferrol, the San Ful-gencio, of 66 guns, is under orders, and is getting ready to proceed for Vera Cruz, from whence she will probably return with treasure. She is reputed one of the fastest failing ships in his Majesty's Navy.

By Letters received lately from Lima, there is advice that three King's frigates were completing their register of money; it will probably run to about three millions of dollars upon each; they were expected to fail about the 15th February, and were to touch at Monte Video for intelligence, and there to put themselves under the command of the Gifu de Esquadra, or Brigadier Don Francisco de Buftamante, who has been the Naval Commander there for some time, who is to take the command, and to return with them for Spain; they may be expected in August, and will come rich.

The /hips which have been iitted out at the Carracca have but few men on board, and no steps taking indicating a desire of soon manning them. Two of them are (till in dock, completing their repairs'. The number of additional carpenters and caulkers lately colieded there, (and which may go to about 1,000,) are employed upon the different vessels laid up there in ordinary, which are all of them to be overhauled, and to have repairs necessary to prevent many of them from sinking. They are about ten in number, exclusive of the fix which have been fitted or are fitting out, and of the Bahama and Argonauta, which came round from Carthagena; four of them are judged to be incapable of being repaired, and only fit to be broken up,

The L’Aiglc, corvette Torche, and brig Argus, French, which have been so long here, are completely manned and victualled for six months, and appear to be now waiting to proceed to sea.

No. 18.

E.xtrad of a Letter from Rear Admiral Cochrane to Lord Melville; dated 15th June 1804.

Your Lordship will observe by the enclosed Paper,.that the French are making every exertion to complete their squadron lying at Ferrol and Corunna. This reinforcement, which I expect to arrive by the 22d, will do much towards it, as hitherto they have been without marines. I make no doubt but seamen will follow the fame rout, if they do not fend them in smallveflels across the Bay, landing them at the out-ports, from whence they will pass by land to Ferrol. Lands-men will answer, as they are by no means deficient of seamen. How far the Spaniards have adhered to their Neutrality, in suffering three hundred men to march from one end *of Spain to the other, in order to complete the equipment of the French squadron, is a matter that is not for me to decide upon.

(Inclosure in No. 18.)

Thirteen boats belonging to the French at Sedera. Each boat has twenty-six men* armed only with small arms. They are under the command ot a Naval Officer, and came from Bayonne, laden with sail-cloth, bunting, cordage, Ac. which is now transporting by land to the French squadron at Ferrpl. Six more are hourly expected. The above boats do not exceed fourteen tons each, and keep close in shore, never leaving port but when the coast is clear. The men are said to be as a recruit to the French ships; and the boats to be sold.

Naval Occurrences at Cadiz for July 1804; reported by Mr. Duff, His Majesty's Consul at that place;

Tiil King's storeship Santa Julia, which arrived latterly with building timber for the Carracca, is under orders to proceed for Trieste, to bring quicksilver.

N. B. The mines of Almaden, which for the last four years had produced any quantity of quicksilver which was wanted here, having in a great degree failed, insomuch that the above-mentioned ship is destined for Trieste, to bring a supply.

His Majesty's ffiip Minho, which arrived latterly from Gallicia, and brought building timber and powder, is to be careened at the Carraccas, as well as the Castilla, which is expected here from Gallicia, and intended also to be Cent for America.

The frigate Lucia is getting ready at Carthagena to come to this department.

The ship San Leandro, sixty-six guns, failed from the Havannah the 20th June, having on board Don Mendimuta, late Viceroy of Santa Fe; flic is supposed to have put into Porto Rico, and was in a bad condition.

The Trinidad and Saint Ann are under orders to proceed for Ferrol, half manned, in order to remain in that department; in like manner the Regia, when careened. Thtfe large ships grounding at low water,

from the creek of the Carracca having too little water for them in its present state, is assigned as the reason.

The fix ships which were armed in this department, viz. the Tri* nidad, Saint Ann, Terrible, San Raphael, Glorious, and Suint Jeno America, continue as before, with few men on board, and little exertion towards manning them.

The Bahama and Argonaut, two of the fix which were fitted out at Carthagena and came round here, have their complement of men on board, and lay in the upper part of the bay ready for service.

They are continuing to overhaul and to careen the remaining ships in the Carracca as fail as they can undertake it. The number of caulkers, carpenters, Ac. (Maiftranzos) actually employed there may be about two thousand five hundred. The ships actually in dock, and repairing in them, arC the Rayo, San Jufle, and Soverano. The department has a sufficient prOvision of pitch, tar, hemp, rope, and cables, and of sail-cloth. I do not find any quantity of naval frores is expected from the Baltic this season, or that there are any contracts.

Nine frigates, of which four from Vera Cruz, are expected soon from thence, Lima, Ac. Three of them from Vera Cruz had failed; the Venganza we learn is arrived at Ferrol, or Vigo, with 3,100,000 dollars. The Sabina and Amphitrite, which failed with her from Vera Cruz, and having equal sums on board, are said to have put into TenerilTe, and all of them with reduced crews, from having lain at Vera Cruz during the sickly season. They left the Rufina, which was to have followed them the 23d June, and may be every day expected. These frigates, and the others from Lima, Ac. it is computed may bring about twenty-four millions of dollars.

The Castilla, from Ferrol, arrived here the 15th.

No. 21.

The frigates expelled from Lima and Buenos Ayres, 4 or 5 in number, and one from Carthagena, are not yet arrived; they may be looked for in what remains of this year, and may be expected to bring in all from 8 to 10 millions for account of the King and of the merchants.

Britannic Majesty s ships, calls upon me to enquire of your Excellency if the above fa#s are true; for should the two squadrons fail in company, I declare to your Excellency that it is my determination to attack that of France and Holland, and I trust in doing so I will not be opposed by the Spanish squadron; the consequences of which may prove fatal to the harmony and good understanding that has so happily subsisted between the two countries, and which my belt endeavours have hitherto been used to preserve. Translation of a Memorandum, without signature or date, from the Chevalier d’Anduaga; received 29th August 1803.

Difference between the Family Compact of 1761, and the Treaty of Alliance of 1796, between Spain and France.

Family Compact. According to the Family Compact, the two Powers will con/i-der as their enemy every Power

Vol.6o..

T reaty of 1796. According to the Treaty of 1796, if one of ti e two Powers finds itself threatened or attacked,

who shall become enemy to one of the two Crowns. Art. 1.

'I he inviolable and mutual guarantee shall be supported by all their forces; and their Majesties, according to the principle which is the basis of this Treaty, agree that whoever attacks the one Crown attacks the other. Art. 2.

(Here follow the articles relative to the first succours).

The first succours are to be cunfidered as an obligation infe-parable from the ties of relalion-ship and intimate union, and thele succours shall be tile least that the Power required can do for the Power who may stand in need of alfifiance; but as the intention of the two Kings is, that a War once begun by or against one of the two Crowns, shall become proper and peifonal to the other; it is agreed, that a? loon as the two Kings ftndl be in a state of War with the fame enemy or enemies, the obligation of the said succours shall cease, and in lieu thereof the two Crowns shall be bound to make war conjointly in employing therein the whole of their force. Art. 16.

In case the motives for hostilities should be so prejudicial to both parties as to induce them to declare war by common content against one or more Powers, the limitations established in the preceding articles shall cease to have effect, and the two contracting Power* shall be bound to employ against the common enemy the whole of their forces by sea and land, and to concert plans to direct such forces, either collectively or separately, towards such points as may be deemed most advisable. They also bind themselves in the case pointed out in this article, not to treat for Peace but by common consent, and in such a manner as that each party may obtain that satisfaction to which they are entitled. Art. 13.

In case one of the Powers should aft only as auxiliary, that Power which alone shall be attacked may treat for Peace separately, but so as to prevent any prejudice relulting therefrom to the auxiliary Power, and moreover so as it may tend as much as possible to its direct advantage: for which purpose not.ee shall be given to the auxiliary Power, of the mode and time agreed upon for the opening of the negotiations. Art. 14.

Remarks.'—By (imply comparing the most striking articles of the two Treaties, it clearly appears that the Family Compact was in reality a Treaty of Alliance offensive and defensive, since it stipulated, that the allied Power who was not at War should consider the enemy of his ally as his own, whilst the alliance of 1796 is in itself merely defensive, inasmuch as it only exacts certain succours from the allied Power who may be menaced or attacked, and that the alliance does not become offensive, unless the motives for hostilities being prejudicial to both parties, they should declare War by common consent. This observation is so much the more necessary, as the first article of the Treaty of 1796 has this expression: " There shall exist a perpetual " alliance, offensive and defensive, between the French Republic and " his Catholic Majesty the King of Spain/' Those who may not attentively peruse the Treaty, and those particularly who may not compare it with the Family Compact, might be led from this vague exprtftion, to believe that an offensive and defensive alliance actually exists at one and the same time; that is to say, that the ally of the Power attacked mult ipso facto consider the enemy of that Power as his own, and believe himself in a state of War with him, and consequently as out of his power to continue neutral towards him.

It is equally important to attend to the text of the nth article of the Treaty of 1796, and particularly to the pbrafe, " shall put in

action the greatest force in their power," for this force is, and can only be, an augmentation of the succours to be made to the stipulated succours; but it is an augmentation which can take place, first, only in the event of the succours furnished not being sufficient; and, secondly, only according to the power and means which the party required may have for making the augmentation. One fees at once that it cannot be otherwise: first, because if by the aforesaid phrase it was meant that the Power required should be considered as bound to put in action all his forces, it would be absurd, since he could not do more even were he himself at War with the enemy of his ally: secondly, because the 13th article of the fame Treaty exacts the cm-

7 L ployment

the Other promises, engages, and obliges itself to be aiding with its good offices, and to affilt it when 16 required, according to the Hi-pulation of the following Articles. Art. 2.

(Here follow the articles relative to the succours.)

If the said succours are or /hould become insufficient, th# two Powers shall put in action the greatest force in their poweiV as well by sea as by land, against the enemy of the Power attacked, which Power shall employ tha laid forces either conjointly or separately, according to a plan that shall be concerted between them. Art. 11.

The succours stipulated by thd preceding article shall be furinshed in any War which the contrafting Powers may have to carry on, even should the party required not be directly interested therein, and should only aft as auxiliary. Art. 12.

Translation of a Memorandum, without signature or date, froifi the Chevalier d’Anduaga; received id September 1S03.

Spain, the Ally of France, and at the same time a friend of England, finds herself at this moment called upon to fulfil towards each of them the respective duties of alliance and of friendship.

The Treaty of Alliance concluded with France in 1796, although termed an offensive and defensive alliance, being only, properly speaking, an alliance strictly defer.five, according to the tenor of all its Articles, and the linking difference which exists between its engagements and those contained in the Family Compact of 1761, his Catholic Majesty trulls, he can reconcile his engagements to furnish to France the succours dipulated by the Treaty of 1796, with his mod ardent desire to maintain his friendly connections with His Britannic Majesty. The perfect harmony and good undemanding which have subsisted between the two Monarchs since the re-establishment of the lad Peace; the reciprocal proceedings, and the principles of the Law of Nations to lie puifued under circumstances similar to those in which Great Britain and Spain are actually placed, are so many reasons which prove the judice and the necessity of the conduct which his Catholic Majesty proposes to pursue at the present moment. France confining herself to the requisition of the dipulated succours, and Spain to furnishing them to her, but without allowing herself to commit any a# of dire# hostility against England; his Catholic Majesty cannot for a moment doubt of His Britannic Majesty's disposition to observe a like condu# on his part.

By such a conduct, His Britishi Majesty would, in the fird indance, afford to Spain, and to all Europe, a proof of his jtldice, of his wif-«bm, and of his impartiality. He would make a didindion between a friendly Power who did not fornish succours to his enemies through ambition, resentment, any vicious views, or others inimical to him, hutfolely to fulfil general eventual engagements previously contracted, and the Power who should form connedions inimical to England with her enemy, in the very moment of War, and with the fame hostile Spirit and views as its ally. His Britannic Majesty would obtain for the people of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland the great advantage of the continuance of their commerce with Spain, not orily during the present War, but also in all those in which neither party having any subject of complaint against the other; England would remain in friendship with Spain, notwithstanding her being at War with France. His Britannic Majesty would, besides, establish from this moment the jud idea which should be entertained, especially in England, that a rupture with France does not neceflUrily produce ipso fado, and, according to Treaties, a rupture with Spain.

His Britannic Majesty and his Minidry are too jud and too enlightened for it to be dipposed that they can entertain an opinion contrary to the principles above dated, or to the advantages which England would derive from them, even should die agree to the fydem of conduct pursued by Spain. So fully convinced is the King of this, that he cannot entertain the smalled doubt upon the subject; and he expects with perfect confidence to receive, in the concurrence of His Britannic Majesty and of his Government in the fydem of the King’s conduct, a new proof of their rectitude, and of their friendly fcuti-ments towards the King and the Spanidr people.

No. 5.

' Translation of a Memorandum from the Chevalier dfAn-duaga, without signature or date; received id September 1803.

Thn quedion, whether England Avail acknowledge the Neutrality of Spain, appears to be reduced to the determining whether the Treaty of that Power with France of the year 1796, is an offensive or defensive alliance. It is agreed, that if this Treaty merely contains stipulations of limited succours, it might be considered as an alliance dridly defensive; hut as it is dated in the first article of the Treaty, " there shall exist a perpetual offensive and defensive alliance u between the French Republic and his Catholic Majesty and moreover, in the fecoud article, that if the dipulated succours were er should become insufficient, the two Powers should put in action the greatest forces in their power: it is pretended, that determined by this new obligation the succours become unlimited, and therefore the alliance takes an offensive chara<der.

With respect to the fird article of the Treaty, it is to be observed, that the offensive and defensive alliance spoken of is in fad two alliances, each of a differenjt kind, and which refer to two different periods,. The fird is that in which the Power, whole ally is threatened or attacked, acts merely as an auxiliary. The fecund is that in which both Powers should declare War by common consent against one or more Powers. The fird period relates to defensive, the second

to offensive alliance; and although the fird article embraces the two periods collectively, the other articles of the Treaty distinguilli them in the cleared manner; and it is evident that the defensive alliance takes place in one case, and the offensive alliance in another; which latter is merely hypothetical, as it cannot take place hut when the two allies diall declare War by common consent; consequently the defensive alliance may exist, without its becoming an offensive one, and without being in contradiction to the fird article, which speaks of the one and the other at the same time.

This fame didindion of the two alliances, and of the two periods, serves equally to explain the eleventh article in its true fenle, and with that judice which is required by the definition of a duty, on the nature and extent of, which doubts have arisen. The Treaty itself fixes and separates in its articles the two alliances, and the two periods, in such a manner as, that on the bare reading of it, one discovers that the Article 12. closes the first period; and that the second commences at Article 13. that is to lay, that Article 11. relates to defensive alliance, and Article 13. to offensive alliance, from which it results, that Article 11. as relating to the period of defensive alliance, should be explained according to the nature of that alliance, and according to the analogy which the accellory condition contained in Article 11. has with the principal conditions mentioned in the preceding articles.

The nature of defensive alliances is to compel an auxiliary to furnish to his ally limited succours: and this is the case in the alliance in quedion; for the expression, M shall put in a#iou the greatest force " in their power/' neither can nor ought to be construed as if the auxiliary was compelled to make the same efforts as the ally, but each one in proportion to the nature of his situation. The one puts in action all his forces to defend himself against the enemy, or to do him all possible injury; the other adds to the succours to be furnished any other in his power, to assist his ally, but always in quality of auxiliary, and in proportion to the dipulated succours. That expression of Article 11, which appears in the fird indance to call upon the auxiliary to furnish ultimately a6 much or more to his ally, has, in fid#, no other meaning than this r " The auxiliary shall make u whatever addition may be in his power to the dipulated feecours;* and, although the amount of the new succours is not fixed in Article

11. it is evident, that it is because much cannot be required of the auxiliary, after having received that which, according to the nature of the alliance, the auxiliary was bound to furnish. And it is also an advantage to the auxiliary, that Article 11. does not specify the amount to be added to the fird succours, for, otherwise, the ally would have the power to prescribe how much the auxiliary ought to furnish him in conformity to the Treaty; indead of which, at present, it is the auxiliary himself who is to fix the extent of the succours, according to his position and his own interests, but, however, without failing in his engagements. The auxiliary being called upon to decide upon this point, can never depart from the rule which he ought to follow in his proceedings, if lie means to preserve his character of auxiliary, and to consult his own interests. One of his first interests is that of preserving his conne#ions of friendship and good understanding with the Power who may be at war with his ally, since, if the auxiliary should exceed the limits of his duty towards the ally, by furnishing considerable succours, he would degenerate into the real enemy of the said Power. This considerotion is likewise the surest guarantee to that Power, that the auxiliary will confine himself within the boundaries which his tituatien preiciibes.

It therefore follows, that conformably to the rules of judice and of equity, and of the position of an auxiliary towards its ally, the proportion of subsidies to be added should rather be leiTened; because in fixing the line of demarcation between a defensive and offensive alliance, the more one shall incline to the latter, the more the auxiliary Power would incur the risk of being forced into a War, and the more would flie deprive herself of those forces of which she would stand in need for her own preservation, in case flie herself should have a War to sustain.

All this reasoning is founded upon the Treaty of 1706 itself; because, after having spoken of the succours to be furnished in the first instance, and afterwords of putting in action the greatest force which loth Powers can bring forward, it is dated in the i^th Article, that, when they declare War by common consent, the " limitations " established w in the preceding articles shall cease to have effect. From whence it is clear, that even, according to Article 23. the additional succours are acknowledged to be limited succours.

After this, how is it poffihle that Mr. Frere, in his Note of the 27th September, has not hefilated to treat as " an hofule aggrenion,*' an armament (if it can be so called) which had ceased for several days, and which by the notoriety of its destination could not have merited, under any case, so extraordinary a denomination? This answer, which is in no degree contradicted by the information received by the British Ministry relative to the pretended armament, being perfectly consonant with the loyal and lyfteraatic cundud which my Court has invariably followed since the rupture between Great Britain and France, ought to inspire the British Government with confidence as to the pacific sentiments which his Majesty has never cealed to cherish with regard to England; Moreover, the King has the welfare of his people too much at heart; be attaches too much interest t»> what he owes to other Sovereigns, to permit him, in the midst of Peace, setting Treaties at defiance, and in oppofilion to his most so learn and sacred promises, to venture on a step which would draw down on his kingdoms the most cruel of all icourges, would deal a deadly blow against his fame, and tear from him that treasura which his Majesty values beyond all others, the testimony of his con* science.

Copy of a LETT Lit of SERVICE to Colonel French, of the late ioed Foot; ami Captain Sandon, of the Royal Wu

Gentlemen, War-Office, 30th April 1S04.

I have the honour to acquaint you, Mis Majesty has been plcufed to appiovc of your railing Five thousand Men, to be turned over to the Regiments of the Lint* in His Majesty's Service, upon the following conditionsThe Recruits are to be engaged without limitation as to time and place of Service. You will be allowed 13 Guineas Levy Money for each Recruit finally approved at one of the following Depotsviz.—The Isle of Wight; Dublin; and Edinburgh ;—put of which Levy Money, a furn equal to what may be fixed by the Recruiting Instructions in force at the time, is to be appropriated to stirmlhing the Recruits with necefihries on their final approval, exchffive of the actual Sum which may have been received determined by the Recruit. The iubfistence of the Recruits; the extra allowance to Innkeepers; the allowance for Rear, and any other daily Charge, will only be allowed to commence from the date of approval of each Recruit. Rut, with a view to cover any extra expellees that you may incur by the Men being enlilteda considerable time before their approval, )ou will be allowed to enlist ten Roys in every joo Recruits, for whom you will receive the same Bounty and Allowances as for Men. The Men and Roys respectively are to be of the age and llze directed by the general Recruiting Intimation* of the Army. No charge for Slop Cloathing for the Non-commissioned Officers, or Recruits, will be admitted; as, on approval, the latter will be clothed at the Depots hv the Regiments to which they shall be at once attached. No intermediate approval of the Recruits is to take place, and conlcqueiitly neither Bounty, Subsistence, nor any other charge, will be allowed for such as shall be rcjedled at the# several Depots. Each Recruit, on approval at the Depot, is to sign a certificate that he received the full Bounty promised to him. You will be allowed to appoint 90 Serjeants, 90 Corporals, and 60 Drummers; who must be previously approved by an inspeeling Field Officer of a Recruiting Di ft rich The Drummers are to be of the age and frandard of Roys, as speeilled in the Recruiting Instructions. The Sublilience of the above-mentioned Non-eoinmillioned Officers and Drummers is to commence from the dates of their actual appointment as inch. Half of them, if finally approved at the Depots, nre to be reckoned as part of the complement of the first Five hundred Recruits for your Levy; and the remainder as part of the full Thousand. The Corporals and Drummers are to be given to understand that they are liable to be draughted as Privates into the old Regiments. The whole of the Non-commissioned Officers, and Drummers, mull, in the fir 11 infiance, he enlifi*d and attelled as Privates; and their atteltation transmitted to this Office immediately on approval. One half of the Serjeants may be enlilled with the condition of their being discharged at the conclusion of the Levy; which cireumftance is to be noticed in their respective attefiations. The Bounty of 13 Guineas will be allowed for such of the Non-commissioned Officers and Drummers as shall be finally approved at the Depots, as part of your Levy. Cloathing will be provided, under the Orders of Government, for the Lffiettive Non-commissioned

gon Traiiii

Officers and Druunners fcmploved as above-mentioned. You will be allowed, during the Lew, the aliifiance <d ten Olhcers, whole names are to be Hated to His Koval I ho ijn ess The Com m an i»i:n in Cnir.r, for- His approbation; and such of thelc Officers us may be on Halt-pay are to receive Full Ray during their feivlce with your Levy, subsequently* to such approval. As the Men are to be passed at the Depots, it is not thought necessary to make vou an allowance for an Adjutant, Paynuilter, Surgeon, or Quartermaster; but an Officer, above the ten, will be allowed, to he relideut at each Depot during the Levy. I11 lieu of giving you pennillion to nominate any Officers for Commissions, an allowance at the rate of (wo guineas per Man, over and above the before-mentioned sum of 13 Guineas, will be made to you, whenever 500 Men shall be puffed at the Depots; and, for every 500 Men iublVquently passed, the like extra allowance of two Guineas per Man will be made to you. 'The liipulated allowance of 13 Guineas each for the approved Recruits will he ilVued immediately on their approval by the Paymafu-rs residing at the respective Depots, l»y drafts upon the Agents of the Corps to which the Men and Boys may be attached, and the Recruits will be afterwards fublified through the fame Channel, or by the Diltnct Paymafiors, until they join Regiments. The Ray of the Comnfffiioned Officers, Nou-commissioned Olhcers, and Drummers, employed in the Levy, is to he received from the Pay matters of the Recruiting District in which they shall be respectively stationed, who will draw for the fame up- n the general Agents for Recruiting in London and Dublin respectively; rendering distincl Ray-Litis of their Expenditures on this head, to tins Office. If however, any of the Commilfiom d Officers should he on Dull Ray in the exiting Regiments, the District Paymasters will draw for the Pay of such Officers on their respective Regimental Agents, in the fame nianneT as for that of other Olhcers employed in the Recruiting Service. In coidequeoce of this arrangement, it is presumed that your advances on account of the Levy will be to incontideruhle as feaiccly to require any imjuelt of Money into your hands, in the fnfi instance; hut, if you should find foine affifiance absolutely necessary, there will ho no ohjedion to your receiving a moderate Sum on account, giving Security for the immediate repayment thereof, when defiled. It is to be clearly understood, that Government reserves to itself the diferation of discontinuing the Levy entirely, in case 4,000 Men are not raised, and passed, within nine months from the date of this Letter; or in case the whole 5,000 Men are not raised, and passed, within thirteen months from the same date. In the execution of this Service, 1 am to allure you of every aliifiance that this Office can afford.

My Lord, Whitehall, 13th July 1804.

I herewith transmit to your Lordship a Schedule of the Levy Money directed by His Majesty to be allowed for each Man who shall be provided or raised under the accompanying Ad of this Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for establishing and maintaining a " Permanent Additional Force for the Defence of the Realm, and to u provide for augmenting His Majesty's Regular Forces; and for the

" gradual Reduction of the Militia of Scotland together with the application and distribution thereof; and also directing the proportion thereof which the person appointed in that behalf shall be entitled to receive for each Man produced by him for such Additional Force, pursuant to the twenty-first clause of the said Act.

No. 3.

Copy of a Circular Letter from Lord Hawkelbury to His Majesty’s Lieutenants of Counties in England 'and Wales; dated Whitehall, 33d of August 1804.

My Lord, Whitehall, 33d August 1804. x

Referring your Lordship to my Circular Letter of the 3d of July, enclosing a Schedule of the Levy Money directed by His Majesty to be allowed for each Man provided or raised under the 44th Geo. II I. cap. 56. I have to request that you will, at your earliest convenience, inform me what steps have been taken in the County committed to your Lordship’s charge, with a view to the carrying into execution the provisions of that Act.

I am, at the fane time, commanded to signify to your Lordship His Majest/s pleasure, that each Recruit produced under that Act by Churchwardens and Parish Officers should be approved, as required by the 33d clause thereof, previous to his being attested; and that the Bounty of two Guineas, directed to be paid to him on such attestation, and the like sum on his being intermediately approved, should, be paid to him together in one sum, as soon as he shall have been both approved and attested, but not before; as cases have frequently occurred where Recruits, after having received the two Guineas directed to be paid to them on their being so attested, have deserted, or been rejected in consequence of being unfit for Service, by the Officer appointed by His Majesty, pursuant to the 33d clause of the Act above mentioned.

I have the honour to be, &c. &c. &c.

Hawkfsbury.

P. S.—With the view of enabling yonr Lordship to make this Regulation public with as little delay as possible, I fend enclosed several copies of this Letter, for the purpose of being transmitted, should you judge proper, to the General and Subdivision Meetings of Lieutenancy in the County under your charge.

No. 4.

Copy of a Circular Letter from Lord Hawkelbury to His Majesty's lieutenants of Counties in Scotland; dated Whitehall, 35th August 1804.

My Lord, Whitehall, 35th August 1804.

Referring your Lordship to my Circular Letter of the 13th of July, inclosing a Schedule of the Levy Money directed by His Majesty to be allowed for each Man provided or raised under the 44th Geo. Ill# cap. 66. 1 have to request that you will, at. your earliest convenience, inform me what steps have been taken in the County committed to your Lordship's charge, with a view to the carrying into executioD the provisions of that Act.

I am, at the same time, commanded to signify to your Lordship His Majesty's pleasure, that each Recruit produced under that Act by Heritors or their Agents, should be approved as required by the 25th clause thereof, previous to his being attested; and that the Bounty of two Guineas, directed to be paid to him on such attestation, and the like sum on his being intermediately approved, should be paid to him together in one sum, as foori as he shall have been both approved and attested, but not before: as cases have frequently occurred, where Recruits, after having received the two Guineas directed to be paid to them on their being so attested, have deserted, or been rejected in consequence of being unfit for service, by the Officer appointed by His Majesty, pursuant to the 35th clause of the Act above mentioned.

I have the honour to be,

&c. Ac. Ac.

Hawkesbury.

With the view of enabling your Lordship to make this Regulation public with as little delay as possible, I fend enclosed several copies of this Letter, for the purpose of being transmitted, should yoo judge proper, to the General and Subdivision Meetings of Lieutenant) in the County under your charge.

No. 8. 1

Copy of a Circular Letter from Lord Hawkesbury to His Majesty's Lieutenants of Counties in England and Wales; dated Whitehall, 25th September 1804.

My Lord, Whitehall, 25th September 1804.

As it is of the utmost importance to the Defence of the Country, that every exertion should be used to complete the Levy of Men to be raised for the Additional Force in the manner prescribed by the 44 Geo. III. cap. 56; and as considerable delays have, from various causes, taken place, it is my duty to call the attention of your Lordship, and, through your Lordship, that of the Lieutenancy of the County, to the geceffity of supplying, without delay, the force which is required of the County of by the above-mentioned Act.

It is distinctly to be understood by the Lieutenancy, that the number of Men to be raised, in the first instance, and until an apportionment shall be made by the Privy Council of the future number, is only the amount of the deficiencies and vacancies (fropn death, desertion, and discharge) existing in the Army of Reserve and the Militia; the amount of which, in regard to the Army of Reserve, will have been VOL. 60.

Circular. tnfpcclor General’s Office,

London, 5th July 1804.

Sir,

By the Inspector General's directions, I have the honour herewith to transmit, for your information and guidance, the Act of Parliament for railing an Additional Force, and also the order, which by virtue of that Ad, authorizes you to attend the General Meetings of the Counties specified in the margin, for the purpol’e of ascertaining the deficiencies existing in their respective quotas for the Army of Re-serve, raised under the Act of the 43d Geo. III. cap. 82. in explanation of which, and other duties connected with the Ad, the following Returns and Papers are inclosed; viz.

No. 1. Copy of the Return sent to the Counties, and corresponding to Schedule (A) of the Ad.

No. 2. Returns from Officers who were employed under the late Ad, in receiving the Men enrolled iu pursuance thereof.

No. 3. County Regimental Rolls.

No. 4. Printed Circular Letter of the 14th July 1803, with the Return it covered.

No. 5. Regimental States.

No. 6. Returns of Casualties from Receiving Officers, &c. &c.

No. 7. Return of Men whole Discharges were not confirmed by the Deputy Lieutenants.

No. 8. Form of the Attestution to be used under the present Act.

No. 9. Description Return to be also used under the present Act.

The Returns, No. 1. are made out from the last and mod coned documents in this Office; they account for all the men who have been at any time received by the Reserve Regiments and Battalions exclusively appointed for the reception of the men of the Counties they respectively refer to, whence it is fair to infer, that any man not included therein, who may have been ballotted and enrolled, are casualties which the Counties have to replace; for if men who w ere at any time enrolled for the Army of Relerve, are not serving in any of His Majesty's Forces, and have never joined any Corps, though they might have been received at the places of assembly, it follows that such men mud have deserted, &c. and, as Deserters, leave the Counties responsible for them.—No. 2. Shews that such occunences were not unfrequent; they are Returns of the Men received at the different Nations by the Receiving Officers, and lent to the corps for which they were designed, being in figures, the General is aware they can be of no further ule than to establish the fad ltated, viz. that ihough jnany men might have been enrolled and taken to the receiving places, they dele) ted without joining any Corps, where alone any satis-fadory descriptions of them could be taken and preserved: should therefore the Return No. 1. prove unfutisiadfcory to the Meetings, the fads to be deduced from No. 2. will, it is hoped, remove any doubts which might be previously entertained.

Although in so novel, complicated, and rapid a measure in its effects as the Reserve Ad was, men were given up by the Civil Magistrates, and received by the Military Officers, without paying due regard to the Instructions contained in No. 4.; yet it is hoped the Regimental Rolls, No. 3, aided by the documents the Clerks of General Meetings arc supposed to poffiefs, will prove sufficiently clear to enable the Meetings to determine for what Subdivisions, Parishes, &c. the men are serving; I mean by their Returns of Men enrolled, for they cannot be at present in possession of records to enable them to ascertain with precision the Casualties to be accounted for in Schedule (C) as directed by the Ad.

No. 5. Are the lad Returns received from the Regiments and Battalions concerned, and give the application of their men.

No. 6. Are the Returns uf Casualties, from various quarters, to the fulled extent reported to the Inspector General; in them many names are repeated, which, if not previously observed and guarded against, may occasion some inconvenience.

No. 7. mod explicitly (hews that the men named in it were, in no one instance, wantonly or improperly discharged; the reasons assigned mud be sufficient to satisfy any impartial mind in the lead degree conversant with Military Service, of the indispensible necessity of the measure, thereby relieving not only the Corps from a great burthen, but the County from a very heavy useless expence.

In furnishing you with this information, the Inspector General desires you will not lose light of the Law, which determines that men so discharged are not legal Casualties, but leave it to the candour, good sense, and uniform loyalty of the Lieutenancy to replace them, which, indeed, the Inspector General flatters himself they will be diL poled to do on the face of the other Returns, without the necessity of your producing those I am adverting to, which are transmitted as private information, to be used as your discretion shall fugged.

Having thus detailed what appeals tiecefTary to the performance of the very important duty intruded to you, the General desires me to express his confidence, that your zeal for the good of His Majesty's Service, with that due regard to the just interests and rights of the Counties, will procure a fair and equitable adjustment of the vacancies to be replaced; nor is he less persuaded of the Meetings being uduated by similar laudable motives, and like yourself, be impartially guided by the real spirit and meaning of the Legislature, in a measure thus left to your mutual arrangement anddecilion.

You will be pleased to lose no time in fixing with the Clerks of the General Meetings whose names and addresses are in the margin, the most convenient days to admit of your attendance on all their Special Meetings, that you may know the General's communications on the

subject to those gentlemen; the letter for Mr.----- is enclosed, to

be forwarded when you have pended its contents. You will have the goodness to avail yourself of these Meeting*, to explain as much as lies in your power, the nature of the Military arrangements to be adopted in carrying this new Act of Parliament into died; you will state what are noted in the margin to be the Receiving places for the Counties (and should any disposition appear on the part of the Meetings to increase their numbers, you will combat that desire by enumerating all the mischiefs which that system produced during the late Ad) at each of which places an intelligent Officer, not under the rank of Captain, is to be ihitioned, under inltrudions from the Inspector General to be communicated through you, for receiving and taking charge of the men who may be raised, and to refuse such as are not conformable in age or stature to the Act of Parliament, as Well as such as may be deemed furgieally unfit by the Military Medical Officer, appointed to insped them under instiudious to be drawn up by the Surgeon General with reference to the Act of Parliament, and not founded upon the extensive and general duties General Service Recruits are subject to; the men will, as heretofore, continue until further orders to be polled to the Corps named in the margin.; And with a view to the most accurate description of their persons and places of residence, &c. it is to be requested that no Overseer or other person sent with men to the Receiving Officer, be ever without the means of giving the information required in the Return No. 9. which the Receiving Officer will be ordered to obtain before he takes charge of the men; and it is of much essential consequence that none but the Attestation, marked No. 8. be ever used. 'You will urge the Meeting to give all possible publicity to these important points, which, well understood and rigidly observed, will ensure such correct documents of the men, as at any future period, shall render their being called out in times of Peace as pradicable and easy as the men of the Militia, should such a measure be deemed expedient.

As keeping Counties divided between two Inspeding Field Officers would create much confusion in this measure, and render the attendance on the General Meetings of greater difficulty, the Inspector General has determined that in the operation of this Act the district shall consist of the Counties named in the margin, but this arrangement is to be confined to the duties required under this Act of Parliament, and not to interfere or create the fmalieft alteration in the Districts as Recruiting Districts, which, for that Service, continu* in every respect upon their present footing.

As soon as the Receiving Officers are appointed, their names, and the inflrudions under which they are to ad, shall be communicated to you. At present I have only to add, that in the execution of this important service, the Inspector General will be at all times happy to afford you every assistance in his power.

Be pleased to acknowledge the receipts hereof.

(Signed) P. Carey,

A. I. G.

(Signed) G. Hewett,

continued, 3* Man.

T II E FU N DS applicable to the Volunteer Service, were, during the period above-mentioned, issued to the Agent General by tha Pay'innHer General of the Forces, to cover the payment of Bills accepted by him, under the direction of the Secretary at War, for whose ihlpetfion Schedules of such Bills, specifying the days on which they respectively became due, were submitted; by these Schedules, the Secretary at Ufur was guided in directing the Paynialter General as to the amount and periods of the Issues. Since the 19th of January 1805, in pursuance of the directions of the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, the Jlllies have been made by the Paymaster General directing the sum required to be written off at the Bank of England from his Account, to the Account of the Agent General; and all Bills, accepted by the latter, are made payable at the Bank.

The ESTABLIS II M ENT of the General Agency Office was instituted (as dated in the Secretary at War’s Letter, dated June 1803), " with a view to Public (Economy and the Good of the Service" the Funds having till then been issued to Agents appointed by the Commandants of each Volunteer Corps respectively, to whom an allowance for Agency, of 2$ per-Cent. upon the amount of the KTues, was paid by Governmer*.
