13* Februarii. RETU RN to the Order of the House of Commons, of the 12th February 1805'—Requiring

An ACCOUNT of the Number of Persons admitted to visit The BRITISH MUSEUM, within the lad Six Months; And the Regulations under which they have been admitted to visit the fame.

I N obedience to the Order of the Honourable the House of Commons, dated the 12th instant, 1 have the honour to lay before them, an Account of the number of Persons admitted to a fight of the British Museum, during the months of October, November, and December 1804, and January 1805; and a copy of the Regulations under which those persons have been admitted. To which I beg leave to add, as being a part of the Regulations for admission, a copy of the Directions respecting the Reading-Room of the Museum.

In order to explain the three different modes of admission to a fight of the Museum, as stated in the Return, I mud beg leave to suggest, that the Regulations herewith laid before the Honourable House have been printed for the information of the Public, and are freely distributed to all who chuse to apply for them; and that, according to these Regulations, 75 persons, in 5 different Companies of 15 each, may obtain admission in the course of every open day; but that, in order 10 accommodate a greater number of persons, in rafe any such fliQuld apply, an additional company of 15 persons may be added on each open day, at 2 o’clock; and that, should still more persons apply, the Officer in waiting may grant Tickets to the Supernumeraries for one of the intermediate, or closedays, in each of which 3 companies, of 15 persons each, may be admitted. The Honourable Housewill please to observe that, according to these Regulations (making allowance for the intervals and days when the Museum is shut, viz. the months of August and September, one week at each of the great Fellivals, on Thanksgiving and Fast-days, and the Saturdays and Sundays in every week) the above three modes of admission may accommodate upwards of 14,000 persons in a year, besides many persons of distindion for

rank or learning, whom the Officers attend occasionally through the House, and who are not required to conform to the above Regulations.

I humbly beg leave to (late, in justification of the non-compliance with the ftrid order of the Honourable House, to return the numbersad-mitted within the last six months, that no Vilitc rs are admitted into the Museum (the Reading-room excepted) during the months of August and September; these two months having been set aside to enable the Officers carefully to insped, to re-arrange where necessary, and cause to be cleaned, the contents of their respective Departments.

I mull also observe, that no period of adin ffiou previous to the month of August, could be added to the return, the present Plan not having been carried into execution till the middle of July lull.

Concerning the above Regulations, 1 have further to lLte, that they have not yet received the formal sanction of a General Meeting of the Trustees; and that a considerable alteration having been Ltely made in the Establishment of the Museum, and there not having been sufficient time to frame a set of Statutes conformable to the new system, the said Regulations were drawn up under the direction of some of the Trustees moll converiant with the aflairs of the Museum, and have hitherto been acted upon by way of experiment; but that a Special Committee was appointed at the last General Meeting, for the purpose of preparing a new set of Statutes; by whom these Regulations will necessiirily be taken into mature consideralion, aid be either confirmed, or properly amended.

British Museum, 7 J. Planta>

The Museum is open for public inspection every Monday, Wod-ticfduy, and Friday; except in the Christmas; Fatter, and Whitsun M eeks, and during the months of August and September.

Persons who with to see the Museum, will applvat the Anti-Room in the House, on any of the above-mentioned open days, between the hours often and two, where each Individual will he required to in-Icribe his or her name and place of abode, in a book to be kept for that purpose.

Five Companies of not more than fifteen persons each, may be admitted in the course of the day; viz. one at each of the hours of tcu, eleven, twelve, one, and two. At each of those hours the Directing Officer in w aiting shall examine the entries in the book, and, if none of the persons inscribed be found exceptionable, he shall deliver to teac.li of them a Ticket for immediate admission.

Should more than fifteen persons apply at any particular hour, the last comers (to the number of fifteen^ and no more) shall he allowed to inlcnbe their names for an extra Company, to he admitted on the fame day, at two o’clock*

It is expected, that Person3 who visit the Museum be decent and orderly in their appearance and behaviour; the Officers being intruded to refuse admission to, or to cause to withdraw, any one who shall dilregard this caution. Pali experience has proved the neceility of this injunction.

No Children apparently under ten years of age will be admitted.

No money is to be given to the attendants or lemints.

Directions respecting the Reading-Room of The British Museum.

The Reading-Room of the Museum is open from teti till four* fcvrrv day, (except oh Saturdays and Sundays, and for one week at Christmas, Latter, and Whitfurttidt, also on ThaukfgivnJg and Fait

Persons desirous of admission are to fend in their applications, in ■writing, to the principal Librarian, who will lay the fame before the next General Meeting or Committee of the Trustees. But as it might he dangerous, in so populous a Metropolis as London, to admit jierfed Grangers, it is expected that every person who applies, if not known to any Trustee or Officer, /liould produce a recommendation from some per Ion of known and approved character.

In aJl cases which require such dispatch as that time cahnot be allowed for making an application to the Trustees, the principal Librarian, or in his absenre, the Secretary, is empowered to grant a temporary leave, till the next General Meeting or Committee.

Permifljons will in general be granted for three months, and none

for a longer term than six months: and at the expiration of each term, fre/h application is to be made for a renewal.

Although the Librarians be strictly enjoined to \ife all possible dispatch in supplying the Readers with the printed books br manu-feripts they may apply for, yet, as in so extensive a Library it may not be possible to find every article immediately, it is recommended to the Readers to allow a reasonable time for the fearth, especially as to the printed books.—It is expected that the Library will soon be in such ix Hate of arrangement, as to render this intimation super-fluous.

No Reader (except in particular cases, at the discretion of the principal Librarian) will he entitled to more thaii two volumes at a time; but they may be exchanged as often as he may require#

Readers will he allowed to take one or mbre extrude from any printed book or manuscript; but no whole or greater part of a manuscript, is to be traitscribed, without a particular leave from the TrUltees. The transcribers are not to lay the paper on which they write on any part of the book or manuscript they are using.

No perfmi is, on any pretence whatever, to write on any part of a printed book or manuscript belonging to the Museum; but if any one should observe a defect, or be able to point out an improvement in such book or manuscript, he is requested to signify the same to the Officer in waiting, who will make proper use of the information;

It may be sufficient merely to fugged, that flence is absolutely requisite in a place dedicated to the purposes of study.

COPY of an ORDER from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to the Commissioners for the Transport Service, dated 23d January 1805, to consider the Officers and Men detained in Spanish Ships as Prisoners of War, and to intimate to them thafc their Private Property will be re dared.

(Copy.)

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, &c.

V here as the Earl Camden, one of His Majesty s principal Secretaries of State, hath, by his Letter of the 22d inffant, signified to us the King's pleasure, that the Spanish Prisoners, as well Officers as Men, lately taken in Spanish vessels detained by His Majesty's ships, should be placed in the situation of Prisoners of War; that they should receive Rations and Allowances in the same manner, and to the fame amount, as in the late War; and that the Officers now in lAmdon should be removed to fneb Towns as may be thought proper for their Residence on Parole, care being taken that an intimation be made to the Spanish Officers belonging to the Frigates which were ordered to be detained, that their private Property will be reffored to them; We do (in pursuance of His Majesty's pleasure, signified as aforesaid) hereby require and direfi you to consider the said Spanish

Prisoners as Prisoners of War; that they be suppliedi with such Ra-tions, and made Allowances in the same manner, and to the fame amount, as in the late War; that the Officers, now in London, be removed to such Towns as you may appoint for their Reffdence on Parole; and that you intimate to the Spanish Officers belonging to the Frigates lately detained, that their private Property will be reffored to them accordingly.

Given under out hands, the 23d January 1805.

x Jtio Cofpoys. '

P. Patton.

To tV. Dickinfin.

The Commissioners for the Transport Service, and for the Care and Custody of Prisoners of War.

RESOLUTIONS reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raism*

the Supply granted to Ills Majesty.

1. RESOLVED, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to Ilia Majesty, the Duties payable on Importation into Ireland of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize (not being the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of Great Britain) and of the Drawbacks to be allowed on the due Exportation thereof from Ireland; and also the Duties payable upon the Exportation of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, of the growth, produce, or manufacture of Ireland; and also the Duties granted by an Act of the last Session of Parliament upon Ships, Vessels, or other Bottoms, trading to Ireland from any Country whatsoever, over and above all other Duties payable on the tonnage thereof, and upon Entries Inwards and Outwards in the Port of Dublin over and above all Fees payable on the fame; and also the Bounties and Allowances granted, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, on the Exportation of certain Manufactures of Ireland, and on the Importation of Bark or Hemlock for Tannen use, do cease and determine; and that the several and respective Duties, Drawbacks, Allowances, and Bounties following, be paid and allowed in lieu thereof; Viz.

RESOLVED, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged a Duty of Six Puunds upon every One hundred Pounds of the amount of the Duties payable by Law on all Goods, Wares, and Merchandise (except Sugar, and except Goods the growth, produce, or manufacture of Great Britain) which shall be imported into Ireland by any pertouu being a Retailer or Consumer of such Goods, Wares, and Merchandize.

3. RF.SOLV E D, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Four Pence per Gallon be allowed on all Spirits distilled in Ireland from Malt made of Corn of the growth of Ireland, w hen the price of Barley lha.ll not exceed Sixteen Shillings British currency the barrel, and which shall be export'd from Ireland, except to Great Britain.

4. RESOLVED, That it is the Opinion of thie Committee, That a Bounty of One Shilling and Nine Pence for every thirty-two Gallons be allowed on all Strong Beer or Ale made wholly from Malt the growth or produce of Ireland, when the price of Barley shall not exceed Sixteen Shillings per Barrel British currency, which shall be exported from Ireland, except to Great Britain.

MINUTE of the Lords of the Council respecting Licences to be granted for the Exportation and Importati

France, Spain, and Holland.

At the Council Chamber, Whitehall, the iStli of May 1803:

Prerent-—'The Lords of His Majesty’s most Honourable Privy Council.

j^5..Al)_Several applications of the Merchants of London trading to the Continent, dating, That their Trade and Commerce is greatly embarralTcd by the late political events between this Country, France, Holland, and Spain, and representing that they have a great deal of Property now lying in the Ports of France, Holland, and Spain, which has in part been paid for, and which is considered as being British Property, and having no means of getting fuel) produce trom those Countries, unless ths Government of this Country would grant

Licences, under His Majesty's Sign Manual, to allow the Importation in Neutral Vessels of such Goods and Merchandize upon the fame terms as during the late war.

Their Lordships came to a Resolution, That it be recommended to His Majesty to grant Licences under Sign Manual, for the Imports tion of Goods from France, Spain, and Holland, of the fame description as were allowed during the late war, and in the same manner; and also to recommend to His Majesty to grant Licences for the Exportation of such Goods, tb those Countries, us were allowed during the late war; and that this be considered as a general rule with respect to Exportations and Importations to and from France, Spain, and Holland, until further Order of this Board.

Note.—In the year 1606, certain Rates of Value were affixed to the several Articles Imported into, and Exported from this Kingdom $ and, consonant to these Eirumtes, the ledgers of the Inspector General's Office are ffill kept, and the Public Accounts Hated accordingly.

The Official Rates are in general much under the true Value, but in one or two Inffances (particularly Coffee Exported) they greatly exceed, and therefore in the foregoing Statement the Price of Coffee has been reduced to as nearly its real Value, in each Year, as could be ascertained.

The Declared Value of British Produce and Manufactures Exported under the Act of the 43d of His Majesty, cap. 43. amounted in the Year ending 5th January 1804, to £.40,100,870, and in the Year ending 5th January 1805, to £. 40,349,642.

The Account of the Value of the Imports from India and China, for the Year ending 5th January 1805, cannot yet be prepared.

He said. That he saw the calculations of Mefirs. The Witness further said. That the price of British Herrings in the London market, at the beginning of 1801, was from 35 to 405*. per barrel, and he believed the Swedish Herrings would have fold for nearly the fame price.

That he (Mr. Cowie) received several Accounts of Tales effected in the West Indies in 1802, which shewed a disappointmenfc and loss in part; but till the Tales more generally arrived in 1803, tlicy could not clearly ascertain the extent of the loss; those further Accounts which came in that year enabled them to make up an Account in July, and they prefen ted a Memorial to the Lords of the Treasury, Hating the circumstances of their loss, some months afterwards, when they could ascertain with sufficient correctneis that no further returns were to be expected.

Mr. Cowie further fiated. That his regular and accustomed tradtand commission business presented sufficient and more certain advantages, but his motives and those of his partner, were to benefit the Country, to follow up the wishes of Government, and open a branch of trade of an important nature, and in a high degree beneficial to the West India

Colonies, as the repeated memorials and folieitations of the Merchanti and Planters to Government for many years past would fully prove.

He further stated, That in communicating the information and plan Messrs. Chalmers and Cowie did to Mr. Mackenzie, and in the subsequent conferences they had with Mr. Wilberforce, and the information given by them in such conferences, they understood they were acting throughout by the with, and at the requeli of the Provision Committee, although through the interference of individuals; and the Witness gave the following reasons for such underffanding,—there was no Swedish merchant, nor any other perl'on who gave information to the Committee but themselves; that information was laid before Mr. Rose and Mr. Pitt, as he was informed by Mr. Wilberforce, and acted upon by Government;—fo that the importation was created by the Act before alluded to.

He also Hated, That from the beginning to the end of the trans-action, in the measures they pursued, they acted in confidence of this underffanding; they were distinctly told by Mr. Role, that tha prohibition against the exportation of British Herrings would continue in force, so that their importation would go to supply the West India demand; and they would not have written a letter on the subject of the importation, had they not understood it was the wish and at the desire of the Provision Committee, and of the Government; and no other mercantile house whatever having acted upon that occasion but themselves, renders theirs an unique case.

Mr. Cowie further Hated, That had the passing of the Act taken off the prohibition and the distress of the Country, and the demand for the West India market been previously known to him, it was not at all in his contemplation that he should have engaged in the importations, without the communications he had with the Committee, and the desire expressed that he should wait upon Mr. Pitt, who hud expressed a wish to fee them upon the subject. That at the time they engaged in that importation, they had no assurance that an embargo would not take place, nothing having palfed on the subject; the embargo was therefore quite unexpected, as the Act for allowing thi importation of Swedish Herrings passed on the 31st of December 1800, and on the 14th of January following the order for the embargo was issued; but during that interval, their property was committed to the extent Hated. The probability of such an embargo did not enter into their consideration at the time of giving their first orders.

Being asked. Whether he received any communication from the Committee, except that the prohibition would be taken off? Mr. Cowie said, That he and his partner received from the Committee, or Members of the Committee, whose names have already been mentioned, the ff rongeff encouragement to import, as the distress at that time was very urgent; that the encouragement held out by those Members was the great demand for the article, as a measure benefiting the poor, and to supply the West India market; and that the prohibition against exporting British Herrings would continue in force.

Charles Chalmers, Esq. the partner of Mr. Cowie, is a merchant in London; and, being examined, confirmed the evidenci of Mr. Cowie, Hating himself to be well acquainted witji all the facts to which Mr. Cowie had been examined, and having been prefeuUt all the conferences referred to in the evidence of Mr. Cowie.

✓The Witness further Hated, that he had several interviews with Mr. Rose when his'partuer was not present, and received upon such interviews, the ffrongelt encouragement to proceed in the importation of Swedish Herrings; that the encouragement so received went farther than an assurance, that the importation of Swedish Herrings should be allowed; and Mr. Rose particularly pressed him to ule every expedition in the power of himself and his partner to bring the Herrings to England.

That, in one of the interviews the Witness had with Mr. Rose, he told him, Messrs. Chalmers and Cowie had dispatched a cutter to Sweden, with orders for the fish; of which Mr. Rose highly approved, and requeiled the Witness and his partner would use every expedition in their power, which would highly benefit the Country at that period; that this latter conversation took place about lour or five days after the cutter had been dispatched.

The Witness further said, that the promise Hated in the e\.m dence of Mr. Cowie, that Licences would be granted lor the ff’.ps engaged by Messrs. Chalmers and Cowie in England, was communicated first, verbally, by Mr. Enos Smith, one of the clerks in H.e Council Office; and then by letter from the same clerk, which the Witness produced; and also by assurances to the Witness by M* Fawkener and Sir Stephen Cottrell; that the assurances given by Mr. Fawkener and Sir Stephen Cottrell were, "That their Lordihps " had considered the application of the Witness and his Partner, and, 4< from the hardship of their case, in not being able to get the " cargoes to market, Licences would be granted* The ltuels said, he had been informed that the delay respecting the Licences h^ been occasioned by His Mcjeffy's then indisposition; but the Wilt'd* lmd no reason to know why the general order or procLroaU»a, spoken of in the evidence of Mr. Cowie, did not appear in the

Mr. Robert George Steele, the principal and confidential clerk of MelTrs. Chalmers and Cowie, was examined; and said, that he was well acquainted with all the mercantile Transactions of MelTrs. Chalmers and Cowie, and with all their operations respecting the importation of Swedish Herrings in 1801; he said, that they had not been engaged in the importation of Herrings before that time.

The Witness then confirmed the evidence of Mr. Cowie, as to the dates of the different arrivals of the Herrings in question; the measures taken by the Petitioners to effell Tales of the Herrings; and the costs and charges attending their purchase and importation; and also the proceeds of the Tales.

Thomas Rowcroet, Esq. a merchant, and one of the Aldermen of the city of London, being examined, Hated, that he saw the Herrings imported determined by Mefirs. Chalmers and Cowie, in the year 1801, which, in their original date, were good and merchantable Swedish Herrings; but when he saw them they did not appear to have been fresh, but to have been delayed in the importation; and the Witness adviied their being Tent to the West Indies for Tale, as the only means of making any thing of them, there being no sale lor them in England.

Mr. Henry Anderson, a dealer in provisions, and wharfinger, being examined, dated, that he had the charge of the whole 19,500 barrels of Swedish Herrings, unported by MelTrs. Chalmers and Cowie. He confirmed the evidence of Mr. Cowie, as to the dates of their arrival; the previous failing of the spring fleets for the West Indies, in 1801; the rish being of a good quality; the endeavours ul'rd to effect sales in England; and the measures taken to render them fit for exportation.

John Foulerton, Esq. a merchant in London, and a Scotch factor, and Mr. Lawrence Bruce, formerly a captain in the Jamaica trade, but since retired, being separalely examined, spoke to the fame fads as Mr. Anderson. The Witness, Bruce, had purchased some of the Herrings prepared for exportation; and the three last Witnesses agreed, that the conduit pui sued by MelTrs. Chalmers and Cowie, in exporting the Herrings to the West Indies for sale on their own account, was proper and prudent; and that this was the only measure which could have been pursued to avoid a total loss of the property.

Mr. Arthur Strother, a merchant in London, being examined, laid, ‘That he proceeded to the West Indies, at the request of MelTrs. Chalmers and Cowie, in the beginning of December 1801, as super-cargo, to efl’ed sales of a quantity of Swedish Herrings imported by them. The Witness dated, in confirmation of Mr. Cowie s evidence, that he had examined the Account of Payments and Receipts hereto annexed, and marked Appendix (N° 1.) which he said was correct, as far as the part of the Herrings under his management.

The Witness further dated, That he was also in the West Indies in the months of May and June 1801, and that he had the strongelt reason to believe, that, had the Herring* been in the West Indies at that tune, they would have fold exceedingly high, from the observations he made on the date of the markets at that period.

The AIT of the 41ft of His Majedv, cap. 10. (passed on the 15th of December 1800) was read; by the 3d fecTion of which a bounty was secured to the Importers of Corn, equal to the difference between the market-price after arrival and the price mentioned in the All of Parliament.

The Ad of the 41ft of His Majesty, cap. 21. (passed on the 3id December 1800) was also read; by the 17th and 18th sections of which, persons entitled to a bounty upon exporting Pilchards were allowed to fell them for home consumption, and receive the bounty as if they had been exported. By the same Act, advantages were also held out to persons engaged, or who should engage, in the Fisheries at ihat period.

Claes Grill, Esq. the Consul General for Sweden, being examined, said, That in January 1801, he made application, through the Swedidi AmbatTador, to the Britidi Government, for allowance for maintenance of the crews of such Swedish ships as were detained by embargo in the ports of Great Britain ajid Ireland; the Witness received from Government, in consequence of that application, at the rate of 3 s. 6<f. per day for each captain, 2$. per day for each mate, and 1 s. 3 d. per day for each of the remaining part of the crew, amounting in the whole to about £. *24,000.

The Witness said, lie had every reason to believe that a similar application was made, and with similar success, on behalf of the Danish drips detained by the fame embargo, as the Witness was pre-lent, and attended with Mr. Wolfe, the Danish Consul, upon Mr. Rose, at the Treasury, when the allowance to be made was settled; and the Witness said, kt believed the sum received by Mr. Wolfe was

about £. 22,000; this money, he said, was given to afford maintenance to the men during their detention by the embargo.

The Witness further dated, That he had always looked upon Messrs. Chalmers and Cowie as merchants in ths commission line; and that he did not know of any instance of their buying goods on their own account.

David Bristow Baker, Esq. a merchant in London, being examined, said, That he had received several Turns of money from J. F. Hage, who was a Commissioner on the part of the Danish Government, to arrange the outstanding claims of the Danish subjects in the West India islands upon the British Government, which Turns were placed in the WitnessV hands on account of the Danish West India Company; and he underdood the Turns were paid by the English Government on account of ships, or other Danish property, detained by British cruizers. The Witness said, he had also received sums on the fame account for other Danish subjects, amounting altogether to £.47,261.

Robert Cowie, Esq. being again examined, said, That, as agent for the Swedish East India Company, he had received various Turns of money of the British Government for Losses fudained by three Swedish Indiainen, one of which was seized at the Cape of Good Hope, another at St. Helena, and a third on the North Seas, and all brought into British ports, under the Order in Council of the 14th January 1801: That there had been an allowance made by Government for Swedidi Tailors impreded and taken to India; for anchors, fails, and cables, and a variety of port charges; besides the maintenance of officers and crews, and the expence of furnishing great part of one of the crews: the whole amount received by the Witness for the three ships was about £.4,200*

The Witness further dated, That he had not received any allowance or compensation for his Losses from the Swedish Government, nor had he any claim upon that Government, as the ships with his property on board were not prevented from failing by any AH of the Swedish Government, but the fear of being captured in England had detained them in the Swedish port.

The Witness further said, That he had never before, or subsequent to the importation of the Herrings in quedion, purchased goods of any description upon speculation; but that his trade had been solely that of a Commission Merchant, except in one indance about twenty years ago, which was a very small purchase.

George Cowie, Esq. a merchant in London, being examined, said, That he had received from the Transport Board, in consequence of an application to the Lords of His Majesty’s Treasury, the fubfldence money for the maders and crews of five diips, detained at Gibraltar during the embargo laid on by His Majest/s Order in Council of the 14th January 1801, amounting to £*731* He also received for the dock hire of the ship Cron Prince Guda Adolph, and for another ship, named the Wanfgapen, her full freight, although her cargo of fruit, which was sold by order of Government, did not produce so much as the freight amounted to.

HEPORT from th* SELECT COMMITTEE on the Tenth Bepokt of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry; respecting the

Office of the Treasurer of His Majest/s Navy.

*tHE SELECT COMMITTEE to whom the Tenth Report Of the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry (respecting the Office of the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy) was referred, to enquire into the Application of any Monies, issued to the Treasurer of the Navy for Naval Services, to Purposes not Naval; and whether any, and what Representations were made to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, or the Chancellor of the Exchequer, respecting the withdrawing from the Bank, any Sums of Money so issued, since the passing of the Act of 25 Geo. 1IL c. 31.; and also into the Proceedings had for the Recovery of the Debt due to the Crown by the late Adam Jellicoe;—Have agreed to the following Report.

Irr taking into our consideration the Three Subjects which are re-ilrred to Your Committee, it occurred to us, that though the First, interms, comprehends an Enquiry, generally and without restriction, into the application of any Monies issued to the Treasurer of the Navy for Naval Services, to purposes not Naval; yet it must necessarily have been the intention of the House to exclude from our consideration ill such Monies so issued and so applied as were to be the subject of sneafnres which the Attorney General was directed, by an Order of thi House, to take " by due course of Law, for ascertaining and re-u covering any Sums of Money that may be due from Lord Melville u and Alexander Trotter, Esquire, in respect of any Profits derived 44 by them from Monies issued for Naval Services, and that may have M come to their hands subsequent to the first of January 1786 —

We, therefore, conceived it not to be our duty to enquire, whether any Sums issued for Naval Purposes had been applied by Lord Melville or Mr. Trotter to their own use, for which they would be responsible in the civil suit to be instituted against them.

In prosecuting our Enquiry with this reserve, it could not be previously known to us, bow any particular sum of money so issued had been applied, till such sum had boSn traced to the actual application of it. We were therefore necessarily, in some instances, led into an examination, which, without adverting to this difficulty, might appear to exceed the bounds of the Enquiry, which vre understood to have been prescribed to ns 5 leaving it to the* Party examined to object to the questions that were proposed to him, on the ground of their tending pesfonally to charge him, whenever he thought fit to do so.

Of the sums issued for Naval Services, and afterwards applied to Purposes not Naval, which the cause of this Enquiry brought into our view, it appears that the sum of £.40,000. came into the Hands of Lord Melville, and was advanced by the joint concurrence of his

Various foifts appear also to have been advanced by Mr* Trotter, during a period of between fourteen and fifteen years, whilst he was Paymaster of the Navy under Lord Melville, to the order of Lord Melville, amounting in all to 22 or £.23,600. which we shall distin-guifti by the name of The Aggregate Sum of 22 or £. 23,000:; about one half of which, Mr. Trotter states to have been advanced exclu-fively from Public Money: the rest from a fund, which is called in Mr. Trotter’s evidence, his Mixed Fund at Messrs. Coutts, confiding partly of public and partly of private money; for which Aggregate Sum of 22 or £. 23,000. no interest was paid.

Iu order to avoid confusion, it may be proper here to state, that Mr. Trotter was desired by Lord Melville to borrow for him, and did advance to him for his private use, a further sum of between 22 and £.23,000. of which he was himself the lender, and for which he charged him with interest at £.5. per cent.; but from what fond the fame was drawn by Mr. Trotter, we did Hot think it proper to enquire.

He was also occasionally in advance iii his Account Current to Lord Melville, in sums to the amount of from 10 to £.20,000. as mentioned in the Tenth Report, which came entirely from the Mixed Fund at Messrs. Contts and Company (the Balance upon that Account beiilg also occasionally in favour of Lord Melville to the amount of 2 or £.3,000.); and for the last mentioned sum of 22 or £.23,000. so lent on interest, as well as for such Balance when it was in favour of Mr. Trottfer, he states, that, he considered Lord Melville as his private debtor; but on such Balances in the Account Current, no interest on either fide was pffid.

Of the specific fom therefore of £.22 or £.23,000 so lent on inte«* rest, and those occafmnal advances in the Account Current from the Mixed Fnnd at MeflVs. Coutts and Company, mentioned in the Appendix to the Tenth Report, we shall abstain altogether from taking further notice; confining our remarks to the several sums of £. 40,000., £. 10,000., and the Aggregate Sum of 42 or £. 23,000.; upon none of which any interest was paid.

As to thfe £:40,oooo.; the diversion of it from Nava! Services to Which it was appropriated, contrary to the provisions and meaningjof the 25th of George the III. C. 31. attracted our earliest attention, and called for a full and minute enquiry into the causes and circumstancc6 of that transaction.

For this purpose, several Witnesses have been called before us; from whose evidence it appears, that in December 1795 a contract was made by Government with the Houses of Messrs. Boyd and Company, Robarts and Company, and Goldsmid and Company, for a Loan 0

That Loan was contracted for conjointly by the fame parties who were concerned in the preceding Loan; all, Houses at that time of unsuspected credit; each House being generally considered, subsequent to the payment of the deposit for which they were all jointly liable, responsible only for the amount of the ffiares then held by them re-speriteely. Of the latter Loan in the beginning of September 1796, two instalments, of 15 per cent, were due.

In the beginning of the year 1796, from the embarrassment of Public Credit, and the decreasing state of the specie at the Rank, the Governor and Directors thought it prudent to restrain their engagements; and upon that account had refuted advancing the progressive payments upon the Loan of December 1795; but in consideration of the purposes for which the Loan of April 1796 had been liiade, as well as of its being comparatively small, they consented to advance to the Contractors, and did advance, the third, fourth, fifth, and Hxth payments; requiring them to make the seventh, being the lait payment, which was to become due on the 26th of October in that year.

It is dated in the evidence given to Your Committee, that the autumn of 1796 was a period of peculiar embarralTinent, both of public and private credit; which led to the reftrtelions of payments in specie at the Bank, that took place in February 1797; that there was a very great run on private commercial houses, a great scarcity of money, and a very heavy prelTure on the Bank for discounts, which they had been obliged materially to narrow, and had thought it ne-celfary to contract their accommodations both to Government and the Commercial World, not however making any distindion between the house of Boyd and Company, and houses of the first mercantile credit in the City of London.

Under these circumstances, at some time before the gth of September 1796, Mr. Boyd appears to have represented to Lord Melville and Mr. Pitt, the great pecuniary difficulty and embarrassment of his house; that the Bank had refuted to discount their bills, and that, with ample Securities in their hands, they were not enabled to raise money to pay the next inHalment on the Loan, which was nearly due, and requested immediate pecuniary affiltance for the purpose of completing their engagements to Government.

It appears to Your Committee, that in addition to these engagements to Government, Messrs. Boyd and Company had large payments to make on account of the Emperor of Germany; that they paid, on the 3ill of October 1796, a sum of £. 186,340. 13. 1. on account of the Director of the Emperor's Finances at Vienna; and that, in the whole of the same year, they remitted, on the fame account, sums amount-% ing to £.4,609,506. 9. o. It appears also in evidence, that it would have been difficult, and perhaps impossible, for Messrs. Boyd and Company to have procured advances upon the securities in their possession (which we shall hereafter mention) or to have converted them into cash; that a payment of 15 per cent, on the Loan of £. 18,000,000. was due on the 9th of September; and that, had they brought to market such a proportion of their Scrip, as was necessary to raise the said sum of £.40,000. in order to make good their engagement, the probable consequences would have been, to increase the discount on Scrip, which at that time amounted on the Loan of April, from 13 to 15 per cent, to uffed injuriously the credit of Boyds house, especially if it had trailfpired that their necellities compelled them to make such disadvantageous fates, and mull thereby have had a general tendency to augment the embarrassinent of Public Credit.

It has also been Hated in evidence to Your Committee, that if a failure in the Loans then in progress of payment, had been ocealioned, either in the whole or in part, by the circumstances above Hated, the deficiency could not have been supplied by a fresh Loan (had it been necessary to resort to such a measure) except upon terms of very con-Hderable loss and disadvantage to the Public.

Under these difficulties, Lord Viscount Melville, then Treasurer of the Navy, appears to have fuggeHed to Mr. Pitt, that the lum wanted by Messrs. Boyd and Company, might be spured, without a probability that the Naval Service would fuller any inconvenience from the advance, provided there was a sufficient security for the repayment; and no other method having occurred, by which much serious mischief to the Public could be prevented, it was thought advisable, by the concurrent opinions of Lord Melville and Mr. Pitt, that the application of Messrs. Boyd and Company should be complied with, and that the sum of £.40,000. should be advanced, upon a sufficient security being given. And it appears in evidence, that, under the orders of I.oid Melville, the sum of £.40,000. was drawn from the Bank, and on the fame day paid over to Mr. Boyd, by Mr. Long, then Secretary of the Treasury, upon Mr. Boyd’s depositing with Mr. Long, securities amounting to about £.40,700. confiding, in part of bills drawn on and accepted by the Kail India Company from their Presidencies abroad, the rest of Government Securities, which Mr. Long tranlinit-

Your Committee, duly considering the reference under which their powers are derived, have not felt themselves at liberty to come to any specific refutations on tim merits of the several transactions which have been the subjects of their Enquiry; they have deemed it even more confident with their duty, to abstain from observations, which might fecin to convey a judgment upon any of the points inquestion.

They have endeavoured to give tLe IJoufe a correct summary of the material parts of the evidence, confining their remarks ftrilUy within the limits of explanation; leaving the conclufious to be deduced therefrom altogether to the wisdom of the House :—But have

thought it right to annex, in the Appendix, the whole of the evidence taken before them; considering this course of proceeding, under all the circumstances, as likely to prove more satisfactory to the House, than if they had omitted those parts, which, upon a minute review, they might have thought not immediately relevant to t’ie object of enquiry; trailing, that if in any instance the examination should appear to have exceeded the ftrid line of investigation prescribed to them, it will be attributed to the desire they have felt to execute, in the fullest manner, the duty intruded to them by tht House.

Boyd and Company, who were Contractors for the Loan; that the Bank had refused to make their payments on the Loan as ulnal, or to discount their bills; and that, with ample securities in their hands, they were not enabled to raise money to pay the next instahnent, which was then just becoming due. That under these circumstances be thought it a public object to support the house; that if the house failed it would involve many others in its ruin, and give a great blow to commercial credit, already very much shaken. lie said they required the sum of £.40,000. to enable them to make good their engagement to Government; that he had found the means of advancing that sum, and which he could do without inconvenience, provided undoubted security was given for the repavroent of that sum within a very short period; that with this view of the subject be would place the sum of £.40,000. in my hands, deffring I would deliver it to Mr. Boyd, upon his giving such security as he had described, and that Mr. Boyd would call upon me at the Treasury tht fame day with such security. I do not ailed to state this conversation with precise accuracy at this period, but as well as I recoiled, tli# above is the substance of it. Upon going to the Treasury I found Mr. Boyd there, and delivered to him the sum of £.40,000. and received the security, amounting to Xomething more than £.40,000; I put these securities into a paper, which I 1‘ealed up, and transmitted them immediately to Lord Melville.

The Examination of Samuel Thorntox, Esq. (a Member of the Committee) taken the 8th of May 1805.

Do you recollect applications made to the Bank by the House of Boyd, to make certain advances upon a loan or loans contrutf ed for by that house in the years 1795 and 1796?—I would premise that the loan taken in November 1795, was taken by Messrs. Boyd and Company, and conjointly with Messrs. Robarts and Curtis, Goldlmid and others, from whom there was a joint application made to the Bank for advances on the said loan in February 1796, but owing to the then state of public credit, and the situation of the Bank with relped to its specie, the Directors thought it prudent to restrain their engagements as much as poffihle; and as a principal means of so doing, and from that cause only, as far as my recollection serves, they declined advancing the progressive payments of the loan for the service of that year.

Were any subsequent applications made by the Contractors in the same year, and of the fame fort?—Two more applications were made, the first of them in May 1796, which was declined by the Bank on the grounds I have already mentioned; the next application was for an advance on a loan of seven millions and an half, which had been negociated in April 1796, for the express purpose of funding j£.7,5°°,o°o. chiefly of Exchequer Bills, and partly Navy Bills, held by the Bank, and for the express purpose of relieving the Bank from its advances to Government, which at that time pressed heavily upon it; in consideration of the nature of this loan, and the comparative smallness of its amount) the Directors contented to advance the 3d, 4th, 5th, and 6th payments, requiring the Contractors to pay the seventh and last, which’becume due on the 26th of October 1796.

Were the difficulties of the Bank then, and the necessity they felt themselves under to narrow their discounts, owing in a great, or any degree, to the advances made to Government, and the failure on the part of Government to repay those advances at the periods stipulated?— It was the prevailing opinion among the Directors, that the cause mentioned was a principal occasion of their difficulties, to which however must be added, a general alarm that prevailed in the Country, from an apprehension of the attacks of the enemy.

Was the step taken by the Bank to narrow their discounts, with & view in any degree to check general speculations, or the speculations of any particular house ?—I believe it was taken solely with the view to contract their own engagements; a house, supposed to be involved in hazardous sperulation, never enjoys the fame credit at the Bank as those who conduct their business in a regular way, hut this circumstance would only restrain the advances of the Bank to that particular house.

Did the House of Boyd enjoy as much of the confidence of the Bank at the time the applications made for the advances upon loans contracted for by them were made and refilled, as any other house, And were they treated respecting their discounts with the fame favour as any other house of the high eft credit in London?—Except their engagements with the Public, Messrs. Boyd and Company had *10 engagements, that were known to the Bank, to be of a nature or Extent that precluded them from receiving the fame accommodation as other houses of the first credit.

Did they in point of fad receive such accommodation?—Except the advances on the Loan they received all, or nearly all the accommodation they aiked for, to the belt of my remembrance.

How long did that confidence in the house of Boyd, on the part of the Bank, and the accommodation consequent upon it, continue ?— Until a few months before their failure, at which time I was so convinced of their ultimate insolvency, that I thought it my duty to apprise the Chancellor of the Exchequer; and at the negociation of a public Loan, which I believe succeeded next to that of 1796, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in my presence, refused to admit Mr. Boyd and others concerned with him as bidders, which they had offered to become.

Could you by reference to any document, give the date of such bidding?—I believe I could.

Was Mr. Boyd present ?—He was not; but two Gentlemen offered a bidding for themselves and him, and Mr. Boyd sent printed circular letters, intimating, that such bidding was to be considered as a continuation of his lifts for the Loan; one of which letters I saw.

Were the securities of the East India Company negociable in the months of August, September, and October, 1796?—The Bank discount only Bills that are payable within two months from the time at which they are offered; if the India Bills in the possession of Melfrs. Boyd and Company had a large time to run, I conceive there might be difficulty in getting advances on them at that period.

Do you apprehend houses of the first credit could not by any means have converted them into cash ?—I think houses, who had not before been under the necessity of railing large supplies, might have got such accommodation.

Do East India Bills, of the nature of those held by Messrs. Boydt as far as the Committee have had any description of them, bear interest?—The Bills drawn by the Presidencies of India are frequently made payable at two periods, at the option of the Court of Directors; if discharged at the first period mentioned in the Bill, no interest is received; but if the later period of payment is chosen by the Directors, the Bills bear interest for the time the payment is so pro traded.

Can information be obtained from any document in the hands of the Bank, of the drafts drawn by the Paymaster of the Navy Pay Office, during the months of August, September, and October, 1796? —From the Bank books, an account may be given of all payments made by them, but the drafts, which are the vouchers of such payments, have always been returned to the Navy Pajr Office, when the account has been liquidated.

Suppofnig the contracts for the two Loans, then in progress of payment, had been dissolved, must not the advance of price to be paid by the Public for any new Loan have at least been equal to the discount on the Loan then existing?—I think there would have been great loss and great difficulty in negociating a fresh Loan for the supplies of that year; but it must be a matter of doubt whether it would bear an exact proportion to the discount on the existing Loan, in the hands of 1 necessitous people, who, from their situation, must press the sale in an. undue degree; I have no hesitation, however, to express my opinion, the cancelling a contract for a Loan at that period of the year would have been as calamitous as it would have beta unprecedented.

Had the practice continued, without interruption, from the period of January 1786 to the period of your discovery of it?—I know nothing to the contrary.

Did the practice appear to you irregular, and contrary to law?— As the practice of drawing money from the Bank into the hands of the different Cashiers, for the purpose of subsequent distribution, had been dated by the Commissioners of Enquiry in 1782 to be absolutely necessary, which practice was perhaps hardly jullifiable according to the drid letter of the Ad that was passed pursuant to their fuggef-tions, and which practice, neverthelela, it was impossible to suppose that Ad was intended to prohibit, it did not immediately appear to me that the practice of drawing money out of the Bank into the hands of a private Banker, if carried on bon& fide for the fame purposes of official convenience, and for those only, was necessarily illegal or unjudifiable; I felt it however to be a confulecable objection to the practice, that it was in fad a substitution by the authority of the Treasurer of the Navy, for however short a time, of the security of a private Banking-house, however respedable, in the room of the security of the Bank, or of the Clerks of his own office; and I was sensible that this practice, in common with that of placing sums of money in the hands of the Cashiers, or of the Clerks at the Out-ports, or even in the iron chelt of the Office, was in fume degree liable to febufc, undoubtedly in a greater degree than the practices lad referred to.

Did you discover that abuse had arisen out of this practice ?—I did not.

Were you ever informed, or had you ever reason to believe that the Public Money had, in consequence of this practice, been used to purposes of private emolument?—I was undoubtedly aware that the habitual passage of considerable sums through the hands of a private Ranker, for however short a time each particular sum might remain upon his books, mud be some advantage to the general concerns of the house, but I had no reason whatever to susped, nor did I in fad susped that any sums of money, after being drawn by Mr. Trotter from the Bank, for Naval Services, and placed in the hands of Messrs. Coutts, were subsequently drawn from that house for any purposes whatsoever, except the Nav^l Services for which they were originally drawn.

Did you ever communicate to the present Chancellor of the Exchequer the irregularity you had discovered?—It is difficult for me, at this distance of time, to recoiled every incidental conversation I may have had with the Chancellor of the Exchequer; the only converlhtion which I recoiled having had with him on that fuljed, while I was in office, was, 1 believe, a lliort time before or after my visit to the Bank, which was subsequent to Mr. Pitts leaving office, and the object of which is fluted iti my Evidence before the Commissioners of Naval Enquiry; the steps I did take will appear in that Evidence, to which I beg leave to refer.

Do you recoiled the terms, or the substance of the conversation that passed between you and Mr. Pitt ?—I only recoiled very generally, that I mentioned to him the nature of the practice, with the reasons which led me to believe it to be irregular, and that I Hated my intention of changing it; and as far as I can remember, Mr. Pitt appeared to agree with me in opinion, that it was desirable it should be changed. I had a subsequent conversation with Mr. Pitt, when we were both out of office, in the Autumn 1802; the only thing I recoiled that the name of Mr. Coutts Trotter occurred in that conversation, and that J mentioned to Mi. Pitt that 1 thought it not improbable that either the circumstance of the Naval Money passing in part through the hands of the house of Coutts, to whicu I found that he belonged, might have led to his introduction into that house, or that the circumstance of his being a partner in it might have led to the feledion of that house for that purpose; I meant this with a reference to advantage derived to the general concerns of a Banking-house necessarily arising from the nature of their business, however cautiously conducted, and not from having any reason to believe that the Naval Money was used for the benefit of Mr. Alexander Trotter; I had the less reafou to susped it, as his fa-lary had been increased, I think, in May 1800 from £. 500 a year to £. 800., on account of its inadequacy to the importance of his office.

The further Examination of James Drummond, Esq.—taken 15th May 1805.

Is that book in your hand the caffi-book of August 1798, of Boyd and Bentield?—Yes.

Can you point out in the books before you, the entry of the sum advanced to Mr. Boyd of £.40,000. in the year 1796, by Lord Melville, or anonymous, which you may conclude to have been such advance upon the security of East India Company Bills and other public securities ?—It appears by an entry in the cash-book of 9th September 1796, that bills to the atnouftt of £. 11,828. 11 s, 9 d. on the East India Company; to the amount of £.5,041. is, 8d, on the Treasury; a further sum of £.11,000. on the Treasury; and £.12,834. 8s. 2d, on the Victualling Office, making together the sum of £.40,704. is, 7d, were delivered to Mr. Boyd to discount, or raise money upon them; that Ivlr. Boyd accordingly paid to the house on account thereof £.30,000.-00 the 9th day of September aforesaid* and a further sum of £. 10/300. on the following day. I wish to (late in explanation of my evidence on a former day, that in the first part of my examination, my mind bore upon an earlier period than I now perceive the question applies to. I was asked concerning the Loan contracted for in December 1795: My answer referred to the preceding lx>an for the service of the year 1795, in which the Imperial Loan of £.4,600,000. was included; the Loan contracted for in November or December 1795, confided only of £. 18,000,000., and did not include any Loan to the Emperor. About the 15th of April following, a further Loan of seven millions and an half was raised for the service of the year 1796; this first erroneous impressioti ran through other parts of my evidence. I do not recollect any difficulty was experienced in money transactions during the year 1795, but it is a fad generally known, that great inconveniencies were sustained from what is usually termed a scarcity of money early in the Spring of 1796; and from the time that the Bank of England came to the resolution of narrowing their discounts, that inconvenience continued to increase until the latter end of February 1797, when an Order of Council was made for suspending the issue of caffi by the Bank; in consequence of this general depredation of credit, the Loan of April 1796 was, in less than six weeks, three and an half per-cent. discount; by the end of July, at seven and three quarters per-cent, discount; and at the end of September, 13 per-cent, discount; the other funds fell in proportion; it was nevertheless always possible to fell funded property, ferip, Arc. at a greater or less discount; but the best mercantile securities, bills of exchange of undoubted credit and solidity, and even the acceptances of Government, and the East India Company, when at long dates, became in a great degree unavailable, that is to say, they could not be difeounted at legal interest. That these general distresses bore with severe pressure on the house of Boyd, Benfield, and Company; I never meant to deny, it was the more felt by them at that time, as their transactions were then of considerable magnitude, having large payments and remittances to make on account of the Emperor, in addition to all the other concerns of their establishment.

In answer to some of the questions, I have stated, that I was in the Constant habit of communicating with Mr. Boyd concerning the affairs of the house, but that I could not be certain whether upon all occasions, his communications to me were unreserved— In saying so, I was very far from meaning to infmuate any thing to the disadvantage of Mr. Boyd, for whose character and abilities I always did, and still do, entertain the highest opinion: I only meant to say, that our situation9 were very different in many respects, mine was that of an acting laborious partner in the executive business of the house, and particularly in the correspondence department; it was my duty to follow his in-struriions, and ta inform him of every tiling that occurred; he, on tfic contrary, was frequently placed in fituauons which might have rendered a full and free communication with roe on every point very improper. I recoiled particularly* that early in the month of June 1796, the Baron de Muller arrived from Vienna on a special million from the direction of his Imperial Majestys finances, and that Mr. Boyd was confidentially employed by him and Count Straremberg in negociating some plan of further pecuniary supplies to the Emperor with His Majesty’s Cabinet Ministers. In consequence of those negotiations, the house of Boyd, Benfield, and Company, were in-struded to facilitate the means of further supplies to the Emperor, and sent a person to Hamburgh about the latter end of July 1796 for that express purpose, with unlimited credit upon the house. Mr. Boyd only communicated to me, on this and other fnuilar occasions, as much As it was necessary I should know, for the purpose of carrying the resolutions into execution.

Do you find any entry of payment on instalmemts on the Loan, corresponding to the entry of the receipt above stated of £. 40,000. ?—

Mr. Pitt’s name is, I pfriume, occasionally inserted in the Minutes as present, if be happens, although not actually in the Board-room, to be in his own house; so that any matter of a very special nature, upon which the opinion of the First Lord of the Treasury should he considered as indispensable, might be immediately referred to him; but I believe it was not customary to insert the names of the junior Lords if they were not actually present.

When are the names of the Lords present put down?—They are put down as the commencement of the proceedings of the day, as soon as the Board begins to ftt, and if during the fitting any Lord should come in, his name 16 added to the rest, which would account for Mr. Sinytil’s name being the lull in the Minute referred to, although that Gentleman was senior to mi in His Majesty’s Cona-miflioiu

Treasury Minute; respecting Paymaster and Treasury of the Navy.

Friday, 3d March 1797.

A Receipt having been delivered into this office from under the hand of Alexander Trotter, Esquire, the Paymaster of the Navy, for the Sum of £.48,995. 13#. 6d. for the following Services relating to this department; viz.

In full of a memorial for £. 70,000. to pay Bills of

Exchange, &c. - - - * - - 35»000 -

In further part of a memorial for £. 150,000, to pay Provisions and Victualling Stores - - 13,995 *3 6

£48,995 13 6

and other ViChi&lting Services of a more pressing nature than Bills of Exchange, requiring the appropriation of the sum of £. 35,000, before-mentioned:

Write to the Treasurer of the Navy, and request he will be pleased to cause the said sum of £.35,000. to be applied to the payment of Victualling Services in lieu of Bills of Exchange.

The Paymaster of the Navy - having also requeued, that £.8,995. *3*- M. may be taken from the Money which has been granted as above Rated, and applied to the payment of Seamens* Wages, for which it is much wanted, thereby leaving only £.40,000. for this department:

Write to the Treasurer of the Navy, and desire he will pay over the said sum to the Deputy Paymaster, for the Service proposed.

Appendix (P.)

Letter from the Commissioners of Victualling, introducing Three Accounts of Victualling Bills which became due in 1796> 1797> and *798, &c.

. * . , .. 4 Victualling Office, 20th May 1805.

In return to two Precepts from the Select Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, on the Tenth "Report of Naval Enquiry, dated the 10th and 17th i lift ant: j

The Commissioners for Victualling'His Majesty's Navy beg leave to tranlinit herewith, " Three Accounts of Victualling Bills, which 44 became due in the years 1796, 1797, and 1798; t>ut which were *4 not paid on the days they respectively became due, on account of 44 their not being assigned for want of Money; shewing the amount of 44 each Bill; the day on which it was due, the day on which it appears Money was received for its Payment, and the day on which 44 the Alignments for Payment took place/'

Independently of the Bills specified in these Accounts, various other Bills, which became due in the same year, were prevented from being assigned for payment on the days they respectively became due; not from want of money, but from irregularities in the Vouchers to which they related; from eircurostances requiring particular investigation; from indispensable forms of office, and from other causes rendering delay unavoidable.—An Account of these last mentioned Bills is in preparation, but, owing to its magnitude, will require considerable time before it can be completed.

John Marsh. G. P. Towry. C. Cunningham. IV, Bofcavcn.

R. S. Moody* John Harrison•

REPORT from the COMMITTEE to whom live several Petitions which have been presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, praying Relief from the Effects of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, M An Act to regulate the Imports " tion and Exportation of Corn, and the Bounties and Duties payable thereon/* were referred*

The COMMITTEE, to whom the several Petitions which have been presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, praying Relief from the Effects of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to regulate the " Importation and Exportation of Corn, and the Bounties and " Duties payable thereon/* are referred; to examine the Matters thereof; and to report the fame* as they shall appear to them, to the House:

Have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the several Matters and Allegations referred to them, and agreed upon the following Report:—

I. That it appears that the Petitions referred to the consideration of the Committee, complain generally against the effects of the Ad 44 Geo. III. c. 109.

II. That the Petitions presented from various places in England complain—First, Of the advanced Rates at which Importation and Exportation are fixed:—Secondly, Of such part of an Act, made in the 31ft year of His present Majesty, as relates to imposing additional Duties on Foreign Corn warehoused in Great Britain, and taken out for Home Consumption;—and, Thirdly, That, certain Petitioners complain of the Alteration that has taken place by the Act of the 44th of His present Majesty, in the mode of ascertaining the Average Prices which regulate the Importation and Exportation of Grain.

III. That the Petitions from various places in Scotland, in addition to the above-mentioned objections, complain—First, That the rates at which the Exportation and Importation of Foreign Grain is permitted, are fixed by the average prices of the four Maritime Districts of Scotland, and not by the average prices of the sixteen Maritime

Districts of Great Britain, and, that in consequence of such separation of England and Scotland, the ports of Scotland have been (hat to Importation, while the market price of Grain has been much higher in many populous places in the western parts of Scotland than th» importation price; and also, that circumstances may arise, by which the free tTanfmission of Grain from one part of Great Britain to another will be prevented :—Secondly, That the ports for the importation of Grain from the British Colonies in America are only open for three months at a time, which the Petitioners contend is not long enough to obtain a supply from thence;—and, Thirdly, that Inih Grain is withheld from the Scotch market until the price advances nearly to that rate at which Foreign Grain may be imported at the lowed Duties.

Your Committee beg leave to date, That, after due deliberation, they have not thought themselves authorized, under the Order of the House constituting them a Committee, to enter upon any general invelligation of the Corn Laws, or to examine such speculative opinions, however respedable, as may be contained in the Petitions referred to them; but have felt it their duty to confine themselves to evils complained of as actually existing, without extending their enquiries to the general tendency of such provisions and regulations upon the subject as the Legislature, in its wisdom, from time to time, has thought proper to enact.

Under this impression, Your Committee have proceeded to examine Documents, and hear Evidence, in support of the various allegations above enumerated; the Minutes of which Evidence, and Documents, they beg leave to annex in an Appendix to this Report, N0s 1, 2, 3, 4>and 5*

Examination of Joseph Dixon, Esquire, a Corn Factor:— Has been in that situation Ten Years in Partntrship with George Dyson.

HAVE you been resident during that time in London?—Yes.

Have you formed any opinion as to the effects of the Corn Ad of last Session, as to prices in London ?—’Hie immediate consequence of the Ad passing w as an advance in the prices.

Do you conceive any part of that effect was produced by the rumour of such Act, previous to its passing into a Law ?—I do; the price began to advance during the time the Act was in agitation.

When you say price, do you allude to Wheat, or to Grain in general ?—To Wheat only; it had no material effect upon any other Grain.

If the price of Wheat rises considerably, has it not a tendency to raise the prices of the oilier forts of Grain ?—I have reason to think that it has.

State the facts on which you ground your opinion, that Wheat rose in price upon the general rumour of the Act of last Session ?— Wheat vole in consequence of the advance of the limits of the price of Importation and Exportation.

When you speakuf the riling price during the passing of the Act, do you know of no other caules of the riles ?—1 know of no other canfes, except in allusion to the general blight, and which was not known till a few weeks before Harvest.

Do you not know that the blight took place in the month of June ? —I do not.

Do yon not know that in the first week of July it was notorious in London that the Wheat Harvest was likely to be defective ?—I cannot call that to my reeolle&ion.

Do you remember the period at which the Bill then before the House of Commons had first an effect on the prices of Grain in Mark-

Lane ?—All prices of Wheat in Mark-Lane began to advance about the beginning of July.

In advising your Correspondents in the Corn Counties of such advance in price, did you, in your circular letters, ascribe it to the Bill then in the House of Commons ?—I never did myself.

Did you ascribe it to any other given cause?—I do not recollect.

Would not the price have risen although the Ad had not passed? —I do not ascribe the high prices which we have witnessed since Harvest to the effect of the Bill, but to the general failure of the lall year’s crop.

Is not Irish Wheat, under the present course of the trade, on its Importation into this country, denominated Foreign Wheat, and does it not thereby enjoy the advantage of re-exportation above what it could enjoy in Ireland, and also above what is enjoyed by any Wheat of the growth of Great Britain?—It is in all respects considered as Foreign Wheat, and under the fame regulations; and as Wheat may be exported from Ireland to Great Britain at a higher average than to any other country, it may be landed under the Kings Lock, and reexported to Foreign countries at times when no direct Exportation from Ireland to such Foreign countries could take place.

When you say it is in all respects considered as Foreign Wheat, do you mean to confine that expredion to the Regulations of Re-exportation, or to your general view of the subject ?—I mean respecting the prtfvision of export, and also as relates to the Warehouse Duty, upon its being taken from under the King's Lock, and afterwards entered for Horne Consumption.

Do you conceive the object: of the Importers of Irish Wheat, fmee November lad, to have been the British Market, or for Re-exportation? —Some of the earliest shipnients from Ireland were certainly with the view of benefiting by the great advance in the Home Markets, but I have reason to believe the shipments would not have been so extensive if there had not been an expectation of its meeting also a demand for F oreign Countries.

Do you believe the quality of such Wheat to have been such as would have made it faieable in "the British Market?—It would not have found a ready sale in the British Markets, except at the time of considerable scarcity, on account of its inferior quality.

Whether the blight which did so much injury to the Crops of Wheat in the southern and eastern counties of England, extended in any degree to Scotland ?—From the heft information I had from that country, it did not.

Whether very unusual quantities of Wheat and Flour have not arrived in the Port of London, from the Ports of Scotland, Berwick* wpon-Tweed, and other Northern Ports, but particularly from Scotland, fmcc last Harvcfl ?—There have been very constant and considerable iupplies of both during the months of November, December, January, February, and March.

W hether those largo quantities of WTheat and Flour have not been the chief cause of the reduced prices in London since November last ? —As the quantities from that country prove much beyond general expectation, and formed the chief arrival at the London Market during that period, they certainly have contributed very much to the decline.

Whether the transporting such large quantities of Wheat and Flour from Scotland to England Tas not occasioned the prices to be much higher in Scotland than otherwise they would have been?—The extraordinary demand for the South of England occasioned a considerable advance in the Scotch Markets.

Whether you conceive the Act of last Section has had any effect in raising the price of Wheat in the London Market?—On the intention of enacting such regulations, there was an inconsiderable advance in the prices, but I do not conceive that the Ad has at all contributed to the advance that took place last Autumn.

Must not the advance in Price in the London Market, from whatever cause, necessarily draw Grain to the London Market from Scotland, or any place where it was to be had?—Certainly, from every Market where the prices were fuflieiently low, to be an encouragement for fending there.

has there been any considerable Importation of other kinds of Grain chides Wheat, from Scotland into the Port of London?—The quantity of other Grain received from Scotland during the period mention'd, has fallen far short of what has been received at many other time*.

Was it not understood in the Corn Market to be the direct object of the Corn Bill to give to the holder of Grain a security for obtaining a price so much higher than the average of former prices, as amounted to the difference betwixt the former Scale of Prices, and the icale created by the Act of last Session?—It was understood to he the declared object of the Ad, to prevent the prices, in plentiful seasons, from tailing so low as they had done under the provisions of the old Lav.*.

Do you conceive it has had that effect?—The Ad, as yet, has never boon in operation; the prices of Grain since the passing of the

Ad, having, from Other causes, ruled much beyondvvhatlheincreiiej Icale would have produced.

1'hough the Act may have never been in operation us to effcal Importation or Exportation, do you not think that the advance in the Icale of price by which Importation and Exportation isreguEtd, and the new Icale of Bounties of the new Ad of last Selhon, mutt contribute permanently to keep up the price ol Grain higher than it

would have been, if no alteration in such feales had taken place r_

Whether, in your own opinion, and in those with whom you have had an intercourse in the Corn Trade, the Icale ot prices in the hut Corn Ad that governs Exportation and Importation is not too hinh for the benefit of the Public ?— My own opinion, and the opinions of moll others with whom I have communicated, certainly are, that tl« scale of prices is too high.

On what grounds do you think the prices are too high?—As the Importation is governed by an aggregate average price of the Maritime Dillrids of England and Scotland respectively, it may often happen, in years of moderate scarcity, that prices much beyond those mentioned in the scale may exist in populous districts before the general average shall be raised to the rate allowing Importation, am] that the surplus of some districts contributing to keep down the general average, may not materially aid those in want; and, that the reverie of this operation in years of moderate plenty, may give opening to Exportation, and lay the foundation of lulsequent Importation that might not otherwise take place, thereby intioJucing into the country a quantity much greater than had been parted with.

Do you coiilider any material rife m price to have taken place in the Market previous to the knowledge of the blight ?—No material advance had taken place previous to the first rumours of an injury to the crop.

Do you think the period of three months, for which the ports ore now open to American Importation, is lutficiently long?—The period is certainly too short for any material supply, provided it depended upon orders to America not sent out till the Ports are actually open.

What period would he sufficient ?—I think four months.

Are we not as likely to have American Grain as cheap under this system, as if it were the practice for the American Merchants to wait for orders from England?—I think quite as cheap; at the same time it must be considered, Great Britain is not the only market the Americans look to, and consequently it could only be occasionally that the prices in England would affect: the value of Grain in America, and also because it is usual, at particular seasons, for the Americans to ship on adventure, without, at the time, having any particular market in view.

Whether a greater extension than three months to the Import from America would not be injurious to the agriculture of the country ?—I think it would; because a sufficient supply for the wants of the country might be received from the Baltic and other nearer Ports, during the period at present allowed, and that a further extension might give opening to America to pour in during the remaining three months a supply no longer wanted, to the detriment of agriculture; and it would also, in my opinion, be an undue preference to admit any country to enjoy exclusively the advantages of the British markets.

If this extension were limited to the Britishi Colonies in America, could it have any pernicious e fie cl on the agriculture of Great Britain?—I think not, because the supply received from the Biitifli Colonies is seldom of much importance, and the quality not generally suited to the British markets.

Examination of Peter Giles, Esq.

A Corn Factor, connected with the Foreign trade, resident in London, and has been so for 25 years.

Did the agitation of the question regarding a new Com Law last year, materially rail'e the price of Wheat and other Grain ?—It had an effect in July of railing it, both as to Wheat and Oats; I think Wheat advanced in July from 8s, to 10s. per quarter, but not wholly occasioned by the agitation of the Bill.

What other cauies?—The appearance of the crops on the ground not being very favourable.

When did you apprehend that the last crop might be defective ?— The report of the blight and mildew commenced the first week in Augnll.

When did that apprehension affect the price of grain ?— It began the first week in August, and continued to advance till the last week.

Do you attribute that fggond nfe entirely to the apprehension of a defective crop?—Entirely.

Has the new Act checked any Importation, or permitted any Exportation that would not otherwise have taken place ?—None.

Do you consider the Scale of Prices in the new Act higher than necessary to entourage the Farmer to raise a sufficient quantity of Grain for Home consumption ?—I cannot give an answer to that question.

Do you think that this Country could feed itself, if cultivation was more extended and encouraged ?—In good seasons I think we should grow sufficient, and in bad seasons we certainly should want Importations; I speak of Wheat.

Do you think that the surplus of the good years, might be made

equal to the deficiency in the had years ?—It is an extensive question, ^ and should wish to decline giving an answer.

since July last ?—It has chiefly gone to Liverpool.

Can you state what price, in comparison with that of British growth, that quantity which has been disposed Of ill the Home market has brought?—It is a difficult question to answer.

Is Irish Wheat, in the present course of the trade, capable of being re-exported as Foreign Wheat?—It is permitted.

Has there mot been an unusual difference of quality in Wheat, tht produce of the last harvest r—Certainly.

What is the greaieft diffeience in price yon recollect in Wheat, the growth of last harvest, on the fame day ?—The best Whfeat has foki for double the price of the inferior Wheat,

Is Foreign Grain permitted to be warehoused in Great Britain when the Ports are Unit from Importation?—Yes, under the King's Lock.

Is not such Grain, so permitted to be consumed, buuhened with a higher Duty than Grain arriving at that time?—Yes; by a Duty father exceeding 3*. per quarter.

Memorandum:

The Custom House Accounts are made up on Saturday in each week, and on the Four Quarter days. The Accounts include the exact Receipt, in the Port of London, to the day of closing, inclusive; and also the amount of all such Bills of Exchange, remitted from the Out-Ports and Plantations, as fall due on or before the Fourth preceding day; four days being allowed for making out an Account of the Appropriation of them, and for examining the fame in the Comptroller General's Office.
